News.title: Widdecombe police reopen investigation into incident at Farage's home, BBC understands
News.content:
Counter-terrorism police investigating the killing of Ann Widdecombe have reopened an inquiry into an incident at Nigel Farage's south London home, the BBC understands.

It is understood to relate to what the Reform UK leader described as a "lit incendiary device" being pushed through his letterbox in April 2025.

Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London said it was looking into an "attempted burglary" at a property as part of the Widdecombe murder investigation, but did not confirm the home was linked to Farage or why it might be connected to the killing of the former MP.

CTP London has also referred itself to the police watchdog over how the initial investigation into the Farage incident was handled.

Police said at the time that "damage was caused to a door but nothing was stolen".

Both CTP London and the Metropolitan Police were involved in enquiries. No arrests were made and the investigation was closed.

But on Friday, CTP London said a new line of inquiry had been identified that was not "pursued by them at the time".

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had "decided to independently investigate the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member following a referral received earlier [on Friday]".

A statement continued: "The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of enquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025."

CTP London said it would "full engage" with the watchdog's investigation, adding: "The victims and families in both investigations have been updated today, and we continue to support them."

Ann Widdecombe, the 78-year-old former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman, was found dead at her home in Devon last month with serious injuries.

Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was later charged with her murder.

Kerry was initially arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July, before being additionally arrested on 13 July on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

Widdecombe had served as Tory MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

News.title: Victims urged to come forward as police accused of 'litany of failures' over murderer and rapist
News.content:
Police have urged more victims of Simon Levy to come forward, as London's victims' commissioner said a "litany of failures" had allowed him to kill two women and rape a third.

Andrea Simon called for a review on the "failure to monitor him appropriately" when the 40-year-old was known to police as a sexual predator.

British Transport Police said women who recognised Levy as their attacker should report it, while the Met Police said it had investigated whether he had more victims, including further murders.

Meanwhile, the Independent Office of Police Conduct (IOPC) said a police constable is under investigation for gross misconduct, and a detective sergeant is facing a misconduct investigation.

On Friday, Levy was found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third in London while he was being monitored by the Met Police for being a convicted sex offender. He had previously committed a string of sex attacks.

Levy is due to be sentenced on Wednesday.

The Met, British Transport Police (BTP) and Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) have all admitted failures in how Levy was monitored between his first conviction in September 2021 on sexual assault charges and his arrest for murder in September 2025.

On Saturday, Simons told BBC Breakfast a "multi-agency review" was needed, saying: "There was a lack of restrictions that could have been placed on him and a failure to monitor him appropriately - so all of those things, I think, we need answers to now."

Simons said public services "have to get better at recognising patterns of offending" before attackers become "emboldened".

The Met said its detectives had "exhausted numerous lines of enquiry - including working with coroners â to identify whether Levy is responsible for any similar, unsolved incidents, including deaths".

No further victims have been identified so far but the force urged "anyone who believes they may be a victim of his to contact police".

Levy is known to have attacked at least 10 women on public transport in London, seeking out busy carriages to assault passengers.

BTP said more women "may recognise [Levy] and have not yet reported what has happened to them".

News.title: Infantino denies claims Uefa paid off alleged 'lover' when he was general secretary
News.content:
Gianni Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment over the affair by Uefa while he was its general secretary, according to a Daily Telegraph investigation, external.

A spokesman for the now Fifa president was reported to have told the paper Infantino "strongly denies these categorically untrue allegations".

Uefa, for whom Infantino was general secretary from 2009 to 2016, issued a statement confirming "a departure payment was made to the individual in question".

The allegations come as Infantino fights for his future as Fifa president following his aborted plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

BBC Sport has contacted Fifa and Infantino for comment.

The Telegraph reported that Uefa paid a six-figure sum to the woman, who had an alleged relationship with Infantino, who is married, during his time at European football's governing body.

"Fifa president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue. Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory," a Fifa spokesman told the Telegraph.

"No employee at Uefa and Fifa has ever raised a complaint regarding Mr Infantino's behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved."

Uefa confirmed a payment was made to the woman in question and that it covered the fees for her to complete an MBA course at a local business school.

It said all payments were in line with regulations at the time, but those regulations have since been tightened and "reflect those found in a modern, high-profile organisation".

News.title: Fifth heatwave of the year likely next week as temperatures could hit 35C
News.content:
Temperatures on Saturday will begin to climb above average again, reaching the mid- to high 20s Celsius in most of England and Wales.

It will be cooler in Scotland and Northern Ireland at 17 to 21C with more cloud, a bit of rain and a blustery wind.

By Sunday and into next week temperatures will rise even further with many parts of the UK exceeding their heatwave threshold temperature of 25 to 28C, depending on location.

With this hotter weather expected to last well into the week, many locations will have the three consecutive days needed to declare the fifth widespread heatwave of the year.

It has already been a remarkable summer in the United Kingdom with multiple records broken.

July has been the sunniest month on record for the UK, as well as the driest July on record for England and Wales.

There have so far been 33 days this year when temperatures have exceeded 30C in the UK. Next week, it is likely the record of 34 days, set in 1995, will be broken.

For the first time ever, a temperature of 35C has also been recorded somewhere in the UK on the three consecutive months of May, June and July.

It is possible August will join that list by the end of next week as some forecast models suggest 35C in central and south-east England.

News.title: Hunter Biden tells BBC his pardon was 'not good' for US or his father's legacy
News.content:
Hunter Biden has told the BBC he was "the most privileged person there is" after receiving a presidential pardon from his father, former US President Joe Biden, acknowledging that it was not a good choice for America or his father's legacy.

In a wide-ranging interview with BBC Newsnight, Hunter Biden defended the controversial pardon, revealed his father's "painful" cancer has spread, ruled out seeking elected office and spoke about helping others recover from addiction.

Asked about the 2024 pardon, he said he understood the criticism but noted: "What would you have thought of my dad if he did not do that for me."

"It's something that is easily criticised and for good reason," he added.

"It's not fairâ¦ All I know is that I'm grateful that he did it for me," he said, acknowledging the pardon was "not good" for the American people, the constitution - or his father's legacy.

He argued to the BBC that his father ultimately acted out of concern that he would become a target under Donald Trump's incoming administration.

"I was the only one in the world that could have gotten what I got from the only person in the world who could give it, my father."

Hunter Biden also insisted he and his father had never discussed the possibility of a pardon before it was granted.

"There is no way that you can have those kinds of discussions that would not become public," he said.

President Biden granted his son a full and unconditional pardon in December 2024, despite repeatedly saying beforehand that he would not use the powers of the presidency to intervene in his son's legal cases. In announcing the decision, the former president said his son had been "selectively and unfairly prosecuted".

The pardon covered his son's federal gun conviction, a tax case he'd pleaded guilty to and any federal offences committed between 2014 and 2024.

News.title: I went for a full body MOT and the results came as a shock
News.content:
Annabel Mason-Thompson went for a Neko Health scan in September last year, knowing she had a suspicious-looking mark on her back - but it wasn't flagged by the technology.

"I felt a bit let down if I'm honest," the 50-year-old says. "Their AI scanner failed to pick up any of my four cancerous lesions.

"It was only when I went into the doctor's room after the scan and I pointed out my red mark did they take a look at it."

Further examination confirmed the mark was suspicious, so Neko Health contacted Annabel to say she would need treatment and wrote a letter to her private dermatologist to say the "lesion requires evaluation with a view to possible excision".

Her dermatologist found three more cancerous marks which needed urgent treatment.

"Luckily," she says, "they were all slow-growing basal cell carcinomas. I had to have two cut out and two taken off via cryotherapy."

Neko Health says "member safety and clinical excellence are at the heart of everything" it does. The company said its clinical team did identify a "lesion of concern" and it was reviewed by two of its dermatologists before a referral was made for potential treatment.

"We know that no one system is foolproof," Nilsonne says, "which is why we have multiple lenses - it is crucial that the technology and human expertise work together."

His company's latest data shows that of the 4,362 scans carried out on clients who visited Neko Health's Stockholm headquarters last year, 1.2% discovered life-threatening conditions such as melanoma and leukaemia. A further 4% spotted significant health conditions that required further treatment, and 1.2% flagged conditions that could be reversed such as pre-diabetic blood sugar levels.

While the figures are not representative of the population and only account for those who can afford to pay for this kind of preventive healthcare, Nilsonne says this is an indicator of how medicine should look in the future.

But GPs disagree. Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs (RCGP), says they haven't seen "convincing evidence" private broad screening tests "improve health outcomes".

She says the results from these private scans can also place an additional strain on the NHS as clients come back for further tests and potential treatment, even "where the findings prove to be clinically insignificant".

News.title: He's been frozen on Everest for 30 years, now 'Green Boots' may finally be coming home
News.content:
For 30 years, a dead body known as "Green Boots" has been lying in the snow, nestled under an overhanging rock, not far from Mount Everest's summit.

The lime mountaineering boots worn by an Indian climber who died in 1996 have been a grim trail marker for many climbers on their way up the world's highest peak ever since.

Now India is looking for a specialist high-altitude recovery team to undertake a complex and risky mission to retrieve what they say is Dorje Morup's body â arguably the most famous of the hundreds whose bodies have been left frozen on the mountain.

Warning: This story contains a picture of a dead body.

They hope they are on the cusp of returning his remains to friends and family who never gave up hope he'd come home.

"On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there," Morup's wife told the BBC.

"When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'"

News.title: Digital cameras and wired earphones are back and 'a bit more real'
News.content:
Luckily I'm out with my photography-loving best friend, who helps adjust the settings on the camera and gets snapping while I'm otherwise engaged on the dancefloor.

The mere sight of us pulling out the camera and squinting through its tiny viewfinder draws attention â "I've not seen one of these in years", a man remarks.

He's right â digital cameras had their heyday in the late 1990s and early 2000s, just before smartphones took off.

There are currently 42 million active film camera users globally, more than a third of these aged 18â30 and largely influenced by social media trends, according to a market research report, external last year.

So why, when we're surrounded by more advanced tech here in 2026, are they seemingly making a resurgence?

For Lily Redman, a 26-year-old content creator from South Wales, digital cameras "capture a quality that my phone just can't replicate".

She's been taking one on nights out and to concerts and feels the flash on her phone "is grainy and too high definition" compared to the "more smooth" finished product on a digital camera.

"I think people are looking for a bit of grit or something that feels a bit more real," she says.

That may also explain why low exposure photos taken on iPhones and Androids â where people dodge ready-made filters to artificially crank down the exposure setting and produce a darker image â are also popular on socials right now.

With digital cameras offering an element of surprise when you plug in the memory card reader to your computer at home, digital cameras capture a moment in time.

"If I look back at photos my mum took when I was two, they look so old but when I look at photos I took five years ago, they look like they were taken yesterday," says Redman.

"Phone photos have warped our perception of time."

News.title: Woman attacked by bed bugs during Travelodge stay
News.content:
Thirteen days after Hannah Stephenson stayed a night in a Travelodge hotel, she is still itching with red lumps over her body - a nightmare she would not wish on her "worst enemy".

The 31-year-old from Bassingbourn had been out with friends in Cambridge and decided to book a one-night stay at the hotel on Newmarket Road on 26 July to save money instead of getting a taxi home.

The next morning, she woke up to a "horrible realisation", feeling itchy with red lumps over her body and blood spots smeared on the bedding â the tell-tale signs of bed bugs, she said.

A Travelodge spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for Ms Stephenson's experience and how distressing an incident like this can be."

Stephenson said a lovely evening with friends had turned into a horrible morning.

"It was just a lovely wholesome time of Cambridge sightseeing and pubs, and now it is tarnished by these bedbug bites," she said.

"It wasn't until I saw the blood and the bugs that I realised what had happened."

News.title: Bristol Airport disruption a 'shambles' as flights restart
News.content:
Widespread disruption continues at Bristol Airport after a runway defect saw all flights suspended.

Hundreds of passengers were stranded after the airport's runway was closed from 18:00 BST on Friday until 08:00 on Saturday. While the runway has since reopened, the airport's website says the majority of flights are delayed or cancelled.

A spokesperson for the airport apologised for any inconvenience caused and advised passengers to check the status of their flight with their airline.

Dave Blackwell, travelling home from the Greek island of Rhodes, said it had been "a shambles" since his flight back to Bristol was diverted to Newcastle.

"We were in Rhodes Airport for three hours with no information. Now we have all been told our flight is going to Newcastle and then a five or six-hour bus ride - why Newcastle? How appalling," he said.

News.title: Strictly dancers Ola and James Jordan separate after 23 years of marriage
News.content:
Former Strictly Come Dancing stars James and Ola Jordan have confirmed they have separated after more than 20 years of marriage.

The former professional dancers were regulars on the show for several series after first featuring in 2006.

The couple's manager Vickie White confirmed the split, which was first reported by the Sun newspaper, external.

She said in a statement: "It is with great sadness that I can confirm that James and Ola began a trial separation some time ago.

"Their shared priority remains co-parenting their daughter, Ella, and they are committed to putting her wellbeing first.

"They would greatly appreciate your understanding as they navigate this difficult time."

Ola Jordan won the Open Polish Championship in 1999 when she was 17 years old and became James' dance partner shortly afterwards in March 2000.

She moved to England a month later and the pair got married in October 2003.

James appeared on Strictly from 2006 to 2013 while Ola appeared on the show until 2015.

Ola's celebrity partners included wildlife presenter Steve Backshall and Welsh sprinter Iwan Thomas, while James danced with former international gymnast and broadcaster Gabby Logan, as well as The One Show presenter Alex Jones.

News.title: Man guilty of fatal shooting of teen outside club
News.content:
A man has been found guilty of fatally shooting an 18-year-old outside a Wembley nightclub.

Tyrece Balcha was found with gunshot wounds outside the Crystal Club in Atlantic Crescent at about 05:30 GMT on 21 September 2025. He was taken to hospital, where he died four days later.

A jury at the Old Bailey found Ashley Wallace, 40, of Shenley Road, Southwark, guilty of murder and possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life.

At the same trial, two men were found not guilty of murder. A woman was cleared of possession of a firearm, possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life, and perverting the course of justice. The jury did not reach a verdict on a fourth man.

CCTV footage showed that Balcha had been involved in an altercation inside the club before being followed outside and shot.

Wallace fled the scene in a vehicle and was arrested on 25 September after police traced the car to south-east London.

A revolver carrying Wallace's DNA was found inside the vehicle, and investigators established that the bullet recovered from the murder scene had been fired from the gun.

News.title: Siân Phillips to step back from acting aged 93 after memory issues
News.content:
One of Wales' most celebrated actresses, Dame SiÃ¢n Phillips, is stepping back from full-scale stage acting after experiencing memory issues during rehearsals.

The 93-year-old made the decision after struggling to remember her lines while preparing for a recent production, according to The Times.

However, Phillips said she would continue performing in smaller projects, including a production with Michael Sheen's Welsh National Theatre next year.

Her career has spanned more than 80 years across stage, television and film.

Phillips told The Times she decided to stop taking on major stage productions after struggling to remember her lines during rehearsals for Atonement at Chichester Festival Theatre earlier this year.

According to the newspaper, she said she would continue performing in her show It's All Greek and is also due to appear in Samuel Beckett's Rockaby for Michael Sheen's Welsh National Theatre next year.

Born in Betws, near Ammanford, Carmarthenshire, in 1933, Phillips grew up speaking Welsh before learning English by listening to the radio.

She began performing as a child, appearing on Welsh-language radio from the age of 11, before studying at the University of Wales and later winning a scholarship to the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art.

She performed in radio productions such as The Archers and an adaptation of John le Carre's Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy, opposite Sir Alec Guinness.

Before her acting career took off, she worked for BBC Wales as a bilingual announcer and newsreader.

Phillips went on to become one of Britain's most acclaimed actresses, appearing in productions including Doctor Who, Calendar Girls, Dune, and I, Claudius.

She won a Bafta for her portrayal of Livia in the BBC's I, Claudius and received a Tony Award nomination for playing the title role in Marlene.

She was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in 2000 for services to drama, and then a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire (DBE) in 2016.

News.title: Passengers 'stranded' at locked train station
News.content:
Translink has apologised after rail passengers were left stranded on a platform when a late-night train arrived into a station that was already shut for the night.

A group of about 30 customers were stuck on the platform at Newry Train Station for more than 45 minutes in the early hours of Saturday.

One of the passengers, Anne Greer, told BBC News NI it raised safety questions for the public transport company as the customers had no safe way to exit the station.

Translink said the firm was "looking into the incident" but added its train crew "remained with the passengers to ensure their safety while the issue was resolved".

The train was among a number of extra late-night services which are running to and from Belfast during the Fleadh Cheoil na hÃireann (Music Festival of Ireland).

It was scheduled to leave Belfast at 23:59 BST on Friday and it arrived in Newry at about 01:20 BST on Saturday.

"To our surprise the entire station was closed, so we couldn't exit," Greer said.

"So we're all trapped on the platforms for over 40 minutes."

She said the train crew "helped as much as they could, but there was nothing they could do".

"They were completely gobsmacked as to why they've arrived into a completely closed and locked train station."

Greer said she and other passengers tried to contact Translink but they could only find phone numbers for call centres which had also already closed for the day.

News.title: Man fundraises for stranger's dream trip
News.content:
A man has run almost 200 miles (321km) to pay for a stranger who has incurable cancer to go on a dream trip.

Giles Richards, from Yeovil in Somerset, completed 192 miles (310km) for Kayleigh Ewan to travel to Australia.

Earlier this year, the 36-year-old was diagnosed with metastatic cancer, which spread to her spine and liver. Doctors have told her the disease is incurable. Richards heard about Ewan through his partner and decided he wanted to help.

Ewan said she was really grateful to Richards, adding: "There's lots of places on my bucket list, but Australia is something I'd need time and money to plan and time is something I might not have."

News.title: Man charged after four killed in lamp-post crash
News.content:
A man has been charged in connection with a crash that killed four people.

James Diggle, 27, of Alundale Road in West Derby, Liverpool, faces four counts of aiding and abetting causing death by dangerous driving.

The charge follows the deaths of four men, Jack Diggle, 23, Benjamin Dooley, 23, Andrew Roberts, 24, and Craig Shackleton-Brady, 26, who were killed when the black Cupra they were travelling in hit a lamp-post in Huyton, on Merseyside, on 24 July.

Merseyside Police said Diggle would be appearing at Liverpool Magistrates' Court later.

News.title: Alarming charts that reveal a planet in peril – as experts warn record-breaking heatwaves are just the start
News.content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

Britain’s record-breaking summer of heatwaves and life-threatening extreme temperatures could prove to be the coolest of our lifetime unless we double down on efforts to tackle the climate crisis, experts have warned.

Back-to-back hot spells, which saw the mercury peak at 37.7C (99.9F) in June, have so far led to nearly 3,000 deaths, half of England and the whole of Wales are in drought and a failure to heed decades of warnings to build climate resilience into our supply chains has left the UK facing food shortages.

The news overseas is even more alarming, with unprecedented wildfires burning thousands of square kilometres of land around holiday resorts in Spain and France, claiming 16 lives, while record-low water levels threaten Europe’s industrial heartlands on the Rhine and exposing lost Nazi warships on the Danube.

open image in gallery People walk on a path between the sun scorched grass, turned yellow-brown by a lack of rain, in Greenwich Park ( AFP/Getty )

And the picture is only set to intensify in the coming months as a record-breaking El Nino – a periodic warming of the Pacific Ocean – wreaks havoc with global weather systems, resulting in extreme rainfall in some parts of the world and devastating drought expected in others.

Experts warn that recent temperatures are no anomaly with worse to come, unless we ramp up efforts to phase out fossil fuels and invest more heavily in renewable energy sources.

“Unfortunately, this will be the least extreme climate we will experience in our lifetimes, certainly until we reach net zero emissions,” warned Hayley Fowler, professor of climate change impacts at Newcastle University. “We need to pressure politicians to do more and faster: to both rapidly reduce emissions and rapidly adapt our infrastructure to cope with more extreme weather.”

Prof Fowler’s comments come as recent analysis from Carbon Brief suggests that the combination of climate change and the super El Niño mean that 2026 is set to be the warmest or second warmest year on record – continuing a pattern of global temperatures increasing year after year.

“What we're seeing now is exactly what climate scientists have been expecting for decades,” adds Dr Friederike Otto from Imperial College London. “But the future is not predetermined: every tonne of carbon dioxide we avoid emitting reduces future warming and limits the severity of impacts.”

Gareth Redmond-King, international lead at think tank the Energy and Climate and Intelligence, echoed the concerns, saying: “This extremely hot and dangerous summer risks being one of the coolest for the rest of our lives if we keep burning coal, oil, and gas and destroying nature.

“But we should by no means feel that hope is lost, because we have a scientific pathway forward in the form of net zero that we need to be pursuing as urgently as possible if we want to bring our climate back into balance.”

Zack Polanski, leader of the Green Party, criticised the government for not doing enough to address current climate, and urged new PM Andy Burnham to do more.

"This is the biggest threat to our country since the Second World War but Andy Burnham is silent on it,” he said. “Worse than that, he's considering restarting drilling in the North Sea – literally pouring fuel on the fire. Where is the action to meet the scale of the emergency?”

Fleur Anderson, Labour MP for Putney and chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on climate change, added: “We need to remember this period when the hot weather goes away. It is important now to join up government thinking between different departments to address all the different areas of our lives that are affected by climate change.”

Her comments come as the latest Met Office data shows that rainfall in July was the lowest it has ever been in records stretching back more than 250 years.

Ms Anderson also criticised the weakening climate consensus among mainstream political parties – with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch pledging to repeal the UK’s Climate Change Act – saying it was “extraordinary in the middle of these heatwaves for the parties to be differing on this”. She added: “I am so disappointed by the fact that the climate deniers seem to be winning the argument on the right in the face of not only scientific evidence, but also what is actually happening to our country.”

‘A new normal’ – that could get even worse

The Met Office has warned that the climate extremes of this summer are becoming “the new normal” for the UK – and the scientific evidence shows that things could get much worse unless the world global emissions continue to increase annually.

A report published by 160 scientists last year warned that even levels of global warming below 2C above the pre-industrial average could see climate systems that humans depend on for their survival – including the Amazon Rainforest, the Arctic permafrost, and the critical Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) – collapse. Scientists currently believe the world is at around 1.3C of warming.

open image in gallery A combine harvester crosses parched fields in Suffolk, England ( AFP/Getty )

In the UK, a report on climate-preparedness published this summer by the climate APPG warned that the country is woefully underprepared for coming climate impacts. Some 6.3 million homes and businesses are at risk of flooding, and the cost of annual coastal flood damage is projected to increase two to three times by the 2080s, the report found.

By 2050, 92 per cent of existing homes could be suffering from overheating, while climate change and ecosystem collapse could mean the UK will struggle to maintain its food supply as early as 2030. Farmers have already warned that drought and heatwaves are likely to result in shortages and they may have to stop growing some vegetables.

Some 46 per cent of roads and 54 per cent of railways will also be at risk of flooding by 2050, the report finds, while direct impact costs from heatwaves over the next 50 years is set to be £64bn.

The cost of heatwaves has been particularly apparent in the wake of record-breaking fires in France and Spain this year. The cost of these fires as well as those in other parts of Europe is currently estimated at more than €3bn (£2.6bn).

open image in gallery Burnt properties in the wake of record-breaking French wildfires ( AFP/Getty )

Members of the APPG are calling on the government to move responsibility for climate resilience from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) directly to the Cabinet Office. “We have always planned historically for the cold in this country, but now we need to be worrying about the summer and overheating. We have to think differently about how we act to overcome these problems,” said Ms Anderson.

Speaking of wildfires that have also hit the UK this year, minister for climate transition Katie White said: “British firefighters are telling us they’ve never seen anything like this. With wildfires across Britain and Europe, we know we're not waiting for climate change, we're living through it.

“We must build our resilience, but critically, also cut the dirty emissions driving this.”

50 million people facing acute hunger

Over the next year, the world is set to experience a climate phenomenon known as a El Niño, which is when unusually warm sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean lead to droughts or increased rainfall in different parts of the world.

This year’s “super” El Niño is set to be more severe due to a particularly high forecast temperature rise, as well as the climate crisis further exacerbating weather patterns. Analysis of El Niño forecasts from Carbon Brief suggests that the El Niño is set to be by far the strongest on record.

In the UK, it risks heightening food shortages, as millions of small-scale farmers around the world that supply the UK with tropical fruits, cocoa, coffee and tea will struggle due to the disrupted weather patterns.

The consequences overseas are set to be catastrophic, with warnings up to 50 million people could be pushed into acute hunger before the end of next year, the World Food Programme warned this week. It comes on top of geopolitical shocks, such as the war in Iran and aid cuts from wealthy countries, which are already piling immense pressure on the poorest parts of the world.

The past ten years has already seen the number of people facing a food crisis double, according to the United Nations, with data also showing that foreign aid has also fallen to a 10-year low.

As warnings about the climate crisis intensify, the impact of how Britons are feeling about the impacts are becoming clearer. A survey published by the think tank IPPR this year found that 81 per cent felt unprepared for the worst impacts of the climate crisis.

But experts stress that there remains every hope that the worst impacts can still be avoided, and the world’s climate can be stabilised, if we continue – as the vast majority of the world outside of the US is doing – to roll out renewables and pursue a goal of net zero emissions.

“There is still time for us to avoid the worst impacts of climate change, and every fraction of a degree of avoided warming matters,” said Professor Elizabeth Robinson, head of the Grantham Climate Institute at the London School of Economics. “But this requires governments not just to stick to their commitments to reducing emissions, but to close the gap between commitments and policies that they are delivering.”

Dr Otto added: “This is a problem that is solvable. We know how to replace fossil fuels with renewables, we know how to lower demand, we know how to redesign cities and landscapes to be much better adapted to increasing floods, extreme heat and drought.

“Climate change is one of the defining challenges of our time, but it is also one where clear, informed decisions and sustained action can shape a much better future for all.”

The UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has been approached for comment.

Andy Burnham made a vow upon entering No 10 that he would “rewire” Britain, with a core aspect of his vision to deliver “the biggest council housebuilding drive since the postwar period”.

The prime minister admitted the country is in the grip of a severe housing crisis, with millions struggling to meet unaffordable rents and a social housing backlog that now extends to more than 1.3million households.

However, the task for Mr Burnham is substantial. The PM’s predecessor Sir Keir Starmer pledged to build 1.5 million houses before the next election, a target that newly reinstated housing secretary Angela Rayner admitted was a “really difficult challenge”.

The government’s target to reach the figure through 300,000 new homes a year is already off pace. Only around 840,000 homes, around half the total target, are expected to be under construction by mid-2029, according to property agent Savills.

The Independent looks at the scale of the challenge ahead and what might need to change to accomplish his goals.

Burnham’s Brexit problem

open image in gallery Andy Burnham has promised a housing revolution, but can he deliver? ( AFP/Getty )

Many point to Britain’s decision to leave the European Union as a key factor in the decline in housebuilding. Brexit is estimated to have reduced the UK construction workforce by more than 200,000 people, a report by training group PfP Thrive found.

At the same time, construction materials in the UK have increased by 60 per cent, according to analysis by the UK Trade and Business Commission, compared to 35 per cent in the EU.

Housebuilding faltering, partially as a fault of Brexit, means that affordable housing is not being delivered. Sir Keir’s government pledged £39bn for the Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP), to deliver around 300,000 properties within the 1.5 million target.

And council housing is another matter altogether. This is technically property owned by local authorities and usually offers a much cheaper “social rent” for residents – around 50 per cent of market rates, compared to around 80 per cent for “affordable” homes.

Rooftop Housing Group’s chief executive Boris Worrall told Inside Housing: “It has played out exactly as feared. Brexit has been a key factor in accelerating inequality and deepening the structural challenges the UK faces – including a shortage of affordable housing and a rising and unsustainable welfare bill [because of falling GDP]… We have built fewer homes than we would have done [had we remained in the EU]. It is that simple.”

Construction downturn

One reason Labour has fallen behind on its housebuilding targets has been due to increased costs in the housebuilding sector, says Steve Turner, executive director of the Home Builders Federation.

He told The Independent: “We did a report recently that showed that it’s now £76,000 on average more expensive to build a house now than it was five years ago, and that’s because material costs have gone up.”

Taxes and policy costs such as building safety levies, landfill taxes and green initiatives are also eating into private-sector margins, he explained.

“These are probably the right thing to do,” Mr Turner adds, “but because you’ve layered them on over recent years, including increased affordable housing, it’s got to the point now where not everything can be funded through development and sites are no longer viable.”

Continued concerns about the impacts of US president Donald Trump’s war in Iran and the political uncertainties festering over the UK for months meant that output from the construction industry declined at the fastest rate since the height of the Covid-19 pandemic.

The S&P Global UK construction PMI showed a reading of 38.2 in May, down from 39.7 in April and indicating a steep drop in overall business activity.

Any reading above the 50 threshold indicates that activity in the industry is increasing, while anything below means that it is contracting.

Can more council housing be built?

During the postwar peak in the 1970s, English local authorities built an average of 103,000 homes every year. In the five years leading up to 2025, they managed just 2,000 completions annually.

This is clearly a low point to start from. But there is a way to increase the amount of social housing and still deliver the target of 30,000 affordable homes a year, a new report from the Resolution Foundation has found.

open image in gallery ( Centre for Policy Studies/Onward )

The crucial measure is to ringfence the £39bn SAHP exclusively for social rent, dropping annual completions by 5,000 to 25,000, the think tank says.

Combined with tweaking developer rules and allowing housing associations to access cheap loans, this could be boosted to just over 30,000 affordable homes, 25,000 of which would be for social rent.

But this is still a “far cry” from the promise made by Mr Burnham, author Hannah Aldridge, senior research and policy analyst at the think tank, writes.

“And with the best will in the world, new homes still take years to build,” Ms Aldridge adds, noting that delivering at scale would require far more funding from the government.

To hit 300,000 homes for social rent, the government would need to boost its spending to £47bn by 2036, the report found.

What do local authorities need to make Burnham’s vision happen?

While town halls have welcomed Mr Burnham’s focus on social rent, council leaders warn that the right message cannot overcome longstanding financial barriers.

Councils across England are grappling with historic housing debt, which has risen from £29bn in 2012 to £31bn. This was meant to be paid off beginning in 2012, but has instead risen as Right to Buy proliferated under the Conservative government, meaning less revenue for councils.

Rent freezes and caps during the pandemic – which protected tenants – meant that councils were forced to lose income from their homes, adding more to this debt.

Many council leaders are calling for the historic housing debt burden to be restructured, so that it is more realistic for councils to build new homes.

open image in gallery Housing secretary Angela Rayner has said delivering Labour’s target of 1.5 million homes is a ‘really difficult challenge’ ( AFP/Getty )

Several have also advised that the playing field should be levelled for councils and housing associations.

Housing associations will soon be able to access £2.5bn of loans at 0.1 per cent, while local authorities are stuck paying Public Works Loan Board rates which fluctuate between 4 and 5 per cent.

James McAsh, the Green Party leader of Southwark Council, said: “We are straightforwardly paying more to borrow than a housing association building the exact same homes. And I can see no justification for why that should be the case.”

His authority has built 689 council houses in 2024-25, making it the top builder of the past few years. But Mr McAsh warns that the work may have to slow down without more support from the government.

Mr McAsh said: “We’re already trying to build as many council houses as we can; we don’t need Andy Burnham to tell us to do that. What we need from Andy Burnham is funding to allow us to do it.”

The new prime minister’s pledge represents a clear political shift toward tackling Britain’s housing crisis through genuinely affordable homes, which policy experts and council leaders have welcomed.

But delivering a postwar scale building revolution may remain out of reach without serious funding commitments.

Many will be hoping that the new Labour government’s first Budget in October may deliver the answers they are looking for.

Jorge Messi, the father of Lionel Messi, has died at the age of 68 at a medical clinic in the Argentine city of Rosario after a long illness, the Argentine footballer's family has confirmed.

Jorge spent his final months alternating between a medical centre in Rosario and his home, accompanied by his ⁠wife Celia and his ​children ⁠Rodrigo, Matias and Maria Sol, the family said.

Lionel Messi spent time with his father after the World Cup before rejoining his club, Inter Miami, for whom he returned to action a week ago.

Jorge closely accompanied his son Lionel throughout his career, beginning with his early ‌years at Barcelona. He acted as ‌a crucial pillar of support and, for several years, served as his representative.

"I always needed my dad's approval, ever since I was a kid. After every match, I'd ask him what he thought of how I played," the Argentina captain said previously.

During the World Cup, Messi experienced mixed emotions after scoring a hat trick in the opening ‌match against Algeria, breaking down in tears ​while celebrating his first goal.

Later, at a press conference, Lionel explained that his tears were due to "something unrelated to football" after going through "a few difficult, complicated days."

Days later, the family ‌issued a statement ​regarding Jorge's "health situation", informing ‌the public that he was ​undergoing medical treatment.

Newell’s Old Boys, Messi’s first side, posted a tribute to a fan of the Buenos Aires club.

“Club Atletico Newell's Old Boys bids farewell with deep sorrow and grief to Jorge Messi, who passed away at the age of 68 in the city of Rosario,” it said in a statement.

“Recognised leproso fan, businessman, and father of the Argentine national team captain, Lionel Andrés Messi.

“Jorge was the pillar and the person who supported with vision, rigour, and affection the career of the greatest player of all time alongside his wife, Celia Cuccittini.

“His constant companionship and behind-the-scenes leadership were essential in backing every step of Lionel, from his beginnings at Malvinas to the pinnacle of world football glory. Thank you for teaching him to love these colours.”

Reuters

President Donald Trump is claiming another election was “rigged” against a Republican candidate, this time pointing to former Rep. Mike Rogers’ narrow loss in the 2024 Michigan Senate race.

Trump made the claim during a new interview with Jake Sherman of Punchbowl News while discussing the Republican Party’s prospects heading into the 2026 midterm elections.

When Sherman said that Rogers lost his 2024 Senate bid while Trump was also on the ballot in Michigan, Trump said, “But I happen to think he won.”

“Ok, well–” Sherman interjected.

“No, no. I think it was a rigged deal,” Trump interrupted. “I think they rigged him out of it.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump claimed in an interview Friday that the Michigan Senate race was ‘rigged’ against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-MI) ( Punchbowl News/YouTube )

“But he’s a very good candidate,” Trump said in the interviewed published late Friday. “I think he should do well if we believe in polls. I actually sort of believe in polls.”

The Independent has contacted Rogers’ representative for comment.

Rogers, a former Michigan congressman, narrowly lost the 2024 Senate race to Democrat Elissa Slotkin. Slotkin received about 2.71 million votes, compared with nearly 2.69 million for Rogers, giving her a victory margin of less than 20,000 votes. The results were certified, and a subsequent standard audit did not uncover evidence that the election had been stolen.

Trump’s claim comes despite his own victory in Michigan in 2024, where he defeated then-Vice President Kamala Harris by about 1.4 percentage points while Rogers lost to Slotkin by about 0.3 points. Trump also made a similar claim in January, saying the Senate race had been rigged against Rogers.

“I’ll be honest with you, Mike. They rigged the election on you. Mine was too big to rig. You won, I’m telling you, you won, but you’re going to do great this time,”

Rogers is getting another chance in 2026. He won the Republican nomination this week and will face Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in November for Michigan's open Senate seat. The contest is expected to be closely watched as Republicans and Democrats battle for control of the Senate.

open image in gallery Rogers will face Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in November for Michigan’s open Senate seat ( AFP/Getty )

During Friday’s interview, Trump also discussed El-Sayed, referring to the Democrat by what the president claimed was his real name.

“It’s ‘Abdul,’ but I call him ‘Abdullah,'” Trump said. “The actual name is ‘Abdullah,’ and then it’s much longer than that. But if you believe in the polls, [Rogers] does better against Abdullah than he did against the young congresswoman [Haley Stevens].”

El-Sayed’s full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed. He has previously accused Rogers and other political opponents of using his full name as a racist dog whistle.

“They think they want to use my whole name against me,” El-Sayed told supporters Wednesday, the day after he won the primary. “Mike, listen, man, if you can’t say the name, it’s Abdulrahman, keep the name out of your d**n mouth. I’ll be happy to give you lessons.”

News.title: Hunter Biden grateful not to be in prison during Trump presidency but admits pardon was wrong
News.content:
Hunter Biden has acknowledged that the presidential pardon he received from his father was damaging to both the United States and Joe Biden’s reputation.

Mr Biden was convicted on three federal gun charges over a 2018 firearm purchase and later pleaded guilty to nine federal tax offences, before being granted clemency by President Biden in 2024.

His gun conviction marked the first time a child of a sitting US president was found guilty of a crime, and at sentencing he faced up to 25 years in prison and fines of up to $750,000.

However, Mr Biden said that if he were in prison now Donald Trump would be able to exert an “unjust” amount of pressure on his father and their family.

News.title: Nigel Farage ‘horrified’ Ann Widdecombe murder detectives probing firebombing on his home
News.content:
The Way Back. Nigel Farage is “horrified” that counter-terror police probing the alleged murder of Ann Widdecombe have reopened a year-old investigation into a “firebomb” attack at his house.

Officers said the incident, which The Telegraph described as a “lit incendiary device” being posted through the Reform UK leader’s letterbox, happened at an address in Greater London and was reported in April 2025.

The Metropolitan Police and Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London said they investigated an “attempted burglary”, but no arrests were made at the time and the case was closed pending any new lines of inquiry.

Mr Farage, who was not home at the time of the attack and found the damage when he returned home, earlier described the alleged attack as an “outright arson attempt”.

“Luckily it had burned itself out on the porch,” he told The Telegraph in April this year.

Reopening their probe, CTP London said they had identified a line of inquiry “which may have been relevant” but was “not identified and pursued by them at the time”.

The police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), is now investigating the “conduct” of a CTP London staff member, following an allegation that the employee “failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry” related to the attempted burglary.

The Independent understands that Mr Farage is “horrified” that the attack on his home in 2025 is being reinvestigated by detectives investigating Ms Widdecombe’s murder.

A source said: “There has been a very serious policing error which is why counter terror have referred themselves to IOPC, which is unprecedented.”

Richard Tice, deputy leader of Reform, said police forces have not been taking threats against his party’s figures seriously.

Mr Tice told The Telegraph: “Only recently have the authorities woken up to the abuse and intimidation I and other Reform MPs have had, despite plenty of real examples that we have provided.

“I was perhaps very lucky with one particular incident I faced last year. For too long, the threats we have faced have not been taken seriously.

“The fact that the police have referred themselves to the IOPC speaks for itself. They recognise that they’ve messed up.”

According to The Telegraph, Mr Tice pressed his panic button at his house last Christmas after by an aggressive man outside parliament. Officers then arrested the person,

Reform UK spokesperson and former Tory minister Ms Widdecombe, 78, died on 8 July after she was hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, a court heard.

Counter-terror police investigating the death of former MP Ann Widdecombe have reopened a year-old probe into an alleged firebomb attack at Nigel Farage’s home ( PA )

Joshua Kerry, 28, was charged with her murder on 20 July. He has not yet entered a plea and has been remanded in custody until his next court appearance.

Reform UK MPs were given round-the-clock security protection, paid for by the party, after Ms Widdecombe’s death over fears of similar attacks.

Mr Farage has previously raised concerns about MPs’ security, including his own, and said after her death: “And I do fear that for anybody in public life, or especially the political space, things have become even more dangerous to them.”

Confirming the reopened probe following the attack on Mr Farage’s home, senior national co-ordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, Vicki Evans, said: “As part of the ongoing investigation led by Counter Terrorism Policing South East into the murder of Ann Widdecombe, officers have reopened an investigation into an incident reported to police last year.

She added: “Given the nature of this matter and the significant public interest in the investigation into Ann Widdecombe’s death, it was of critical importance for us to provide this update.”

CTP London said it made a “mandatory conduct referral” to the police watchdog on Friday.

An IOPC spokesperson said on Friday: “We can confirm that the IOPC has decided to independently investigate the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member following a referral received earlier today.

“The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of enquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025.

“Counter Terrorism Policing London has been notified of our decision, and no further information is available at this early stage.”

Dame Mary Berry has explained how she is being pragmatic about the future when it comes to designing her garden.

The former Great British Bake Off host, who turned 91 in March, is a keen gardener, and earlier this year published My Gardening Life, an account of her lifelong love of horticulture.

Speaking on the Grow, Cook, Eat, Arrange podcast, the cooking show star revealed that she has to take her advanced years into account when planning how best to use and enjoy the grounds of her riverside home in Henley-upon-Thames.

Berry told the hosts that she and her husband Paul, 93, chose to buy yew trees that were already “fairly big” rather than waiting for them to grow, as they might not be around to see them.

“Obviously you should buy evergreens like a yew, I suppose, about two foot high and wait,” she said.

“Well I’ll be in heaven then so we had to buy them fairly big,” she continued. I suppose they were about four foot because we needed them to get to the top of the tennis court netting.”

open image in gallery Berry suggested that she now has to take time into account when she plans her garden ( Getty Images )

She also revealed that she and Paul wanted to install the tall trees “at the front of the house” for privacy reasons, “because people walking along outside could peer in and now, in six years, it’s well about six foot, which is a joy”.

The baking expert and her husband moved to Henley in 2019, downsizing to a Grade II listed property with four bedrooms, which is reportedly worth £2.6 million.

open image in gallery Berry and her husband Paul have lived in Henley since 2019 ( Getty Images )

The couple previously lived at a six-bedroom residence in Penn, Buckinghamshire, where they were based for three decades. The property featured in Berry’s solo cooking show Mary Berry Cooks, with the kitchen Aga getting plenty of screen time.

Speaking of their decision to move to Henley, Berry previously explained: “We didn’t want to move too far from our friends, and Henley is only a 35 minute drive.”

“The town is beautiful, It has the river, and there are lots of interesting walks to do. As the years go, we will be able to walk into the town, and it will be nice to not have to get the car out.”

The U.S. Senate has confirmed Todd Blanche as Attorney General in an early-morning vote.

It cements the authority of Donald Trump’s former personal attorney over a Justice Department that the president has sought to bend to his will.

In a narrow 50-49 vote, the Republican-led Senate approved Blanche, making him the second Attorney General confirmed since Trump returned to the White House in 2025.

Trump has previously stated his desire to use the law enforcement agency to investigate his political enemies.

While Blanche has already been leading the department in an acting capacity, his confirmation could free him to pursue the Trump administration’s agenda even more aggressively.

Blanche said on social media that he was “deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me.”

He added that he was “grateful” to senators for working late to confirm him.

open image in gallery Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche was confirmed by the Senate by a one-vote margin ( AP )

The vote followed a tumultuous confirmation fight that exposed deep concerns — from some Republicans as well as Democrats — about installing Trump’s close ally atop a Justice Department that historically prided itself on its independence from the White House.

In the end, Blanche was confirmed by the narrowest of margins, opposed by two Republicans — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska — and by every Democrat.

The path to confirmation for Blanche was unusually rocky, due in large part to Republican concerns about a controversial settlement of Trump’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service.

An under-pressure Blanche publicly promised in writing that the department would abandon Trump’s proposed $1.8 billion compensation fund for the president’s allies, including those who attacked the Capitol on January 6, 2021, and rein in another piece of the settlement designed to shield Trump and his family from IRS tax audits.

His appeals were enough to win over Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, the decisive vote who threw his support behind Blanche Friday morning. Cassidy said no other nominee may be able to run the department better under Trump and suggested Blanche’s role as Trump’s former criminal defense lawyer can make him more effective at pushing back on the president’s demands.

“This is not a referendum on President Trump. It is a decision regarding Mr. Blanche in very specific circumstances,” said Cassidy, who lost his primary earlier this year to a Trump-backed challenger.

Sen. Dick Durbin of Illinois, the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee, said that confirming Blanche would be a “serious mistake.” He begged his colleagues not to be on the “wrong side” of history.

“If there is ever a moment in history when we need an Attorney General above reproach, who is clearly dedicated to ending corruption, even at the highest level of our government, it’s right now,” Durbin said.

The vote capped off a bruising confirmation fight, with Blanche’s loyalty to Trump at the center of the stalemate.

Blanche was elevated to the top Justice Department post in an acting capacity after Trump fired Pam Bondi in April. Blanche moved swiftly to advance the president’s interests, accelerating investigations into Trump’s perceived foes and announcing the settlement that created the $1.8 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund” to compensate people who feel mistreated by the criminal justice system and provided Trump and family members with immunity from tax audits.

The controversial settlement threatened to torpedo Blanche’s nomination until he formally rescinded the fund in writing under pressure from Republican Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina. The deal reached between the senators and the department unlocked a vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee, which advanced Blanche’s nomination earlier this week.

Even after the deal, Blanche faced opposition from some Republican senators who were concerned with the “Anti-Weaponization Fund” and the tax audit immunity deal.

open image in gallery In the end, Blanche was confirmed by the narrowest of margins, opposed by two Republicans — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska (pictured) — and by every Democrat. ( AP )

Murkowski announced early Friday that she would join Collins in opposing Blanche’s nomination, saying the country needs an attorney general “who will check the worst impulses of this administration.”

A former federal prosecutor in New York, Blanche rose to public prominence as a lead attorney on Trump’s defense team, including during the Republican’s hush money trial in New York. He also defended Trump against criminal charges in the two federal cases brought by the Biden administration’s Department of Justice — an experience Blanche has said provided him a firsthand look at what he contends was the weaponization of the criminal justice system against Trump.

Blanche entered the Justice Department in 2025 as deputy attorney general under Bondi, overseeing the agency’s day-to-day operations and serving as the public face for high-profile and controversial matters, like the release of millions of investigative files related to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.

Democrats have accused Blanche of prioritizing his loyalty to Trump above all else through investigations against Trump foes such as former FBI Director James Comey and a radical reshaping of the department. Under Bondi and Blanche’s leadership, the department has lost thousands of employees through firings, resignations or voluntary departures.

Blanche’s supporters say that his experience as a federal prosecutor and the trust he earned from Trump in the courtroom make him better equipped than Bondi to explain to the White House the legal constraints of its demands. Republicans have also touted his efforts to bring down violent crime, tackle illegal immigration and combat violent cartels and drug trafficking.

Sen. Chuck Grassley, the Republican chairman of the Judiciary Committee, gave a full-throated endorsement of Blanche ahead of voting, saying that he has led the Justice Department with distinction. “Mr. Blanche is the right choice,” he said.

But it remains unclear whether Blanche will fare any better in delivering on Trump’s desire for retribution than Bondi, whom Trump fired amid resistance from judges, grand jurors and the department’s own workforce as prosecutors sought to establish criminal conduct by one Trump foe after another.

Shortly after Blanche took the top post, the Justice Department moved to indict Comey on charges of threatening the 47th president by posting a social media photograph of seashells in the numerical arrangement of “86 47.” Comey’s lawyers are pressing to have the case dismissed, accusing the department of misleading judges, submitting documents containing false statements and withholding key facts.

Blanche has also appointed Joseph diGenova, a former Justice Department prosecutor from the Reagan administration, to oversee a Florida-based investigation into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired over the last decade to undermine Trump. But it remains uncertain whether that probe will result in any criminal charges.

News.title: Joao Pedro double and Caicedo stunner give Chelsea win over AC Milan
News.content:
Chelsea 3 AC Milan 0

Chelsea cruised to a 3-0 victory over Ruben Amorim’s AC Milan in Jakarta, Indonesia, on Saturday. Goals from Moises Caicedo and a double from João Pedro either side of half-time led Xabi Alonso’s side to their second win on their Far East tour.

The game was fairly even in the first half and looked set to head intothe break level at 0-0 but Pedro’s header from Moises Caicedo’s corner put Chelsea in front.

The London side then doubled their advantage seconds into the second half as Pedro scored his second, assisted by Pedro Neto. Just minutes later, Chelsea had their third courtesy of a well-worked corner routine. Romeo Lavia’s delivery was met by Caicedo on the volley, with the Ecuadorian’s finish with the outside of the boot finding the bottom corner.

Chelsea had further chances to extend their lead in a dominant second-half performance but were unable to add to their three goals.

Chelsea conclude their tour of the Far East with a game against Johor Darul Ta’zim on Sunday in Malaysia before returning home.

Their final pre-season game will be against Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge before beginning their Premier League campaign at Fulham.

AC Milan take on Amorim’s former club Manchester United next Saturday before they kick off their Serie A campaign at Torino on August 23.

News.title: Gomes scores for Aston Villa in defeat by Bayern Munich in Hong Kong
News.content:
Aston Villa 1 Bayern Munich 2

Aston Villa’s tour of the Far East ended in defeat as they lost 2-1 to German champions Bayern Munich in a pre-season friendly at the Kai Tak Sports Park in Hong Kong on Friday.

Bayern took the lead inside the final 10 minutes of the first half, with defender Kim Min-jae heading in from Tom Bischof’s sublime free-kick. Villa goalkeeper Marco Bizot made a string of saves in the second half to keep Bayern’s lead at one goal until former Liverpool forward Luis Díaz smashed in Bayern’s second off the underside of the bar.

Just as the game appeared to be out of reach for Aston Villa, who had struggled to create much going forward for most of the game, Unai Emery’s side showed some life late on. Summer signing João Gomes’s goal from the edge of the box gave them hope before Tammy Abraham nearly brought them back onto level terms, only to be denied by a fine save from 40-year-old Manuel Neuer.

Aston Villa are next in action in six days’ time when they take on Paris St-Germain in the Uefa Super Cup before kicking off their Premier League campaign at Brighton. Bayern have one more friendly to come against RB Leipzig before the DFL-Supercup against Borussia Dortmund. They then kick off the defence of their Bundesliga crown against Stuttgart at home on August 28.

News.title: Suspected Ebola case on packed Congo river boat sparks testing rush
News.content:
Congolese health authorities have intercepted and detained a river boat on its way to the capital after a suspected Ebola case onboard.

Authorities have set up a mobile clinic to test more than 200 passengers after one of them disembarked and died earlier on the voyage.

The boat travelling from the northeastern commercial hub of Kisangani was stopped and held in Maluku, some 40 miles from Kinshasa.

Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is dealing with its worst ever outbreak of the viral haemorrhagic fever, which has seen nearly 4,000 cases and killed around 1,801 people according to the latest government figures.

Samuel Roger Kamba, the health minister, said a 32-year-old man had disembarked in Pimu in Mongala province, before developing ‌suspected Ebola symptoms and dying.

“We did not say it was Ebola. We said there was a suspected case for which we are being cautious,” the health minister told a press conference, according to MediaCongo, a local news site.

He said there had been no other reports of deaths among travellers.

The virus has so far spread to five provinces, though more than 90 per cent of cases have been recorded in the north eastern Ituri region.

News.title: El Nino could cause explosion of rabid seals, animal health experts warn
News.content:
This year’s El Nino weather event risks propelling an outbreak of rabid seals around the world, the world’s animal health body has warned.

Countries in South America and Australasia are being urged to look for signs the deadly infectious disease has reached their waters, only two years after it was first confirmed in South Africa.

The 2024 discovery of rabies in South Africa’s Cape fur seals was the first significant outbreak ever found in marine mammals and has been described as a “significant shift in rabies ecology”.

More than 100 cases have been confirmed in South Africa and Namibia since then, raising fears that aggressive rabid seals could infect humans, pets and other wildlife.

Changing patterns in fish stocks caused by the El Nino phenomenon now potentially risk widening the spread, as uninfected seal populations migrate for food and come into contact with rabid colleagues.

Scientists believe warming sea temperatures off Antarctica could send seal populations northwards into Southern African waters, where they could be exposed to rabies.

They could then return to their home waters, taking the virus with them and infecting other seal populations.

News.title: ​Arteta’s ‘dynasty’ dream collides with Arsenal’s harsh reality
News.content:
Arsenal 1 Real Betis 3

Mikel Arteta says he wants to create a “dynasty” at Arsenal as he threw down the gauntlet to his players to retain their Premier League title and reach a “different level”.

Arsenal are on the verge of completing a £75m deal for Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimãraes from Newcastle and have not given up hope of landing Real Madrid winger Vinícius Júnior, who has been offered an improved contract by the Spanish giants.

The Premier League champions slumped to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night, when they paid the price for individual errors and a lethargic, sloppy defensive display.

But that did little to quell Arteta’s ambitions for the new season. “I’m even more excited [about this season], and we’re going to go and attack every possible title because that’s the ambition that we have,” he said.

“We know that we have the ability. We will go from a strength to a strength as well, whether it’s with the players that we have to take them to a different level, and with the market that is still open to recruit as well, so we are very optimistic about it.

“All the work that we’ve done – that I’ve done through the summer – is to understand what we need to do to win again and to create a dynasty in this football club. That’s the aim.”

Despite Arteta’s bullishness, he conceded Arsenal would have to be a lot better than they were against Betis. When asked about the mood in the dressing room, he said: “Very upset, given a hard time. They are fuming, but this is good. That’s what we need.”

Telegraph Sport analyses some of the talking points from a disappointing evening at the Aviva Stadium.

No Saliba a concern

The importance of goalkeeper David Raya and centre-backs William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhães to Arsenal hardly needs overstating. Their title success was built on the foundations provided by that triumvirate at the back.

Raya has yet to report back from holiday after Spain’s World Cup triumph and Saliba is facing an extended spell on the sidelines with a back injury. Gabriel did appear for the second half but, watching this, Arteta is unlikely to have been dissuaded from the belief he needs another top defender to compensate for the loss of Saliba.

It may have been only Arsenal’s second game of pre-season, so a degree of legginess was understandable.

But the ease with which they were cut open and overloaded by the Spanish side, and the volume of individual errors, did not sit comfortably with Arteta with just over a fortnight until they kick off their title defence at home to newly promoted Coventry City.

Only once in 63 matches last season did Arsenal concede three goals in a single game but they were fortunate Betis did not score more. “In the first half there are two different things: to play well and to compete,” said Arteta, who saw his side trail 3-1 at the interval.

News.title: Ebola outbreak outpacing containment effort, WHO chief warns
News.content:
Caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which there are no vaccines or treatments, it has been extremely difficult to contain, according to experts on the ground.

“The outbreak is spreading faster than our scale-up of the response, with new cases doubling in some hotspots over the past week alone,” Dr Tedros said on X.

Part of the difficulty is that the virus was circulating undetected for weeks before the outbreak was formally declared in mid-May, leaving health officials even now racing to catch up with the spread.

Prof Placide Mbala, director of research, clinical trials and innovation at Africa CDC, told the Telegraph: “It’s mostly the fact we arrived a bit late. It took us some time before we detected this virus outbreak. And when we detected the outbreak, we already had a total of I can say more than 200 suspected cases. It’s been difficult to catch up. That’s where we are.”

While the DRC has a wealth of experience in tackling haemorrhagic fever outbreaks, the effects of that initial delay are still being felt.

Prof Mbala said: “We have some experience dealing with the cases, the labs, the communication, the infection prevention and control.

“We have some experience... But my observation is that we were very slow, and it’s why we’re in this situation.

“We are slow detecting the people, slow responding, we are slow deploying people, we are slow to recruit the community healthcare workers to improve contact tracing, we are slow to deploy the safe burials.”

DRC’s largest outbreak had previously been from 2018 to 2020, when 3,481 cases were recorded.

The West Africa outbreak recorded 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths according to the WHO.

Prof Mbala said insecurity was also severely hampering attempts to curb the virus. The outbreak epicentre is in Ituri province, which has been wracked by ethnic strife for decades and is also home to militias competing to control mining.

He said: “There are many, many mining groups controlling most of the mining places. We have a big issue with those places, because they are places where the response team cannot go.”

Medics and aid workers have also been undermined by violent public distrust of their efforts.

Locals in the area have either doubted the existence of the virus, or have accused health teams of deliberately spreading the infection, or somehow benefiting from it.

More than a dozen health facilities have been set alight and several health workers have been killed.

Prof Mbala said: “The local people, they also sometimes are very upset, because they believe that it’s a kind of a business, and people who are coming here, they are getting a lot of money, [so] don’t want this disease to stop.”

He said he hoped that immunity was starting to rise in some areas and this would start to curb transmission.

However there was also a risk that people fleeing the outbreak would spread the virus further afield.

He said: “The second scenario is the fact we are seeing people moving from the affected area to new areas, to run away from the response team because they do not want to go to the treatment centre.

“And in complicity with their family members living in other areas, they are now the ones who are spreading the disease to new areas

“So we’ll see new places affected because people are moving around from the affected zone to the non-affected zone.”

News.title: Mykhailo Mudryk returns as Chelsea slip to Juventus defeat
News.content:
Chelsea 0 Juventus 1

Mykhailo Mudryk made his first Chelsea appearance since November 2024 as Xabi Alonso’s team succumbed to their second pre-season defeat.

Mudryk replaced Nicolas Jackson in the 82nd minute against Juventus, marking his return to competitive football after a long doping ban that was resolved this week thanks to changes in Wada regulations.

There were a couple of crosses delivered from the left flank by the Ukrainian winger, who could yet leave Chelsea on loan or on a permanent basis before the close of the transfer window.

Juventus were the victors though, thanks to a sumptuous 68th-minute goal by Kosovo winger Edon Zhegrova.

Alonso had 21 players on his bench, and made 12 second-half substitutions.

Levi Colwill and Cole Palmer featured in the defeat by 10-man Spurs on Saturday, but sat this game out as they continue to build fitness. Danny Welbeck did start though, reunited with former Brighton team-mate Joao Pedro up top.

Chelsea scored just one goal against Spurs and Juventus, but the thrust provided by right-back Marco Palestra in tandem with first Geovany Quenda and then Estevao was a bright spot for Alonso.

Chelsea continue their pre-season against AC Milan on Saturday, before they host Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge on August 15.

They begin their Premier League campaign at Fulham in the Monday night slot on the opening weekend.
