World.title: The federalism that promotes productivity (2), By Dipo Baruwa
World.content:
Ultimately, federalism succeeds not merely because power is decentralised, but because authority, incentives and capability are deliberately aligned to make productivity the basis of political success. When states compete to build institutions, attract investment, develop people and expand their productive frontiers, rivalry becomes developmental. It is through that alignment, not constitutional perfection, that productive capabilities are built, locational comparative advantages emerge and sustainable development becomes possible.

Productive Federalism

Productive federalism is not a race to duplicate identical industrial parks, airports, universities or government-owned enterprises. While such investments are not inherently negative, the use of scarce resources requires a more strategic rather than reactive process through which states identify their economic opportunities, coordinate public and private investment around them, develop the required capabilities, and progressively construct locational advantages. The aim is not competition for appearances but for measurable outcomes.

How many sustainable businesses have been created? How many firms have expanded or reinvested? Has agricultural output per hectare improved? Have logistics costs declined? Are technical institutions producing the skills demanded by local industries? Has the state attracted complementary firms around an emerging sector? Has internally generated revenue expanded because productive activity has increased, rather than merely because taxes and levies have multiplied? This requires capable institutions that can identify external opportunities, connect them to local capabilities and ensure that the benefits become embedded within the domestic economy.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

This distinction is important because Nigeria has sometimes confused productive rivalry with politically motivated aggrandisement. States compete to announce the largest airport, the most imposing government building, the newest university or the most ambitious industrial project, even where the economic foundations required to sustain those initiatives are absent. The result is rivalry in expenditure, rather than in capability.

A productive federation would reward governments not for the scale of their announcements but for the durability of the economic systems they create. Public investment would be judged by whether it reduces production costs, improves access to markets, expands knowledge, raises labour productivity and attracts further private investment. Political success would be increasingly connected to economic outcomes, rather than to the ability to distribute patronage or commission conspicuous projects. Unfortunately, the latter is the lived reality of the Nigerian polity.

What is Behind the Cry of Local Government Autonomy?

This also has implications for the relationship between states and local governments. The same authority–incentive–capability framework that applies between the federal and the state governments must also apply within the states themselves. Nigeria cannot build a genuinely productive federation, while local governments remain institutionally marginal to development.

Many services closest to communities, including basic infrastructure maintenance, local markets, primary healthcare support, community libraries, sanitation, local economic information and aspects of agricultural extension, require functioning local government institutions. Yet state governments have progressively absorbed functions and revenues without always providing a more effective replacement. Authority has become concentrated, accountability has become blurred, and local governments have been left with limited incentives or capability to shape development within their jurisdictions.

States should be able to compare themselves transparently on investment attraction, education quality, healthcare delivery, agricultural productivity, infrastructure maintenance, business survival, internally generated revenue and employment creation. Successful reforms undertaken by one state should be documented and adapted by others. Governors should face not only electoral comparison within their states but developmental comparison across the federation.

The question is, therefore, not simply whether local governments should receive allocations directly. It is whether authority, revenue, responsibility and accountability can be aligned at the level in which particular public services and developmental functions can be performed most effectively. Direct funding without capability and accountability may simply reproduce the same distributive weakness at a lower level. But denying local institutions meaningful authority also removes an important layer of experimentation, information gathering and development implementation – basic ingredients for building the federation’s institutional capability to generate, synthesise, and utilise local economic information for national development.

Productive federalism, therefore, requires clarity about who is responsible for what, the resources available for performing those responsibilities, and the outcomes by which performance will be assessed. Where authority is assigned without financial or administrative capability, failure becomes inevitable. Where revenue is provided without responsibility and accountability, distribution becomes an end in itself.

This is also where institutions such as the Nigeria Governors’ Forum should assume a more developmental role. The Forum should not function principally as a platform for political bargaining with the Federal Government or for coordinating common positions on revenue allocation. It could become an institution for productive peer review among states.

States should be able to compare themselves transparently on investment attraction, education quality, healthcare delivery, agricultural productivity, infrastructure maintenance, business survival, internally generated revenue and employment creation. Successful reforms undertaken by one state should be documented and adapted by others. Governors should face not only electoral comparison within their states but developmental comparison across the federation.

Kenya’s experience with county-level devolution offers a useful, though imperfect, illustration. Counties have increasingly been compared on healthcare, agriculture, infrastructure and service delivery. Rwanda, although not a federation, has used performance contracts to connect subnational administration with measurable outcomes. The lesson for Nigeria is not to copy either country, but to recognise that decentralised authority becomes developmental only when performance is visible, comparable and consequential.

The Federal Government also has an indispensable role. Productive federalism does not imply a weak or indifferent centre. It requires a centre that concentrates on functions that benefit from national coordination: macroeconomic stability, national infrastructure, interstate commerce, competition policy, national standards, external trade relations, security coordination, research and the provision of public goods that individual states cannot efficiently supply alone.

The debate before Nigeria is therefore not simply whether to restructure the federation, but what kind of federalism the country wishes to practise. A federation organised predominantly around distribution will continue to produce political competition for existing wealth. A federation organised around productive capability will encourage competition to create new wealth.

The centre should also generate and distribute economic information, coordinate national and subnational institutions, remove barriers to interstate production and trade, and ensure that equalisation supports minimum standards without extinguishing incentives for subnational initiative.

Redistribution remains necessary. Nigeria’s states possess different resource endowments, populations, revenue capacities and historical advantages. A federation cannot ignore these differences. However, redistribution should provide a foundation from which less-advantaged states can build capabilities; it should not become a permanent substitute for productive effort. Equalisation should enable participation in development, not institutionalise dependence on allocation.

The debate before Nigeria is therefore not simply whether to restructure the federation, but what kind of federalism the country wishes to practise. A federation organised predominantly around distribution will continue to produce political competition for existing wealth. A federation organised around productive capability will encourage competition to create new wealth.

Conclusion

The argument throughout this series has been simple. Many of the constitutional and institutional ingredients for productive federalism already exist within Nigeria’s governance framework. What remains deficient is not merely constitutional design, but the governance architecture needed to align authority, incentives and institutional capability.

As Nigeria approaches another general election cycle, this debate should not be ethnicised or reduced to slogans about “true federalism.” Nor should it become a contest between those who support redistribution and those who advocate production. Every viable federation requires both. The real task is to design a system in which equitable redistribution strengthens rather than weakens the incentive to produce.

Ultimately, federalism succeeds not merely because power is decentralised, but because authority, incentives and capability are deliberately aligned to make productivity the basis of political success. When states compete to build institutions, attract investment, develop people and expand their productive frontiers, rivalry becomes developmental. It is through that alignment, not constitutional perfection, that productive capabilities are built, locational comparative advantages emerge and sustainable development becomes possible.

Dipo Baruwa is a business climate development analyst.

World.title: NYSC, khaki and the fight against drug abuse, By Fatih Lawal‑Garu
World.content:
Many young Nigerians see NYSC as a one‑year ritual — khaki, clearance, CDS, and monthly allowances. But my experience taught me something deeper. National service is not about the uniform. It is about the impact made while wearing it… It is about recognising problems around us and choosing to act. It is about using our skills, creativity and passion to improve communities. It is about leaving behind footprints that outlive the service year.

A week before the United Nations International Day Against Drug Abuse and Illicit Trafficking, I walked into the PRNigeria Centre expecting nothing more than another ordinary newsroom assignment. I had no idea that a simple instruction — “Put on your khaki; we’re heading out” — would pull me into an experience that would redefine my understanding of national service and the responsibility that comes with wearing the NYSC uniform.

The PRNigeria Centre is not a typical newsroom. It is a place where ideas breathe, where books are born, and where young people are challenged to think beyond headlines. Corps members do not just file reports; they write books, lead campaigns and contribute to national conversations. I had seen this culture firsthand through publications like Youth Service for National Stability, Diplomacy and Digital Innovation, and anti‑drug, anti‑smuggling campaigns. These works, authored by corps members, made me quietly determined to leave my own mark before my service year ends.

But I did not expect that opportunity to arrive so suddenly.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Our destination was the NDLEA FCT Command, where Deputy Commander Aliyu Omama joined us before we proceeded to Parliament Secondary School and Government Secondary School, Apo. The mission was simple: educate students about the dangers of drug abuse under a campaign titled “Promoting Drug‑Free Schools: A Corper Initiative.”

The initiative was led by Abdulhameed Yushau Shuaib, a fellow Mass Communication graduate from Bayero University, Kano, serving at NITDA. Listening to him speak, I realised this was not just another awareness programme. It was a heartfelt intervention driven by a young Nigerian who refused to watch his peers fall victim to addiction, peer pressure and the deceptive glamour of drug use on social media.

What struck me most was his conviction. He was not complaining about the problem — he was confronting it.

Deputy Commander Omama delivered a message that was both sobering and necessary. He explained how drug abuse fuels domestic violence, armed robbery, kidnapping, banditry and other crimes that plague our society. He listed commonly abused substances — cannabis, cocaine, methamphetamine — using both scientific names and street slang the students recognised instantly.

Yet he did not present addiction as a dead end. He spoke about rehabilitation, recovery and reintegration, reminding the students that help exists, but prevention is always better than cure. His final message was simple: never experiment with drugs.

Representing NITDA’s Director General, Mrs Deborah Dada urged the students to reject drugs and embrace digital skills. She reminded them that technology offers limitless opportunities, which are far more rewarding than any temporary high. Her praise for Abdulhameed’s initiative underscored a powerful truth: national service is not about where you are posted, but what you choose to do with your posting.

Their engagement surprised me. They asked thoughtful questions, exchanged contacts, and expressed genuine interest in future programmes. I left the schools convinced that something meaningful had begun.

But the campaign was only halfway done.

Then came a competition that became a movement. An essay and quiz competition was announced across FCT schools. The response was overwhelming: 87 essays submitted. Editors reviewed each one carefully, screening out plagiarism and AI‑generated content to reward originality and genuine understanding.

On 26 June — the UN Day Against Drug Abuse — the grand finale took place at the PRNigeria Centre.

Ozor Kamsy of Federal Government Boys College, Wuye won the essay competition, followed by Arafat Ismail and Nafisat Abbas. Their presentations showed depth, clarity and a maturity far beyond their age.

The quiz competition was equally intense. Questions covered causes, consequences, prevention, rehabilitation and global efforts against drug abuse. As I watched, I realised how much I still had to learn.

Jamal Oyawoye of Badr Integrated School emerged winner, with Nicodemus Gideon and Salma Musa taking second and third place.

This is a campaign with a future. Partner organisations pledged to sustain the initiative. The Programme Coordinator of Youth Against Disaster Initiatives (YADI), Umar Farouk Bala, announced plans to expand future editions to include disaster preparedness, digital citizenship and public safety. NYSC representative, Mrs Rukayya Abu, praised the organisers and described Abdulhameed’s project as a shining example of meaningful national service.

Her words captured the essence of everything I had witnessed. The True Meaning of National Service.

Many young Nigerians see NYSC as a one‑year ritual — khaki, clearance, CDS, and monthly allowances. But my experience taught me something deeper. National service is not about the uniform. It is about the impact made while wearing it.

It is about recognising problems around us and choosing to act. It is about using our skills, creativity and passion to improve communities. It is about leaving behind footprints that outlive the service year.

That single instruction to wear my khaki took me beyond the newsroom and into a movement. It showed me the power of youth-led advocacy and reminded me that the true measure of NYSC is not the duration of service, but the difference made during it.

I arrived expecting a routine assignment. I left with a renewed understanding of responsibility, purpose and the transformative power of national service.

Fatih Lawal‑Garu is a Corps member serving in Abuja. Email: [email protected]

World.title: “Aren’t We All PR People?”: Setting a new benchmark for communicators, By Yushau A. Shuaib
World.content:
For emerging communicators, this book will serve as a mentor. For educators, it will be a teaching companion. For practitioners, it will be a reminder of the discipline’s core values. And for the profession at large, it will be a contribution that strengthens the intellectual and practical foundation of PR in Nigeria.

Ahmed Balarabe Sa’id’s new book, Aren’t We All PR People?, is one of those rare works that immediately announce themselves as more than textbooks. It is a field guide, a mentor in print, and a career compass for anyone stepping into the demanding but rewarding world of Public Relations. After carefully reviewing the book, I am genuinely tempted — without any flattery — to call it the definitive PR career guide for emerging communicators. It is a standout resource that sets a new benchmark for the field.

Balarabe, a Mass Communication graduate of Bayero University Kano (BUK) more than two decades ago, is not merely a communication scholar, he is a true PR professional in every sense of the word — far beyond regulatory certification. Calling him a practitioner feels almost inadequate because he breathes, speaks, writes, and conducts himself with the instinctive discipline of someone who genuinely lives and promotes Public Relations through his relationships, engagements, and professional ethos.

What makes this book remarkable is not only its breadth but its narrative style. Balarabe writes with a clarity that demystifies PR practice and a warmth that draws readers into the profession’s human side. His storytelling approach, just like my recently released memoir, MNI Versus MNIPR in NIPSS, creates curiosity, making even foundational principles feel fresh and urgent. For budding communicators who often encounter PR as abstract theory, this book offers something different: a vivid, practical, and relatable journey into the craft.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Several chapters carry uniquely crafted titles that immediately spark curiosity and offer clear glimpses into their thematic direction. Chapter One, “From Ancient Rhetoric to Digital Dialogue,” sets the tone by tracing the evolution of communication from classical persuasion to today’s fast paced digital exchanges. Other standout chapters — “A Constellation of Concepts,” “Professionalising the Practice,” “That Good PR Practitioner,” “A Universe of Opportunities,” “Some of Your Mentors,” “Ethical Traps and Hidden Dangers,” “You and AI,” and “PR Shots” — present their subjects with clarity and creative framing. PR Shots, in particular, is an engaging compilation of short, sharp professional posts originally shared on social media, now curated into a chapter that reads like a pocket guide for daily practice. The final chapter, which foregrounds the emerging role of Public Relations in Nigeria’s national project, provides a thoughtful and forward looking conclusion — positioning PR not just as a profession but as a strategic pillar in nation building.

The book succeeds on multiple fronts. First, it bridges the gap between theory and practice. Many PR texts lean heavily on academic frameworks, leaving young practitioners unsure how to apply them in real world situations. Balarabe flips that script. He grounds every concept in lived experience — crisis moments, ethical dilemmas, communication landmines, and the subtle art of managing reputation. The result is a book that teaches not only what PR is but how PR is done.

Second, the book is structured to guide readers through the profession with increasing depth. From foundational ethics to the anatomy of a good practitioner, from crisis communication to the evolving role of AI, each chapter builds on the last with intentional clarity. The inclusion of real personalities — role models whose careers illuminate different pathways in the field — adds a human dimension that young readers will find both inspiring and instructive.

Third, Balarabe demonstrates a rare courage in addressing contemporary issues. His challenge to the Nigerian Institute of Public Relations (NIPR) on the absence of AI regulation is bold and necessary. His exploration of digital crises, misinformation, and emerging technologies shows a practitioner who understands that PR is evolving rapidly — and that the next generation must be prepared for a landscape far more complex than what existed a decade ago.

The book also shines in its treatment of ethics. Balarabe does not present ethics as a checklist but as the backbone of professional credibility. His insistence that ethical grounding must precede technical skill is a message young communicators urgently need. In a world in which speed often competes with accuracy, and visibility competes with integrity, this emphasis is both timely and timeless.

One of the book’s strongest features is its use of narrative to teach principles. Balarabe’s stories — of practitioners, crises, institutions, and turning points — are not decorative. They are instructional. They show how PR works in real life, how reputations are built and broken, and how communicators must think, act, and adapt. This narrative approach makes the book accessible without sacrificing depth.

The book is also refreshingly honest. It does not romanticise the profession. It acknowledges the pressures, the politics, the ethical crossroads, and the emotional labour involved in communication work. Yet, it balances this realism with optimism, reminding readers that PR remains one of the most impactful careers for those who master its principles.

For emerging communicators, this book will serve as a mentor. For educators, it will be a teaching companion. For practitioners, it will be a reminder of the discipline’s core values. And for the profession at large, it will be a contribution that strengthens the intellectual and practical foundation of PR in Nigeria.

In my sincere assessment, this book is more than a guide. It is a benchmark. A resource that will inspire, instruct, and challenge. A book that emerging communicators will return to repeatedly as they navigate their careers.

And truly, Aren’t We All PR People is a book our profession has been waiting for.

Yushau A. Shuaib, an award-winning PR practitioner, is the author of MNI Versus MNIPR in NIPSS- Tackling Institutional Bullying. Email: [email protected]

World.title: The memoir on NIPSS, NIPR and an AI study that outlived institutional setbacks, By Kabir Abdulsalam
World.content:
The enduring strength of MNI versus MNIPR in NIPSS lies not in its recounting of institutional disagreements but in its demonstration that resilience can transform disappointment into lasting contribution… The closing reflection captures this beautifully: “Institutions may grant opportunities, but they do not own ideas. Once knowledge becomes a mission, it acquires a life of its own. No withdrawal letter can take that away.”.. That single sentence summarises not only Chapter Nine but also the relationship between the memoir and its companion volume on artificial intelligence.

When I received copies of MNI versus MNIPR in NIPSS: Tackling Institutional Bullying and AI in Crisis Communication in Nigeria: Challenges and Prospects, both authored by Yushau A. Shuaib, managing director and chief executive officer of Image Merchants Promotion Limited (IMPR), I expected two very different books. One appeared to be a memoir of institutional conflict; the other, an academic work on emerging technology and crisis communication.

Having read both, I discovered they are, in many respects, companion volumes. Together, they tell the story of how personal adversity can become intellectual opportunity, and how an interrupted academic journey can ultimately produce work of lasting national and international significance.

As Associate Editor of Spokespersons Digest — the publication behind the National Spokespersons Awards — I was naturally drawn to Chapter Eight of the memoir, “The NIPR Betrayal” in MNI versus MNIPR in NIPSS, spanning pages 139 to 161. Having covered the activities of the Nigerian Institute of Public Relations (NIPR) for several years, I approached the chapter with professional curiosity. What I found was an emotionally compelling account that raises broader questions about institutional relationships, professional loyalty, and the delicate balance between organisational discipline and support for members.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to the memoir, shortly after his withdrawal from the Senior Executive Course (SEC) 47 at the National Institute for Policy and Strategic Studies (NIPSS), Kuru, Shuaib was invited to appear before the Ethics Panel of the NIPR Council over actions arising from the dispute.

For someone whose professional life had been closely intertwined with the Institute for more than three decades, the experience was understandably painful.

Shuaib traces his relationship with the NIPR back to his undergraduate days at Bayero University, Kano, where he specialised in Public Relations and, in 1992, became the first recipient of the NIPR President’s Prize for the Best Graduating Public Relations Student. Three years later, he was honoured as the Kano/Jigawa Chapter’s Public Relations Person of the Year.

His career subsequently expanded beyond Nigeria through advanced studies, including a Master’s degree in Public Relations from the University of Westminster, London, professional research in online public relations, and affiliations with international organisations such as the Chartered Institute of Public Relations (CIPR), the Public Relations Society of America (PRSA), and the International Public Relations Association (IPRA). Under his leadership, IMPR also earned multiple international recognitions, including the SABRE Awards Africa and IPRA Golden World Awards.

Against this backdrop, one seemingly minor incident in the memoir becomes symbolically significant. The invitation from NIPR reportedly addressed him as “ANIPR” rather than “MNIPR,” the professional designation he had used for many years and which, according to him, had previously appeared in official correspondence from the Institute.

At first glance, it appears trivial. Yet anyone familiar with public relations understands that titles, professional designations and institutional language often carry symbolic meaning. They communicate recognition, identity and belonging.

Shuaib writes that after drawing the Registrar’s attention to the issue, another invitation was issued, this time omitting any professional designation altogether.

Whether intentional or not, the incident deepened his perception that his decades of contribution were no longer receiving institutional acknowledgement.

Equally striking is the memoir’s account of the National Spokespersons Awards.

The book explains that the initiative was conceived in 2019 during the tenure of Mallam Mukhtar Sirajo as President of the NIPR. Its inaugural edition was independently organised by IMPR in 2021, with the Institute’s endorsement, before both organisations entered into a formal partnership through a Memorandum of Understanding in 2023.

The awards have since grown into one of Nigeria’s foremost platforms for recognising excellence in strategic communication; honouring spokespersons, public information managers, corporate affairs practitioners, military communicators and crisis communication professionals.

According to the memoir, however, the partnership was terminated before the expiration of the agreement by the Ike Neliaku-led NIPR.

What surprised me further was when the institute, following the termination, introduced another awards platform under a different name.

Reflecting on the episode, Shuaib writes: “Organisations can withdraw endorsements. Partnerships can be terminated. Titles can be withheld. But one’s name — carefully built over decades — must remain answerable first to conscience, history and truth.”

That statement captures the emotional centre of Chapter Eight.

If that chapter represents the wound, Chapter Nine — “A Blessed Disappointment” — represents the healing. In my view, it is the memoir’s most inspiring chapter.

Rather than dwelling on conflict, it chronicles how an interrupted academic journey became the catalyst for some of the author’s most significant professional achievements.

Shuaib begins by acknowledging the personal toll of the crisis. The combined effects of the NIPSS withdrawal, the NIPR investigation, and the ensuing legal battles, resulted in something he had never previously experienced — hypertension.

His opening reflection is both simple and profound: “As someone who had spent decades helping individuals and institutions navigate reputational crises, I suddenly found myself at the centre of one.”

Yet, the chapter is far from a catalogue of grievances. Instead, it documents how adversity redirected his energy towards new opportunities.

One source of encouragement came from his family, whose support inspired him to take a restorative vacation in Canada. Equally moving were the visits and messages from graduates of the Young Communication Fellowship, many of whom travelled long distances simply to encourage their mentor.

These moments reinforced one of the book’s enduring messages: “True success is not measured by certificates, titles or institutional recognition. It is measured by the positive impact one leaves in the lives of others.”

The memoir also recounts how the NIPSS experience unexpectedly strengthened his vision for expanding the Young Communication Fellowship.

Inspired by the residential model at NIPSS, he developed plans for hostel facilities at the PRNigeria Centres in Kano and Ilorin. During a visit to the Kano Centre, Professor Adamu Abubakar Gwarzo, President of MAAUN, asked whether similar facilities existed in Abuja.

When Shuaib explained that such a project was beyond his financial capacity, Professor Gwarzo donated a large building in Lugbe, Abuja, to serve as a training and residential centre for the Fellowship.

It is an extraordinary example of how one setback unexpectedly created room for another opportunity.

Perhaps the chapter’s most compelling narrative, however, concerns the research project that eventually became AI in Crisis Communication in Nigeria: Challenges and Prospects.

Originally approved as a research proposal during SEC 47 at NIPSS, the study was titled “Artificial Intelligence and Crisis Communication in Nigeria’s Public Sector: An Assessment.”

Following his withdrawal from the programme, the institutional framework supporting the research disappeared. Many scholars would understandably have abandoned the project.

Shuaib chose otherwise. Driven by professional conviction and encouraged by colleagues at the Centre for Crisis Communication, he completed the study independently within three months.

The findings proved remarkably relevant. The research identified what he describes as Nigeria’s “awareness-adoption gap.” While many communication professionals are increasingly familiar with artificial intelligence, institutional use remains largely limited to drafting documents, monitoring media content, and generating reports.

More advanced applications — including predictive analytics, crisis forecasting, sentiment analysis and misinformation detection — remain significantly underutilised.

The study also highlights a “trust paradox.” Although AI improves speed and efficiency, communication professionals remain cautious about relying on it during crises because of concerns over deepfakes, misinformation, algorithmic bias, and the irreplaceable role of human empathy and judgment.

Its central conclusion is both balanced and timely: artificial intelligence should enhance human decision-making, not replace it.

Beyond diagnosis, the research identifies structural barriers to AI adoption, including inadequate digital infrastructure, inconsistent electricity supply, limited broadband penetration, shortages of specialised expertise, weak institutional coordination, and underdeveloped policy frameworks.

Importantly, the work did not remain confined to academia. It informed discussions at the Centre for Crisis Communication and the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), contributing to the National Symposium on Artificial Intelligence and Crisis Communication held at the National Defence College, Abuja, in November 2025.

One outcome of that symposium was the establishment of the Crisis Communication Hub (CCHub), a multi-stakeholder platform aimed at improving crisis management and combating misinformation in Nigeria.

The research subsequently evolved into the 200-page book AI in Crisis Communication in Nigeria: Challenges and Prospects, endorsed by NITDA Director-General, Malam Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi; Major General Chris Olukolade (Rtd); Professor Abdalla Uba Adamu; and Professor Abiodun Adeniyi.

Its most remarkable achievement came when the book was shortlisted as a finalist for the 2026 International Public Relations Association (IPRA) Golden World Awards in Athens, Greece.

There is considerable irony in this outcome. A research project interrupted within one institution ultimately gained wider relevance beyond it.

Had it remained solely an academic exercise at NIPSS, it might have concluded as another research paper in an institutional archive.

Instead, it became a national symposium, a published book, a catalyst for policy conversations, and an internationally recognised work.

That is perhaps the memoir’s greatest lesson. Institutions undoubtedly create opportunities. They nurture ideas, shape careers, and provide platforms for scholarship. But ideas, once fully developed, often transcend the institutions that first gave them life.

The enduring strength of MNI versus MNIPR in NIPSS lies not in its recounting of institutional disagreements but in its demonstration that resilience can transform disappointment into lasting contribution.

The closing reflection captures this beautifully: “Institutions may grant opportunities, but they do not own ideas. Once knowledge becomes a mission, it acquires a life of its own. No withdrawal letter can take that away.”

That single sentence summarises not only Chapter Nine but also the relationship between the memoir and its companion volume on artificial intelligence.

Together, they tell the story of an interrupted journey that ultimately reached destinations far beyond where it first began.

Kabir Abdulsalam is Associate Editor of Spokespersons Digest. He can be reached via [email protected].
