World.title: Election promises: Do they really influence voters?
World.content:
With polling day fast approaching, Zambians are once again weighing a familiar question: do campaign promises actually shape how people vote? Writer and political commentator Alfred Sayila argues that the electorate has grown far more discerning since independence, no longer taking rhetoric at face value regardless of which party makes the pledge.

Since 1964, campaign promises have been used unsparingly by ruling parties to win support, and at times those promises have helped opposition parties ascend to power. But voters have come of age. They now sift through political rhetoric with far greater discernment, separating substance from spin.

Founding President Kenneth Kaunda used to say no one can take Zambian people for granted. He learned this the hard way in 1991, when the crowds he had commanded at rallies for 27 years turned against him at the ballot box, handing victory to Fredrick Chiluba, a man Kaunda had once dismissed as a political dwarf because of his short stature.

If that rejection could befall a leader who delivered real development, peace and unity, the consequences for candidates offering only unfulfilled pledges could prove far harsher. Voters increasingly ask a pointed question before casting their ballots: what did previous leaders fail to do that they now claim they will finally accomplish? Unfulfilled promises, in the eyes of many voters, carry little more weight than lies, and no late window-dressing can restore lost confidence.

Cheap electioneering built on empty promises breeds suspicion among an electorate that has already walked that road before. Rallies, dances, hymnals, handouts and donations often amount to little more than vote-chasing theatre, while the real decision in most voters’ minds is settled long before polling day.

Several campaign pledges circulating this election season raise questions about feasibility. These include promises to build universities in rural capitals, construct skills centres nationwide, build an international airport in a terminus town, further increase the Constituency Development Fund, install solar plants everywhere, employ millions of people and pay farmers within three working days of submitting claims. Such promises invite an obvious question: where would the funding come from, since many are not backed by demonstrated fiscal detail?

Some pledges being presented as new are, in fact, programmes with long historical roots. Free education, for instance, existed in a form during the colonial era through Native Authorities, which offered access to schooling with only small fee contributions, alongside bursaries for vulnerable children. School feeding programmes for boarders also existed under colonial-era grants administered through native authorities, structures that functioned similarly to today’s Constituency Development Fund. The first post-independence government under Kaunda largely consolidated and diversified what it inherited rather than inventing entirely new systems.

The point extends even to the “One Zambia, One Nation” ethos some politicians now invoke. Cross-country transfers of civil servants during the colonial period, though designed to serve a divide-and-rule strategy, inadvertently mixed tribes and cultures across regions, a process the mining industry on the Copperbelt also accelerated. That intermingling laid groundwork Kaunda later built on with his unifying slogan, and its legacy persists in families that settled far from their ancestral regions, illustrating that many of today’s talking points describe processes already well underway long before current candidates entered public life.

Politicians should therefore be cautious about presenting themselves as pioneers of ideas that predate them. Making a promise is one thing; having the resources to deliver it is another. Pointing to numbers of newly employed civil servants offers little persuasive weight, since recruiting public workers is a routine government function and a perpetual drain on the treasury rather than an extraordinary achievement. A more meaningful measure of good governance lies in creating conditions for private-sector job creation and supporting small and medium enterprises.

A genuinely good government also lightens the burden on citizens through subsidies on food, medicine, fuel, fertiliser and seeds. Free education alone means little if households sending children to school are stalked by hunger, and in some areas free education has led to overcrowding, poor facilities and staff exhaustion, undermining the quality of instruction it was meant to improve.

Campaign messaging, Sayila argues, would be more credible if grounded in physical projects already initiated or completed, rather than repeated promises. Voters today want to see improvement in living standards through affordable prices, not abstract statistics about inflation or exchange rates; they want that progress reflected in real purchasing power and reduced cost of living.

Ultimately, elections are rarely won through last-minute campaigning, colourful posters, slick s or borrowed slogans. They are won when politicians own their mistakes and credibly promise to do better. A candidate’s underlying character tends to show through regardless of rehearsed charisma, and unconvincing promises rarely manage to sway voter judgement in the end.

Given the closeness expected in this race, with no single presidential candidate likely to muster the 50-plus-one threshold in the first round, the Electoral Commission of Zambia carries a democratic duty to ensure the process remains free and fair, with the possibility of a run-off remaining real.

World.title: Mast Editorial: Police IG must prove critics wrong on election violence
World.content:
The Inspector General of Police, Graphel Musamba, issued a statement condemning the wave of violence linked to United Party for National Development (UPND) cadres in the run-up to Thursday’s general election. A Mast Editorial said the statement was welcome, but warned that words alone would not be enough to convince a sceptical public.

The piece argued that with polling day approaching, police carry a constitutional and moral duty to ensure all candidates, particularly opposition contenders, can campaign without being attacked or threatened by either cadres or officers themselves. It noted that the ruling party had campaigned largely unimpeded, while opposition figures had repeatedly found themselves on the receiving end of disruption.

The real test now, the editorial said, was whether Musamba’s officers would act against identifiable UPND cadres accused of targeting the campaign of NRPUP presidential candidate Brian Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu. It linked the pattern of violence to what it described as divisive rhetoric from President Hakainde Hichilema at rallies, and to instructions allegedly issued by a Nigeria-based figure calling himself Prophet Seer 1.

Several specific incidents were raised, demanding direct answers from the IG. Where were police, the editorial asked, when officers reportedly tried to stop an Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) sanctioned opposition rally in Ndola, and when cadres allegedly descended on a hotel and lodge in Kitwe housing members of Mundubile’s campaign team, damaging vehicles while officers looked on.

An incident in Solwezi was also raised, where musicians supporting Mundubile’s campaign were allegedly attacked by people travelling in UPND-labelled vehicles, alongside a case in Mwembeshi East, where cadres reportedly raided a rally for an independent candidate and assaulted musician Clifford Dimba, known as General Kanene, leaving him with head injuries from a machete attack.

Further questions concerned Northern Western Province, where cadres allegedly trailed Mundubile’s entourage, and Luampa in Western Province, where his convoy was reportedly blocked and stoned, injuring a police chief inspector. A separate reference was made to Mongu, where officers reportedly detained members of Mundubile’s musical entourage, including a comedian, and where the candidate was allegedly forced to flee a peaceful rally under tear smoke.

Musamba was called on to respond directly to Mundubile’s claim that UPND cadres have been absorbed into the Zambia Police Service, issued uniforms and firearms, and deployed to obstruct his campaign while concealing their identities behind face masks. These allegations, the editorial stated, remained unanswered by the IG.

While acknowledging that video and photographic evidence of the cited incidents circulates on social media, the piece stressed continued confidence in the Zambia Police Service, adding that the institution’s conduct, not its statements, would be the true measure over the remaining election period.

World.title: REA Completes Luwingu’s K19.4 million  Grid Extension
World.content:
The Rural Electrification Authority (REA) has completed the implementation of the over 19.4 million Kwacha Tungati Grid Extension Project in Luwingu District in Northern Province.

Rural Electrification Authority Chief Executive Officer Alex Mbumba says the project is aimed at increasing the number of households connected to the national grid.

Engineer Mbumba says the project which was awarded to a Turkish based contractor Laatu Energy Solutions Limited is expected to benefit about 636 beneficiaries who will be connected to the supply of electricity which has been constructed in the area.

The Chief Executive Officer was speaking when he paid a courtesy call on Luwingu District Commissioner Chomba Chileshe in Luwingu.

He added that the project has given electricity supply to Tungati Combined School, Local Court, Market, Tungati Min Hospital, Kuta Primary School, Chibofwe Primary School, Sokontwe Primary School and Surrounding areas.

He explained that the supply of electricity to the area is expected to enhance the existing economical activities currently taking place on a micro scale such as retail trading, alcoholic beverage trading and maize-milling in the community.

Engineer Mbumba stated that the completion of the Tungati Grid Extension Project will encourage entrepreneurs in the area to set up businesses which communities had challenges accessing.

He emphasized that the implementation of the Tungati project will bring social and economic benefits which will improve the livelihood of the people of Tungati Chiefdom.

The Chief Executive Officer also highlighted that over 41 beneficiaries are expected to get connected under ASCENT subsidy program which is currently in force

And Luwingu District Commissioner Chomba Chileshe Commended government for completing the project on time saying people can now start benefiting from it.

Mr Chileshe indicated that since independence people of Tungati Chiefdom used to cover long distances to acquire services which need electricity.

He also disclosed that health facilities in the area used to have problems keeping vaccines and other essential drugs which needed refrigeration and that with the completion of the project these services will no longer be challenging to them.

Mr Chileshe further indicated that even vulnerable people in communities are now able to have their houses connected to electricity because of the subsidy programme which has been introduced.

He urged communities where REA has installed the electricity infrastructure not to vandalize the infrastructure aimed at improving their livelihood.

World.title: VEEP Urges Clergy to Pray for Peaceful Elections
World.content:
Vice President Mutale Nalumango has called on the clergy to continue praying for unity, peace and love ahead of next Thursday’s general election, saying the values are essential for peaceful polls and national development.

Mrs Nalumango urged church leaders to pray for the country’s leadership and the nation as a whole to ensure Zambia holds peaceful elections.

Speaking when she met members of the clergy in Mkushi, the Vice President said love, peace and unity were critical to promoting national development, adding that Zambia needs God’s intervention to achieve its development aspirations.

She further urged Zambians to reject the spirit of division, confusion and disunity.

Mkushi Ministers Fellowship Chairperson, Reverend Adams Chilowana, said the church remains committed to praying for peace and unity as the country heads to the general election.

Reverend Chilowana disclosed that church mother bodies in the district will next week hold special prayers for peaceful elections.

Meanwhile, traditional leaders in Mkushi have commended the government for the prompt payment of farmers supplying maize to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA).

Speaking on behalf of seven chiefs who met the Vice President, Senior Chief Shaibila said farmers are receiving their payments on time and appealed to the government to maintain the status quo.

World.title: Government hails Joseph Katema’s enduring development legacy
World.content:
Government has eulogised the late former Cabinet Minister, Joseph Katema, as someone who made a significant contribution to the development trajectory of the country, through implementation of sound policies that attracted donor funding.

Speaking during the burial ceremony in Lusaka, Deputy Secretary to Cabinet, Oliver Kalabo, who was speaking on behalf of the government, has since called on the public service to emulate his selfless service to the country.

Dr Kalabo said that the late former cabinet minister facilitated mobilisation of donor support to complement government efforts in implementing policies and programmes targeted at improving the livelihood of the citizens.

“The nation may wish to know that the late Honourable Dr Joseph Katema, was admired for embracing servant leadership, when he served as a cabinet minister,” said Dr Kalabo.

Widow to the late cabinet minister, Antonette Katema, whose speech was read by her close friend, Suzyo Simbyakula, remembered her late husband as a humble man with a heart without limits when it came to helping others.

Mrs Katema said that the departure of her late husband has left a vacuum that cannot be expressed in words.

Cathedral of the Child Jesus Administrator, Benedict Chanda, said that the church has embraced the bereaved family with prayer, and asks God to strengthen them with his grace.

Fr Chanda also called for the need to honor the memories of Dr Katema with tribute and commitment to living a life of honesty, justice, reconciliation and service.

World.title: Africa: A Landmark for African Finance - Europe's First African Sovereign Bond ETF Opens a New Chapter
World.content:
For years, African finance ministers have made the same case at investor conferences and multilateral summits: the continent is not short of bankable projects, it is short of affordable capital. This week, that case took a tangible step forward. Legal & General Asset Management, one of Britain's largest institutional investors, launched the L&G LSF African Government Bond (USD) UCITS ETF — the first exchange-traded fund of its kind available to European investors — built on the iBoxx LSF USD African Sovereigns Index and developed in partnership with the Liquidity and Sustainability Facility (LSF).

It is a milestone worth pausing on. For the first time, a European investor can gain diversified exposure to African sovereign debt with the same ease, and through the same familiar mechanism, used to buy an S&P 500 fund or a German bund tracker. That simplicity is the point: it is precisely what has been missing from African capital markets, and precisely what has made a real difference in other regions that have walked this path before.

From a single transaction to durable market infrastructure



The achievement did not happen overnight. In 2024, the LSF worked with S&P Dow Jones Indices to build the iBoxx LSF USD African Sovereigns Index, developing a proprietary methodology to curate a standardized, investable benchmark for African Eurobonds. That index has now matured into a retail-accessible fund — proof, as Dr. Vera Songwe, the LSF's founder and chair and formerly the United Nations' top economist for Africa, put it, of the growing appetite among private investors for African securities. Songwe singled out Afreximbank's early support as instrumental in building the momentum behind the milestone. Prof. Benedict Okey Oramah, Afreximbank's former president and board chairman, said the bank's original ambition reached beyond a single instrument toward a lasting foundation for deeper, more resilient African capital markets — and called the ETF's launch tangible evidence that African sovereign debt can now attract the same caliber of standardized, investable products found in the world's mature markets.

That shift — from bespoke, one-off transactions to standardized, repeatable financial infrastructure — is what economists who study emerging markets consider the real prize. Indices and the funds built on them aggregate exposure to many issuers inside a single, tradable structure, opening the door to institutional investors who allocate capital through recognized benchmarks and would otherwise find it difficult to build African exposure bond by bond. As that investor base broadens, secondary-market trading tends to deepen, improving price discovery and gradually narrowing the liquidity premium that has long made African governments pay more to borrow than the underlying risk alone would justify.

The beginning of a market infrastructure, not just a fund

What distinguishes this launch from a one-off product announcement is the architecture behind it. Since its establishment, the LSF has worked with African and international partners on a structural problem, not a single transaction: the illiquid secondary markets that have long translated into higher borrowing costs for African sovereign issuers. The ETF is the visible, investable output of that longer effort — but the more consequential piece is what sits underneath it. An index, a curation methodology, and now a public-market vehicle built on top of both form the early layers of something African capital markets have never had: durable, replicable financial infrastructure, the kind that can support the next index, the next fund, and the next generation of instruments, rather than a single deal that expires once it settles. It is, in that sense, less a product launch than groundbreaking — the pouring of a foundation that future African bond funds, corporate debt indices and structured products can be built on for years to come.

A path other regions have proven works

Africa is following, and can now build on, a trail blazed elsewhere with striking results. After the 1997 Asian financial crisis exposed the dangers of financing long-term projects with short-term foreign-currency debt, ASEAN nations joined with China, Japan and South Korea in 2003 to launch the Asian Bond Markets Initiative, an effort to deepen local-currency bond markets as a durable alternative to bank borrowing. The results, over two decades, were transformative: by 2018, the region's local-currency bond markets had grown to more than $12 trillion outstanding — approaching the scale of the entire euro-denominated bond market. A companion Asian Bond Fund initiative, run through regional central banks from 2005, is credited by the Bank for International Settlements with driving marked improvements in liquidity and far more reliable government yield curves across the region.

Latin America's experience is, if anything, an even sharper illustration of what standardized, tradable instruments can unlock. The 1989 Brady Plan converted defaulted Latin American bank loans into tradable, dollar-denominated bonds, turning a small and illiquid market for developing-country debt into a thriving one within a few short years: sovereign bond issuance by developing countries rose from roughly $1.5 billion in 1985 to more than $200 billion by 1992, while bid-ask spreads — the standard measure of how efficiently a market prices risk — fell by more than half. Mexico, Brazil, the Philippines, Colombia and Venezuela all eventually retired their Brady bonds entirely, having graduated into full, normalized access to global capital markets. It is a case study in how a single well-designed financial innovation can rewrite a region's relationship with global investors.

What it means for the factories, mills and industrial zones Africa is building now

For a continent working to move from exporting raw commodities to building the mills, ports and industrial zones that turn them into finished goods, the relevance of a more liquid sovereign bond market is direct and consequential. Every basis point shaved off a government's borrowing cost is capital freed for the roads, power and industrial-zone infrastructure that projects like Benin's Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone or Senegal's cotton-spinning mills depend on. Sovereign yields also set the floor beneath which corporate and infrastructure borrowers price their own debt, so a more liquid, better-priced sovereign curve tends to lower financing costs across an entire economy — for the private manufacturers and agro-processors driving Africa's industrial ambitions, not just for finance ministries.

Close 

It is a case Dr. Songwe has been making for years well before she built an institution around it: that mobilizing private and institutional capital, not waiting on aid flows that have plateaued, would ultimately decide whether African industrialization succeeds. The African Development Bank and Afreximbank have each echoed that argument in recent years. Measured against the goal Songwe helped put at the center of that conversation, this week's launch is exactly the kind of instrument that, in Asia and Latin America, proved able to compound into something much larger than its starting size. If the ambition she has championed through the LSF holds — and the early signs, from a $12 trillion Asian bond market to Latin America's full return to global capital markets, suggest it can — this ETF may be remembered in African finance as the moment the continent's capital markets began to be priced like the mature markets they are increasingly built to resemble.

World.title: Africa: Africa Has Ideas - What It Lacks Is a Fair Hearing from Global Capital
World.content:
Africa Has Ideas - What It Lacks Is a Fair Hearing from Global Capital

guest column

Why good African businesses and projects can struggle to cross the funding redline

Africa has never suffered from a shortage of ideas.

It suffers from a shortage of capital willing to believe in those ideas.

Across the continent, entrepreneurs are building businesses, engineers are designing infrastructure, farmers are developing agricultural value chains, innovators are creating technology solutions and governments are proposing projects capable of transforming entire economies.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Yet again and again, they encounter the same wall:

Where is the money?

This is one of Africa’s great economic paradoxes. The continent has enormous natural resources, a young and expanding population, growing consumer markets and extraordinary entrepreneurial energy. Yet many African businesses and projects that could create jobs and generate wealth struggle to obtain the capital required to move from concept to implementation, or from a small enterprise to a large-scale business.

The uncomfortable truth is that Africa’s financing problem is not simply a shortage of capital.

There is plenty of capital in the world

The problem is that too much of that capital sees Africa first through the lens of risk — and only afterwards through the lens of opportunity.

That distinction matters.

The African funding redline

For years, African countries have effectively operated under a financial redline.

The language may be sophisticated: sovereign risk, country risk, credit risk, currency risk, liquidity risk and political risk.

But the consequence is simple:

Money becomes more expensive.

When the perceived risk of a country is high, investors demand a higher return. Governments pay more to borrow. Local financial institutions operate in a more expensive funding environment. Businesses then face higher interest rates and tougher investment requirements.

A project that might be financially viable at one cost of capital can become impossible when the financing cost rises significantly.

This creates a vicious circle.

A country perceived to be risky pays more for capital.

Higher borrowing costs put pressure on public finances.

Weak fiscal positions reinforce perceptions of risk.

Investors demand even greater returns.

And the cycle continues.

The entrepreneur at the end of that chain is often the one who pays the price.

This is not an argument that Africa has no risks.

Of course it does.

Every investment has risk.

The question is whether the financial system is sophisticated enough to distinguish between risk and opportunity — and between one African project and another.

Are we rating Africa instead of rating projects?

Perhaps one of the most important questions Africa should now be asking is this:

Are we properly assessing African projects, or are we allowing the reputation of the continent to influence our assessment before the project has even been examined?

A renewable-energy project backed by credible long-term agreements is not necessarily the same risk as a speculative start-up.

A profitable agricultural-processing company with established export markets is not the same proposition as an untested business.

An infrastructure project with predictable revenues is not the same as a project that exists only on paper.

Yet the African label can sometimes become an additional invisible risk premium.

This is where the conversation around international credit ratings and financial institutions becomes important.

Credit ratings have a legitimate purpose. Investors need independent mechanisms to assess creditworthiness.

But ratings also influence the cost of capital.

And when a continent is repeatedly perceived through a high-risk lens, the consequences extend far beyond sovereign borrowing.

They affect banks.

They affect businesses.

They affect infrastructure.

They affect entrepreneurs.

They affect the ability of African economies to convert natural resources, human capital and good ideas into productive investment.

The cost of being misunderstood

The greatest danger is not that investors identify genuine African risks.

The danger is that perceived risk becomes detached from actual opportunity.

Consider the African entrepreneur who has developed a viable business but cannot obtain expansion capital.

Consider the manufacturer who wants to build a factory but faces financing costs that make production uncompetitive.

Consider the farmer who wants to move from exporting raw commodities to processing them locally.

Consider the engineer who has designed an energy project but cannot secure affordable project finance.

In each case, the problem may not be the absence of an opportunity.

It may be the cost and structure of capital.

And this has consequences for entire economies.

If a factory is not built, jobs are not created.

If a processing plant is not financed, raw materials continue to leave the continent without capturing their full value.

If infrastructure is delayed, businesses face higher operating costs.

If businesses cannot scale, governments collect less tax.

If young people cannot find productive employment, demographic growth becomes a social challenge rather than an economic dividend.

So the financing question is not merely a question for bankers.

It is a question for anyone concerned about Africa’s development.

Something important may be changing

This is why a development announced by the Liquidity and Sustainability Facility deserves considerably more attention than it is likely to receive outside financial circles.

The LSF has welcomed the launch of the L&G LSF African Government Bond (USD) UCITS ETF, developed by Legal & General Asset Management and described by the LSF as the first of its kind available in Europe.

To the average African entrepreneur, an African government bond ETF may sound remote from the daily struggle to raise capital.

But it represents something much bigger:

an attempt to change the financial infrastructure through which the world accesses African markets.

The LSF has been working to address the structural problem of illiquid secondary markets for African sovereign debt, which can contribute to higher borrowing costs.

In 2024, it collaborated with S&P Dow Jones Indices to create the iBoxx LSF USD African Sovereigns Index, providing a standardized benchmark for African sovereign Eurobonds.

Now that benchmark has become the basis for a publicly accessible ETF.

That matters because capital likes familiarity.

Global institutional investors managing billions of dollars cannot individually analyse every African bond or every African opportunity.

They need benchmarks.

They need transparency.

They need liquidity.

They need standardized investment structures.

And when those structures exist, African assets become easier to access.

This is bigger than one ETF

The LSF says indices and ETFs can help broaden the investor base, increase secondary-market activity, improve price discovery and, over time, potentially reduce the liquidity premium paid by issuers.

That is an important development.

But it should also provoke a much bigger question:

What happens if this thinking is extended beyond sovereign bonds?

What if African infrastructure can be packaged into investment structures that global institutional investors can understand?

What if African renewable-energy projects become part of standardized investment portfolios?

What if African agricultural value chains can attract pension and insurance capital?

What if African companies can increasingly access corporate bond markets?

What if African pension funds can invest more effectively in African infrastructure?

What if global investors can obtain exposure to African growth through transparent, liquid and professionally structured vehicles?

That is where the conversation becomes transformational.

Because Africa does not merely need more money.

It needs better channels through which money can reach productive opportunity.

The entrepreneur is waiting

Somewhere in Lagos, Nairobi, Accra, Johannesburg, Kigali, Lusaka, Harare, Dar es Salaam or Dakar, there is an entrepreneur sitting on a business idea that could employ hundreds or thousands of people.

Close 

Somewhere there is an engineer with a viable energy project

Somewhere there is an agricultural entrepreneur who knows how to turn raw commodities into higher-value exports.

Somewhere there is a technology founder building a solution for a market of hundreds of millions of people.

Somewhere there is an infrastructure developer who has completed the feasibility studies, identified the market and assembled the partners.

And somewhere there is a banker telling them:

“The project is good. But the risk is too high.”

That sentence has probably killed more African opportunities than a lack of African ingenuity ever has.

The answer should not be to pretend the risks do not exist.

The answer is to build financial mechanisms capable of distinguishing between bad projects and good projects in difficult markets.

That is a very different proposition.

Africa should not have to beg for capital

There is another mindset Africa needs to abandon.

The continent should not have to spend eternity travelling around the world asking investors to “believe in Africa.”

At some point, Africa must be able to say:

Here is the opportunity. Here is the data. Here is the structure. Here is the return. Here is the risk. Make your investment decision.

That is what mature capital markets do.

They do not require investors to fall in love with a continent.

They provide investors with information and instruments through which they can make rational decisions.

The LSF describes its ambition as moving beyond individual transactions and creating durable financial-market infrastructure for African economies.

That is the direction Africa should pursue.

The continent does not need another room full of people promising to invest.

It needs financial plumbing that makes investment possible at scale.

And if that plumbing can eventually connect global capital to African businesses, infrastructure and productive industries, the consequences could extend far beyond the financial markets.

Because the real prize is not an ETF.

The real prize is what happens when capital starts building an African industrial economy.

That is where the next conversation must begin.

World.title: Nigeria: Women Lead Campaign Against Open Defecation in Abuja
World.content:
Abuja — Women leaders from 16 communities in Kundu Ward of Kwali Area Council, Federal Capital Territory (FCT), have launched a community-driven campaign aimed at ending open defecation and improving hygiene practices across the ward.

The initiative, being implemented by the Resource Conservation and Development Initiative International (RCDI), seeks to harness the influence of women at the grassroots level to promote sanitation awareness, encourage toilet use and strengthen healthy behavioural practices within households and communities.

The intervention is being carried out under RCDI's ThriveFlow programme on women's health, dignity and community resilience, with support from ActionAid Nigeria through the Renewed Women's Voice and Leadership-Nigeria Project funded by Global Affairs Canada. The programme is being implemented in partnership with the FCT Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Agency (RUWASSA).

Speaking during the training of women sanitation champions in Kwali, RCDI Programme Officer, Mary-Jane Adaku Ukaegbu, said the project was designed to place women at the forefront of efforts to achieve Open Defecation Free (ODF) status in Kundu Ward.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

She said women play critical roles in household hygiene, childcare, water management and community mobilisation, making them effective advocates for behavioural change and improved sanitation practices.

According to Ukaegbu, 80 women drawn from the 16 participating communities will be trained and deployed to conduct house-to-house sensitisation campaigns, educate families on proper sanitation and monitor progress toward ODF attainment.

She explained that the women would serve as sanitation champions, encouraging residents to consistently use toilets, wash their hands at critical times, maintain clean surroundings and eliminate open defecation.

The programme also incorporates menstrual hygiene education and support for women and adolescent girls. As part of the intervention, reusable sanitary pad kits will be distributed to selected beneficiaries to improve menstrual hygiene management and promote dignity among women and girls.

The WASH Coordinator of Kwali Area Council, Mrs. Aminat Dada, commended RCDI, ActionAid Nigeria and FCT RUWASSA for supporting efforts to improve sanitation standards in the area council.

She noted that Kwali Area Council had continued to implement sensitisation programmes to encourage toilet construction and usage, adding that the women-led intervention would complement existing government efforts and accelerate progress towards ODF status.

Close 

Dada described the initiative as timely and urged traditional rulers, community leaders and residents to support the women champions in their mobilisation activities to ensure lasting behavioural change.

One of the participants, Mrs. Ruth Abu, Women Leader of Sadaba Community, said the training had equipped participants with practical knowledge on hygiene, environmental sanitation and disease prevention.

She pledged to take the lessons learnt back to her community and mobilise households to adopt healthier sanitation practices.

Stakeholders expressed confidence that the women-led approach would strengthen community ownership of sanitation programmes, improve public health outcomes and contribute significantly to the attainment of Open Defecation Free status across Kundu Ward and neighbouring communities.

World.title: Nigeria: Osun Election - Police Will Be Apolitical, Impartial - - IGP Disu
World.content:
The Inspector-General of Police (I-G), Mr Olatunji Disu, says the police will be professional, apolitical and impartial before, during and after the Aug. 15 governorship election in Osun.

Disu made the pledge on Friday in Abuja during a courtesy visit by representatives of Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) led by Mr Auwal Rafsajani, the Executive Director, Civil Society legislative Advocacy Centre (CISLAC).

The CSOs had visited the I-G to deliberate on issues of election security ahead of the Aug. 25 governorship election in Osun.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Disu said the meeting was a reflection of a shared commitment by the Nigeria Police Force and the CSOs to ensure a peaceful, credible, free and fair governorship election in Osun.

Disu said he was aware of the concerns expressed regarding election security, violence, voter intimidation, the activities of thugs and the neutrality of security agencies.

According to him, these concerns are legitimate and deserve to be addressed through dialogue, transparency and practical action.

"I want to assure Nigerians that the Nigeria Police Force has taken these concerns seriously and has put in place comprehensive security arrangements for the election.

"The Nigeria Police Force remains a professional, apolitical and impartial institution.

"We have no candidate, no political party and no vested interest in the outcome of the election other than ensuring that the lawful choice of the people prevails," he said.

He said all the police officers to be deployed on election duty had been reminded of their constitutional responsibility to uphold the law without fear or favour.

The I-G said the police would provide a secured environment for eligible voter to exercise their constitutional rights freely and without intimidation.

Disu said adequate personnel and operational assets had been deployed ahead of the election across the state.

According to him, intelligence gathering and threat assessments have been intensified to identify and neutralise potential threats before they escalate.

"We are working closely with other members of the InterAgency Consultative Committee on Election Security (ICCES), INEC and other relevant stakeholders to ensure effective coordination.

"Anyone found engaging in vote buying, voter intimidation, ballot box snatching, thuggery or any other electoral offence will be dealt with in accordance with the law, irrespective of political affiliation or status," he said.

The I-G call on political parties, candidates and their supporters to conduct themselves responsibly before, during and after the election, adding that, elections should be contests of ideas and policies, not violence or intimidation.

He said no political ambition was worth the loss of a single Nigerian life and therefore urged political leaders to prevail on their supporters to reject violence and respect the rule of law.

Disu urged the people of Osun to come out peacefully and confidently to cast their votes.

"Do not allow yourselves to be intimidated by rumours, misinformation or the actions of a few individuals who seek to undermine the democratic process.

"Where you observe any suspicious activity or violation of the law, promptly report to the nearest security personnel," he said.

Earlier, Rafsanjani said the visit was to foster collaborate with the Nigeria Police Force in the provision of election security and ensuring free fair and credible elections in the country.

He said the CSOs were worried about the political tensions in this country, adding the safety and security of Nigerians during elections are very important.

"Our work as CSOs is to ensure that we support the security agencies to be able to do their work without bias or partiality or anything that will create or erode confidence of Nigerians and international community.

"We believe that with your track record, you will be able to lead this very important national assignment that we are going to have come 2027.

"As CSOs, we have met, discussed, and have come up with some key important recommendations and suggestions to have free, fair, credible election that is free of violence, free of rancour," he said.

He said the recommendations and suggestions were could be achieved with the support of the various agencies and institutions.

IMr Samson Itodo, the Executive Director, Yiaga Africa, said the CSOs had independently monitored development around Osun governorship election over the past months.

Close 

"Whether it is incident tracking or public perception surveys or pre-election observation, we have consolidated some of the findings.

"We have also collected evidence from these different methodologies deployed to observe the pre-election environment.

"Our purpose here today is to share principal election security risks that are emerging from our observation and building up to the Osun elections," he said.

He said the Osun election was important because it would mirror the 2027 general election.

"Therefore, it has a lot of significance. It is a unique opportunity to inspire public trust, not just in the management of the election, but in election security," he said.

He said the electorate would want to see institutions demonstrate neutrality so they could have confidence in them.

He said the neutrality of the police and other security agencies was of particular concern to the public.

(NAN)

World.title: 'DEI queen': Virginia Dem's past embrace of far-left prosecutors unearthed
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Shannon Taylor, now the Democratic nominee in the race for Virginia’s First Congressional district, once endorsed progressive prosecutorial blueprints, advocating for less incarceration and more diversity as a Henrico County commonwealth attorney — some of the same "Democratic values" that ended in tragedy in other parts of Virginia.

Shortly after coming into the role in 2012, Taylor fired seven prosecutors under her.

"I stated publicly that the office needs to have more diversity and I’m going to keep to that public statement," Taylor said in an interview ahead of the firings.

Her track record is sparking criticism that she used her role to prioritize ideological and political views at the expense of public safety. It’s also clashing with portrayals from her campaign, highlighting her work as a tough-on-crime figure as she looks to win over a Republican-leaning district.

FORMER PROSECUTOR WHO ACCUSED TRUMP OF WEAPONIZING DOJ WINS DEM PRIMARY

Taylor highlighted her work as she topped a crowded field of Democratic candidates vying to challenge Republican incumbent Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Va.

"As Henrico’s top prosecutor for the last 14 years, Shannon has tried thousands of cases and put violent criminals, drug traffickers and abusers behind bars," Taylor states on her campaign website. "She has a record of shutting down fraudsters trying to take advantage of working families and locking up violent criminals who threaten our safety."

But that hasn’t always been the appearance she’s given.

After her seven firings, Taylor faced blowback for trying to hire a woman named Misty Whitehead as a police oversight prosecutor. However, before the role could be made official, social media posts from Whitehead surfaced that seemingly showed a pattern of attacking police.

Taylor faced backlash from the town’s county manager over her selected candidate.

"A county manager can’t tell a commonwealth’s attorney who to hire, but he can recommend whether or not local funds are included to supplement that salary. And in this case, I absolutely will not do it under any circumstances," County Manager John Vithoulkas said at the time.

Whitehead had a history of voicing concerns about police behavior and social justice that raised concerns for at least one county official, according to local reports.

Taylor defended her pick, telling local outlets that she believed the posts were "thoughtful analysis of the current events we are all living through."

Taylor also has ties to similarly-minded prosecutors in other counties — some of which entered the public eye recently due to tragic circumstances.

SPANBERGER'S ICE ROLLBACK TO BLAME FOR TODDLER KILLING, VIRGINIA 'HOTBED' OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CRIME: DHS

In Fairfax County, Virginia, news broke that Abdul Jalloh, a 32-year-old illegal alien from Sierra Leone, stabbed a Virginia resident to death at a bus stop despite over 30 prior arrests and a known tendency for violent behavior.

Jalloh’s criminal record included charges of rape, malicious wounding, assault, drug possession, identity theft, trespassing, larceny and firing a weapon.

Even so, prosecutor Steve Descano had dropped many of them, prompting concern and outrage from lawmakers.

"You dismissed the case, and it’s shameful," Rep. Brad Knott, R-N.C. said at a hearing where Descano was summoned to Congress to explain a series of similar cases.

Knott had been highlighting one such instance involving a child predator.

"When you dismiss a case, what happens to that defendant? He walks free. A disgusting, perverted individual preying on children, that you dismissed," Knott said.

Long before Descano’s time in the spotlight, Taylor had endorsed Descano, supporting his bid to become county prosecutor in 2019, citing shared outlooks.

"I am excited to endorse Steve Descano for Fairfax County’s Commonwealth’s Attorney because I know he will prioritize the same Democratic values we all share, making Fairfax a safe and just place for everyone and I am looking forward to working with him," Taylor wrote.

Taylor and Descano would go on to champion their shared values in a 2021 letter to the Biden Administration.

In it, the two joined 100 other district and county attorneys in championing a set of "21 principles for the 21st-Century prosecutor." The authors claimed that "tough on crime policies" had been "anathema to justice," championed an end to mandatory minimums and three-strike laws, advocated for taking immigration status into consideration when negotiating sentences and plea deals, and opposed calling rapists "rapists," drug dealers "drug dealers," and convicted criminals "felons" or "inmates."

"A number of elected reform-minded prosecutors are boldly redefining what it means to be a prosecutor," the letter states.

OKLAHOMA TEEN ACCUSED OF RAPING TWO GIRLS WALKS FREE; DA FURIOUSLY CALLS IN FEDS: ‘MADE MY BLOOD BOIL’

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

At least one Republican onlooker blasted Taylor’s record.

"She spent her time reshaping the prosecutor's office around identity politics, pushing a far-left agenda that put woke activism ahead of public safety, and fighting to turn Virginia into a far-left hellscape," Emma Hall, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee (RNC), said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Instead of prosecuting criminals and making Virginia safer, DEI queen Shannon Taylor chose to be a diversity, equity, and inclusion consultant."

Having secured the Democratic nomination, Taylor now heads to the general election on Nov. 3. Wittman, the district’s incumbent, last won re-election in 2024 in a 56.3% to 43.5% victory over Democratic challenger Leslie Mehta, an attorney.

World.title: Lawyer-turned-social media sensation is betting it all on God, love and grief
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

In a digital landscape often dominated by outrage, carefully curated perfection and fleeting trends, Davide De Pierro has built an audience by doing something refreshingly simple: telling honest stories about his experiences that make people feel seen. The New Jersey attorney-turned-digital creator joined Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview to discuss why authenticity — not algorithms — has become his greatest asset in a world where millions of people (six million who follow De Pierro, to be exact) are still searching for genuine human connection.

The 38-year-old was born in New Jersey and spent his early years in Italy before returning to Jersey City, where he still lives today. Though he continues to practice law at a family firm with his father and brother in Bloomfield, his career took a turn when he found success on TikTok and Instagram — pulling viewers in with his sometimes sarcastic, always profound reflections on work, life, love and faith.

"Being a person has been the same, always. What's changed is what you're wearing and what technology you're using," De Pierro said. "But really, I'm just talking about the human condition."

The self-described "half Italian/half Jersey boy" is now poised to re-release his self-published audiobook with HarperCollins in both a new audio edition and a hardcover version. The novel, "The Letters I Never Sent," will also heavily feature in his upcoming international tour, which will include stand-up comedy, live readings of excerpts from his book, a Q&A session and a meet-and-greet.

The world as seen from Davide's car

De Pierro is best known for his single-shot vlogs taken in his car, branded with captions like, "If I saw an alien I wouldn't even care honestly I got too much going on right now," "Started using my own money and realized my mom was right, we do have food at home," and "No matter what I have God."

On the heels of his life-changing success, De Pierro has remained humble — in fact, when asked what he believed made him so popular on social media, he found himself at a loss for words.

CANCEL ME IF YOU CAN: DAVE PORTNOY TAKES AIM AT CANCEL CULTURE CRITICS WHO 'ALREADY DECIDED' THE VERDICT

"I don't know why people are following me. I mean, I know what I do. I go on there and I talk about stuff. And maybe it's, in part, it could be the delivery. In part, it could be the actual language. In part, it could be the way my face looks in the car. I don't know. But I think it just happened."

"I'm happy that I won this little social media lottery, because otherwise I wouldn't be able to put my book out there and go on tour and meet people and have fun. And I'd be stuck in the law office all the time... Now I have to leave for other reasons, so my father permits me to go out and do a tour," he joked.

The creator described his success as "accidental" and said there was no "influencer strategy." Ironically, he used to consider himself "chronically offline."

"I was 37 years old. So, you know, I felt like that ship had sailed. I wasn't going to go dance on TikTok. Probably not for the best."

He credited an ex-girlfriend with the initial idea of posting his reflections on the internet.

"I thought that was a ridiculous idea. But I eventually took her advice, especially after the breakup — that's when men always take all the good advice from their exes. And it worked. And it kept working."

Authentic exhaustion

Millennials — the generation to which De Pierro proudly belongs — have been experiencing burnout for years, with research reported from Gallup to even the National Institutes of Health supporting the claim.



De Pierro told Fox News Digital he often posts about "workplace malaise," dating fatigue, and other kinds of exhaustion because he finds it's not just relatable, it's real.



"I think that you can't fake the authenticity of exhaustion. I think the relatability is that it's real. And so I am a person who has worked and who has gone through relationship problems. I'm not an inexperienced, younger man who's just kind of making things up that might be relatable. And I guess you just can't fabricate that kind of authenticity," said De Pierro, musing on how what some might call his late arrival to social media makes him stand out from other career influencers.

"The authenticity is not special, this isn't unique to me. I'm just describing what we all go through, but you have to go through it first. And so, certainly, there is an advantage to being a content creator in your late 30s if you're going to be talking about the struggles of being alive."

The TikToker pointed to the prolific nature and timelessness of William Shakespeare as an example of connection.

"What does he have in common with me, a 15th century English guy?" he posited in the wide-ranging interview. "In reality, he has everything in common with you, because he's a human being."

COMEDIAN DES BISHOP ON HOW AMERICA MADE HIM FUNNIER AND HIS 'HEALTHY COLLABORATION' WITH WIFE HANNAH BERNER

De Pierro's own audience is further evidence of this hypothesis, he said.

"My following is really a social experiment, if you look at it. I mean, there are people from all over the world and on all different spectrums. And I wonder if they know that they're following the same person, because I'm just talking about being a person. And everyone can relate to the experiences that we all go through every day, which are universal."

Attorney by day, influencer by night, Italian 24/7

As a working attorney, De Pierro made it clear that his online ponderings should not be taken as legal advice.

"I would never call what I'm doing online advice. Especially being a lawyer, I'm so afraid of the word ‘advice.’ We never advise you unless you are our client."

"I don't want people to listen to it as advice. I'm not an expert on anything. I'm sharing observations, sharing experiences, sharing thoughts, but certainly not advice. No, don't do anything I say," he joked.

VIRAL BOY BAND INSISTS IT'S REAL AS IMMIGRATION FIGHT PUTS INTERNET FAME TO GOVERNMENT TEST

He attributed his contemplative style more to his Italian-American heritage than to his career in law, labeling Italians as "natural storytellers" and "expert complainers."

"I think it's part of the Italian identity to be a little bit playfully pessimistic. There might be even a superstition in that. You don't want to assume success."

"And so, I think that that plays into my character and my personality even in my videos. There's an exhaustion, there's a playful sense of pessimism there sometimes. A negativity almost. But it hides a more profound, I think, joy and optimism that Italians do have."

Despite referring to his portrayal in his social media videos as a "character," De Pierro told Fox News Digital that in the age-old Instagram vs. Reality — a concept that contrasts real-life with people's online personas — the lawyer-turned-comedian remains authentically himself.

"I mean, we all contain multitudes, right? So I think one of my personalities involves what I do in the car... All these little accents and modes of speaking are real to me. It depends on who I'm with. If I'm with my Jersey City friends, it's going to sound like "Goodfellas." But if I'm in a court of law, then I have to rein in it a little bit."



Add professional code-switcher to his growing list of accolades.

Public thoughts, private life

Despite often baring his soul online, De Pierro said sharing his thoughts for all the world to see hasn't affected his personal life much — yet.

"It is real, it is authentic, and so it doesn't affect my life because I'm already being myself on camera. So it's not like I'm suddenly unrecognizable to my friends and family, they know that guy intimately," De Pierro maintained.

"But on the other hand — I'm not dating much — but I suspect that it will affect my dating, because I think people are starting to get the impression that I'm this enlightened man, and maybe they're going to have expectations of me in dating that are unrealistic.

"I'm just as much of an idiot as the men that I talk about in my videos."

JEFF FOXWORTHY PULLS BACK THE CURTAIN ON COMEDY'S CREATIVE PROCESS FOR WHAT COULD BE HIS LAST SPECIAL

It is always easier to give advice than to take it, he added.

"I'm still a person. And also, by the way, that wisdom is for everyone else. I'm just good at giving other people advice as opposed to living it myself. I've always been that friend that's really good at telling you what's wrong with you. But if I have to apply it to my own life, I'm probably going to fail nine times out of ten."

For someone who speaks openly about relationships and the roller coaster of emotions they bring, the Heartbreak Heartthrob reveals relatively little about the concrete details of his private life.

That's intentional.

"What's funny about all this is that I'm incredibly public in the sense that I am constantly sharing my thoughts, but I'm almost never sharing my life. I'm just in the car. No one knows where I live. No one's ever seen my family. No one has ever seen the lower half of my body. So I'm extremely private while at the same time having a therapy session in my car," De Pierro told Fox News Digital.

'No matter what, I have God'

De Pierro now speaks openly about many subjects with his growing following, but there is one he had to work his way up to: his faith.



He told Fox News Digital he is "100%" a Christian man, having gone to church every Sunday with his family all his life.

"My faith plays a huge role in my personal life. And so it was just a natural transition for me. As soon as I saw that I had this following and this kind of engagement, I thought, 'Wow, this is a perfect opportunity to speak about something that's really important to me.'"

De Pierro was inspired by the story of his grandfather, who died shortly after De Pierro was born.

FROM ‘SCREAM’ TO STREAM: JAMIE KENNEDY REVEALS HOW HOLLYWOOD LOST ITS WAY AND WHY HE WON'T GIVE UP ON LA

"He was a preacher, and apparently — at least from the stories I've been told — a beloved man in the very small community that he lived and worked in. And a part of me thought, 'Here was this incredible man that I never met who only was able to speak to a few hundred people, maybe a thousand, over the course of his life.'"

"So I saw the opportunity that I had, and I thought to myself, 'Here I am, not even a tenth of the man that my grandfather was. And I have the opportunity to speak to millions of people at times. I have to use this opportunity, even if I could just plant a little seed of faith in these invisible people that are watching me from wherever they may be.'"

He has received no shortage of warm messages from viewers saying his posts have touched them and even helped them through hard times.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"And that's gratifying, too, of course, to feel like you're doing something more than just entertaining. Because it's great to get people to laugh and to get to feel seen and understood."

"But if you could also help people in a way that, again — it sounds crazy to me. I mean, I don't think that anything I'm doing is particularly helpful. But when I see those messages, I believe them. If they felt that way, then it's gratifying to know that I'm doing something, hopefully, useful."



HarperCollins imprint Hanover Square Press announced Monday it is set to publish De Pierro's debut novel, "The Letters I Never Sent," now on pre-sale and set for print and ebook publication on December 8, 2026. The audiobook version, De Pierro told FOX, will be available this October. Additionally, he will embark on his first-ever stand-up tour beginning late September.



The writer, performer, and viral content creator also shared his biggest icks and ticks, what he really thinks of modern dating, and the best advice he's ever received with Fox News Digital. But when asked if he had one final message he'd want to leave behind for his followers, it's a sentiment as refreshingly simple as he is: "God loves you."

World.title: Carmen Electra says 'Baywatch' pushed boundaries without crossing the line: 'It wasn't porn'
World.content:

Carmen Electra is reminiscing about her days starring in the original "Baywatch."

In a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 54-year-old "Nation's Dumbest" contestant discussed the success of the original series, saying, all "the cast members made it special."

"It's hard to replace Pamela [Anderson] and Yasmine [Bleeth] and all those people. And there was just a certain tone. I don't know how to explain it," she said. "It had a certain tone to it that it was just such a fantasy, and maybe it was the first time on television you could see so much skin because we really were playing lifeguards right so we could be in these skimpy outfits."

She went on to say that the show possibly left people thinking, "Oh my God, what is this? We can see nipples."

BROOKS NADER SIZZLES IN ICONIC RED SWIMSUIT AS SHE SHARES BEHIND THE SCENES SNAPS FROM 'BAYWATCH' REBOOT SET

"And it wasn't porn. You know, what I mean? They didn't have to sneak away and find a VHS tape to like, sneak and put in. You can watch this," she added. "You can also learn something. Because, we heard from a lot of people, a lot of fans out there, that they learned so much watching the show."

Electra credited the show's sexy nature as one of the reasons it became the global phenomenon it is, saying they were "sometimes trying to be sexy, sometimes not trying to be sexy" and that "all of a sudden, you get these guys on there with these gorgeous bodies."

In addition to the sexy aspect of the show, Electra attributed its success to the fact that fans could learn something from the show, including how to give CPR, adding she also "learned how to give CPR," and joked, "I could save someone right now if I needed to."

The actress and model joined the show in 1997 for its eighth season, after gaining exposure from posing for Playboy in a 1996 pictorial.

CLICK HERE TO 

In terms of returning for the new reboot of the series, Electra is open to putting on the iconic red one-piece once again, since her former love interest on the show, David Chokachi has signed on to return.

"I could do something. Come in, have another love scene with David Chokachi. Just something really cute and fun. I would be down to get into the water again," she said. "I think it would be fun it makes sense I was David Chokachi's love interest way back then. I think it would be really fun and why not, you know?"

His character, Cody Madison, is now the owner of a beachside bar, The Shoreline, and also acts as a mentor to the younger new lifeguards.

"I think it would be so cool if I just came in for an episode to surprise him and say hi. They fall in love again, who knows," Electra said.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

One thing the actress is not willing to go through again is "the schooling that I did when I first joined the cast," noting, "that was really tough."

Following her time on "Baywatch," Electra had a successful career in both film and television, appearing in films such as "Scary Movie," "Cheaper by the Dozen 2," "Meet the Spartans" and others.

She also recently appeared as a contestant on "Nation's Dumbest," a new celebrity competition show. She told Fox News Digital she originally didn't want to do it, saying, "I didn't pay attention in school" and that she "didn't have a good feeling about it."

"Fox kept getting on the phone. They're like, it's gonna be so easy. It's gonna be fun. It's like acting think of it as an acting role," she said. "Once I was not there anymore, I kind of missed it...and there was a lot of fun. I did miss the cast a lot but yeah, I think we were all sitting there going, 'What? Why the hell did we subject ourselves to be on this show?'"

"I definitely had a lot of anxiety and I would freeze. As soon as we would have to rush and say something, answer a question really fast or there was something weird we had to do," she added. "It could be very stressful and I would freeze."

When it came to a moment that still haunts her, Electra couldn't believe she couldn't remember what BBL stood for, saying the producers threw in "a really easy question that she's gonna get and I got it wrong. I couldn't believe it."

The show features celebrity contestants who undergo pop quizzes and physical challenges with the ultimate goal of being eliminated as early as possible, in order to avoid being the last one standing and being named the nation's dumbest.

Electra was ultimately eliminated after the fourth episode of the show, which aired on Aug. 5.

World.title: $20 avocado toast fuels outrage as travelers say airport food prices are out of control
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Travelers are increasingly questioning why a quick bite at the airport can come with a restaurant-level price tag, according to several reports.

A recent viral post on X added to the frustration after a traveler slammed a nearly $20 avocado toast purchased at an airport in the South.

The traveler said the $19.64 breakfast was supposed to include toasted sprout bread, avocado, extra virgin olive oil, bacon and crushed red pepper — but many commenters said the dish looked far less appetizing than the price suggested.

CROWDED AIRPORT LOUNGES FORCE AIRLINES TO RETHINK FUTURE OF TRAVEL PERKS FOR FLIERS

California chef and restaurateur Andrew Gruel looked at photos of the avocado toast and said he was not impressed.

"It [is] probably sold as avocado purée. ... They took a disposable plastic knife, and they wiped it on a piece of toast," Gruel told Fox News Digital in an interview.

"But it doesn't surprise me, and I don't put it on the actual worker who made that," he added.

AIRPORT LOUNGE CHAOS GOES VIRAL AS KIDS RUN WILD AND PASSENGERS DITCH BASIC ETIQUETTE

Gruel believes the quality of food at airports is going down as the prices are going up.

"Nowadays, all you're getting is just prepackaged, co-packed foods at airports," he said.

"You'll have one vendor that's going to prepackage sandwiches and wraps and hard-boiled eggs, and maybe some meat and cheese platters," he added.

Gruel said he believes much of the food at sit-down restaurants in airports is "overpriced garbage."

THE BIGGEST FOOD AND DRINK MISTAKES TRAVELERS MAKE ON FLIGHTS, EXPERTS WARN

"That is rarely cooked from scratch," he said. But "I don't want to say that there's no good food at airports."

Texas-based travel industry expert and author of the blog "View From the Wing" told Fox News Digital that the issue goes well beyond one expensive breakfast.

Airport restaurants contend with higher rents, limited storage space, stricter security requirements for deliveries and higher labor costs, all of which contribute to higher menu prices, Leff and Gruel said. "It's expensive to operate there," Leff said.

CO-PILOT BECOMES SICK MIDAIR AS CREW ILLNESS REPORTS EMERGE AFTER OVERNIGHT LAYOVER

He added that some airports advertise "street pricing," but the wording isn't always clear.

"They never really tell you which street," Leff said.

The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey even allows airport concessionaires to charge up to 15% more than comparable off-airport "street prices," according to the official Port Authority of New York and New Jersey Concessionaire Street Pricing Standards and Procedures Manual.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"More expensive, not as good," Leff said about all airport food in general.

The pricey avocado toast is far from the only expensive item travelers find at airport restaurants.

A burger at Paris Cafe in New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport costs $34, according to the restaurant's online menu.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Barney's Beanery at Los Angeles International Airport charges $21.30 for its Barney Breakfast, which includes eggs, hash browns and toast, according to the airport's Shop & Dine website.

"Even if you just want a bottle of water, you're paying $5 or $6 for a cheap bottle," Gruel said. "That's where they're making their money."

The viral avocado post prompted travelers to share their own frustrations.

"Airport food prices are absolutely out of control," one Reddit user wrote.

"Even if you just want a bottle of water, you're paying $5 or $6 for a cheap bottle."

"Breakfast burrito to go ... $36 bucks. I thought maybe I broke a window or something, and they added that on," one Reddit user quipped.

CLICK HERE TO 

While some airport lounges offer quality meals, Leff said he wouldn't recommend purchasing lounge access just for the food.

Gruel agreed. "I'd say be careful of the airport lounge food because, most of the time, it's just sitting out there, you know, under a sneeze guard and everybody's putting their hands all over it," he said.

Leff suggested eating before arriving at the airport or bringing food from home.

Additional advice: Look for sandwiches.

"I would never spend $25 on pizza like that. But I've actually had a few good sandwiches at airports," Gruel said.

He added, "Frontega Grill, which is Rick Bailey's shop in Chicago airport — they make a pretty good sandwich. Granted, it's $25 for a sandwich, maybe $20, but it's a good quality product."

British political commentator and Mideast expert, Tom Gross, told Fox News Digital: "Europe’s ruling classes need to be honest. It is not racist to point out the obvious: that most terrorism in Western Europe today is being fueled by radical Islamic mosques and teachers."

GERMAN OFFICIALS WANT TO KNOW WHY BERLIN ATTACK SUSPECT WAS FREE DESPITE ALLEGED ISIS SUPPORT

He added, "Leaders in Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Egypt acknowledge this. Why can’t Western leaders?"

Gross said, "Politicians such as new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, London Mayor Sadiq Khan and Spanish PM Pedro Sanchez, need to stop fueling the propaganda of radical Muslims by implying that there has been some kind of genocide against Muslims in Gaza, when there has been nothing of the sort."

He continued, "If they really want to help push back radical Islam, European leaders should be assisting, not criticizing, those in Washington and elsewhere calling for the downfall of Iran’s Islamic dictatorship."

In April, the U.K. raised its national terror threat level to "severe" following an antisemitic attack in London when a Somali immigrant stabbed two men. A "Severe" warning, according to authorities means another terrorist attack is considered "highly likely" in the next six months.

A spokesperson for London’s Mayor Khan told Fox News Digital that "The Mayor has invested £16 million (approxmiately $21.5 million) – more than any other Mayor – to support grassroots community groups to stand up to hate and intolerance. GERMAN OFFICIALS WARN ISLAMIST, FAR-LEFT RHETORIC DRIVING SPIKE IN ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS

Late last month, the alleged Islamist State terrorist, the 21-year-old German-Lebanese man, Abdul Ballout, drove a van into the Berlin Pride Parade event, murdering one woman and injuring nearly 30 people. The German authorities had released Ballout despite his recent conviction related to supporting the Islamic State.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told public broadcaster ZDF during an interview that in light of the 21-year-old suspect's conviction and record of backing the Islamic State, it did not make sense that the man was roaming free.

"You can assume that it certainly would have made sense to put this person in custody," he noted.

Khan’s spokesperson also cited an X Post from the Mayor following the Berlin Pride attack: "My thoughts are with everyone affected by the horrific attack in Berlin and their families. This appalling act of violence has no place in our society. London stands in solidarity with Berlin’s LGBTQ+ community. This is why Pride matters. Those who seek to spread hatred and division will never win."

SCATHING REPORT CALLS ON US TO LABEL ISLAMIST GROUP INFILTRATING ALL ASPECTS OF AMERICAN LIFE AS TERRORIST ORG

A new report by Germany’s federal intelligence that documents threats to the constitutional order estimates that there are roughly about 28,000 members of Germany’s Islamist scene. Approximately 9,110 are currently assessed to have an "orientation to violence. "The type of violence is defined as jihadi violence."

Germany’s federal interior ministry, which publishes the annual domestic intelligence threat report, notes that crimes attributed to "religious ideology" have climbed from 134 in 2022 to 998 last year. Radical Islamist crimes are reportedly understood to make up the main portion of the "religious ideology" category.

Germany’s neighbor, France, experienced another stabbing just days after the attack in Germany. A suspect reportedly stabbed three women in Paris and declared as people captured him after the attack, "it is Allah who commanded me."

Vidino said, "The incident in Paris it seems one of the cases" regarding the how an attack is classified: "Is it terrorism? Is it a crazy guy? Often times, Europeans play down the ideological motive and cite mental health. Some countries tend to do it more than others. Most Europeans go for downplaying of the ideological component."

AMERICAN ‘JIHAD’ FUELED BY 'RISKY SOURCE' INSIDE US BORDERS, WARNS NATIONAL SECURITY EXPERT

Austria’s intelligence agency announced in May on its website that it arrested a group of suspected Islamist terrorists, which included five males aged between 14 and 45 and one 16-year-old female. "The individuals concerned are suspected of having committed offenses related to Islamist extremism and terrorism in Austria, for example through membership of a terrorist organization, incitement to terrorist offenses, dissemination of IS [Islamic State] propaganda, and approval of terrorist offenses," wrote the Austrian agency.

In June, Swedish authorities arrested a teenage boy who pledged allegiance to the Islamist State and idolized suicide bombers, according to Swedish media. He issued death threats to students at school and showed pictures of beheaded people.

Nervana Mahmoud, a British-Egyptian medical doctor who has written extensively about Islamist terrorism and indoctrination, told Fox News Digital that "The current challenge facing Europe is, in many ways, a battle over Islamist extremism and its place within Western societies. To address the threat at its source, European governments need to focus on preventing radicalization and disrupting foreign funding and ideological networks that fuel extremist movements. Without tackling these root causes, the risk of future terrorist attacks will remain."

SENATE CLEARS WAY FOR TRUMP'S TOP SPY AS KEY ANTI-TERROR PROGRAM REMAINS IN LIMBO

Mahmoud said, "The United States should learn from Europe’s experience rather than simply criticize it. It has an opportunity to strengthen prevention efforts early by fostering a shared American identity within immigrant communities, disrupting foreign funding that may promote extremist influence through universities and think tanks, and working with Muslim Americans who reject Islamism and uphold democratic values. Long-term success will require not only strong security measures but also sustained efforts to prevent radicalization before it takes hold."

The United Kingdom’s judicial system recorded a series of convictions of Islamist terrorists in July. Abdullah Bin Yasir was imprisoned for two and a half years after admitting he had bomb-making guides linked to an Islamic State-aligned entity. The construction of bomb material was designed to carry out a terrorist attack.

Late last month, in Wigston, Britain, the authorities arrested a 27-year-old man for supporting the Islamic State.

According to the Crown Prosecution Service, the 31-year-old Mohammad Bashir "pleaded guilty to preparing an act of terrorism" against a British defense target.

A spokesperson for the British Home Office told Fox News Digital, "The United Kingdom has one of the most robust counter-terrorism systems in the world. We remain committed to ensuring our Police and Security Services have the tools and powers they need to prevent the spread of violent ideologies and keep the country safe."

UK PINS STRING OF ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS ON IRAN-LINKED GROUP, BANS IRGC

The spokesperson added, "This includes a wide range of terrorist offenses and specialized powers designed to risk, support prosecution, and strengthen management of terrorist offenders. Islamist terrorism remains the primary domestic threat to the United Kingdom, accounting for roughly three quarters of the Security Service’s casework."

Northern continental Europe is also facing a serious Jihadi terrorist threat. According to a late May Danish Security and Intelligence Service statement, the "CTA [Center for Terror Analysis in Denmark] assesses that the terrorist threat from militant Islamists remains at the level of significant."

Vidino said there has been a silver lining since the outbreak of the Islamic State terrorist attacks in Europe. "I would say I do think most European law enforcement agencies and security forces have gotten better over the years. When the big ISIS radicalization took place, small countries were completely unprepared to deal with it." He cited Switzerland, Austria and the Scandinavian countries.

"They did not have legal capabilities and mindset. That has changed and it is not perfect."
