As the rain subsided, the grounds crew scrambled to prepare the field. Players stepped in to help roll up the tarp covering the field as the sold-out crowd settled into damp seats.

Meanwhile, on the third base line, 3-year-old Lenore Wooten took in the view of the field. "She'll never know this was never not a thing," said her mother, Jess.

Jaclyn Licht is a freelance photographer based in Brooklyn, N.Y. Find more of her work on her website, JaclynLicht.com, or on Instagram, at @shwaclyn.

World.title: Federal funds can't be used to give test strips to drug users, raising overdose fears
World.content:
Federal funds can't be used to give test strips to drug users, raising overdose fears

toggle caption Bebeto Matthews/AP Photo

Last year, Baltimore had three mass overdose incidents in the span of three months in its Penn North neighborhood.

In one incident, more than two dozen people were hospitalized after many were found unresponsive, lying in the streets or on sidewalks. No one died, but some came close.

This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News.

Follow-up testing found that the street drugs contained high levels of N-methylclonazepam, a benzodiazepine that operates similarly to Xanax or Valium.

Like opioids, benzodiazepines suppress breathing. When they're combined, the risk of overdose goes up. And benzodiazepines don't respond to opioid overdose reversal drugs.

Afterward, the Baltimore Harm Reduction Coalition created test strips specifically for benzodiazepines. The group distributed them — along with test strips that identify other harmful adulterants, such as fentanyl, xylazine, and medetomidine — at clinics and neighborhood events.

Sponsor Message

The strips, available at no cost, can also be found in bars and spread out on street corners. People testing drugs mix a small amount with water and then dip a test strip into the liquid. The strip will change color if it identifies an adulterant.

"Nobody really knows what they're getting whenever they're getting stuff off of the street," said Candy Kerr, a spokesperson for the coalition. "Having the test strips available for the general public gives them the option to move slower if they're going to use whatever they're going to use."

But a new federal policy could make it harder for organizations such as Kerr's to give out the test strips, and they're worried that overdoses could increase.

In late April, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration banned the use of federal grants for distributing strips to the public and for some other harm reduction practices that have been credited with saving lives. Test strips have been used for nearly 10 years to identify adulterants.

toggle caption Scott Muacione

/WYPR

A letter sent to local health departments and nonprofits that provide addiction services explained that the Trump administration believes those harm reduction practices "facilitate illicit drug use and are incompatible with Federal laws."

Sponsor Message

According to the letter, grants from the Department of Health and Human Services also cannot be used for programs that support the use of clean needles or drug paraphernalia such as pipes, or to fund a type of specialized hotline that people can call while taking drugs, so someone is aware and can call for help if they overdose.

The Trump administration wants to focus more on other techniques, such as giving out naloxone, an overdose reversal drug available as a nasal spray, according to Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokesperson.

"It is critical that federal funding provided by the American taxpayer goes to effective, common-sense solutions that have been proven to save lives and keep people out of an endless cycle of addiction and moves them into a life of recovery," she said.

toggle caption Scott Maucione/WYPR

The new policy does not prohibit federal funds from being used to purchase test strips for use by law enforcement officers, public health officials, EMTs, or other medical professionals.

That creates an important exception for government agencies that test drugs and send out regular reports on what adulterants are saturating the drug supply in certain locations.

Still, Yngvild Olsen, who oversaw SAMHSA's Center for Substance Abuse Treatment in the Biden and Trump administrations, says there is a substantial body of evidence that shows giving test strips to people who use drugs can change behavior.

"There's some people deciding not to use the substances, some people deciding to reduce, to use less, or take other types of precautions, including naloxone, and making sure that there are people around that can actually then help in the case of an overdose," Olsen said.

toggle caption Scott Maucione/

WYPR



Kerr said the best approach would be to continue to promote the use of test strips while also continuing to give out lifesaving medications like naloxone. She believes that working on all fronts has helped lead to Baltimore's decline in overdose deaths, which havedropped more than 40% since 2023.

Sponsor Message

Under the new policy, nonprofits will still be able to hand out test strips, but they will have to find other funding for that work, which Kerr finds worrisome.

"We've been making these strides forward because we've had these things, because we've been funded," she said. "We're going to have to pull money from other places."

To pay for the test strips, Kerr said, the Baltimore Harm Reduction Coalition will have to cut back on services such as giving out hygiene and wound care kits. But she said that option is better than risking another mass overdose in Baltimore — or allowing even just one preventable fatality.

This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with WYPR and KFF Health News.

World.title: Private prisons announce $1.4 billion in revenue as immigration detentions climb
World.content:
Private prisons announce $1.4 billion in revenue as immigration detentions climb

toggle caption Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images

America's two largest private prison companies, CoreCivic and GEO Group, are reporting a combined $1.4 billion in quarterly revenue over the spring as immigration detention closes in on record levels.

Those revenues announced Thursday do not include net proceeds of $1.6 billion made by CoreCivic after the recent sale of four of their facilities to the Department of Homeland Security. Patrick Swindle, CoreCivic's President and CEO, told investors on an earnings call that that works out to an average rate of $307,000 per bed.

The earnings — from April through June of this year — come as the U.S. is holding almost 66,000 people in immigration detention , nearing record levels not seen since January, according to Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, a nonpartisan research center. Both companies say they're also finding other revenue opportunities, like ankle monitors for Haitian immigrants who recently lost their protected immigration status.

Sponsor Message

Swindle said that CoreCivic's total revenue went up by just over 27% this spring compared to the same quarter last year, for a total of $684.9 million. CoreCivic exceeded expectations in a period that included the government shutdown, Swindle said. This was accomplished in part by lowering operating costs — meaning the business of detaining people is becoming cheaper — and because of more people being put in detention.

CoreCivic's sales of detention centers to the government won't be reflected until next quarter — but they are part of a larger strategy to meet President Trump's goal of having 100,000 people in detention at once. CoreCivic made a deal to continue operating the detention centers and also hopes to build more. Meanwhile, GEO Group says they're also in talks to do the same.

GEO Group's Trump administration ties

GEO Group CEO George Zoley said in his company's earnings call also on Thursday that thanks to 2025 contracts, total revenues are up to $732.1 million — an increase of nearly $96 million or 15% — over the same period last year.

GEO Group's government ties run deep. Former GEO Group executive David Venturella is the acting director of ICE. In a recent letter, he told lawmakers he has divested his GEO Group stock.

toggle caption Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images North America

President Trump's border czar Tom Homan was also a paid consultant for GEO Group before joining the government, and former Attorney General Pam Bondi lobbied for GEO Group before she was appointed.

Sponsor Message

President Trump also has financial stakes in the two companies, according to Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics. An analysis of Trump's most recent financial disclosure by CREW last month found that the president's brokers have made 29 trades of private prison stocks since he returned to office. According to the study, the first purchases were made on the 10th day of his second term. The total amount bought and sold was in the hundreds of thousands of dollars split between GEO Group and CoreCivic.

More revenue streams

In Thursday's call, GEO Group noted that their ankle monitoring sales are up. The electronic devices are part of the Intensive Supervision Appearance Program contract it has with ICE, along with smartwatches and the SmartLink phone app that help the government keep tabs on immigrants outside of detention, Zoley said.

Zoley also told investors that GPS-tracking ankle monitors in particular will likely keep climbing now that Temporary Protected Status for Haitian immigrants has ended.

"Because of this new policy shift as to who will be subject to this immigration enforcement like … the Haitians, we could see a significant increase in the number of people in the ISAP program," Zoley said, adding "most of them, we believe, would be placed under the ankle monitoring supervision." He noted that "the app is far less expensive than the ankle monitors."

World.title: Data centers are a political issue crossing party lines, driving voters to candidates
World.content:
Data centers are a political issue crossing party lines, driving voters to candidates

toggle caption Mario Tama/Getty Images

Two months after OpenAI and Oracle broke ground on a massive data center campus in Saline Township, Michigan, Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed held a rally in front of the site, using the controversial project as a backdrop for his insurgent campaign.

"I stand with local and state elected officials saying that we cannot approve any more of these until we have federal-level guardrails," said El-Sayed with community activists standing by his side.

Data centers, the giant, windowless, server-filled buildings are the backbone of the AI boom. They are also deeply unpopular. A Gallup poll from earlier this year found 7 in 10 Americans oppose the construction of an AI data center in their area. So, perhaps it's not a surprise that candidates across the political spectrum are trying to tap into the backlash.

Sponsor Message

El-Sayed narrowly won his primary earlier this week, and while data centers weren't the centerpiece of his pitch to voters, they do tie into key themes of his campaign — populist economics and getting money out of politics.

"Unless and until we protect local communities from the power of corrupting money and politics, we're going to continue to see projects like this get pushed on to local communities despite themselves," El-Sayed said.

In Ohio, the Republican nominee for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy, released an "Ohioans-first data center pledge" this week, which called for legislation and, until it passes, a moratorium on data center construction in the state.

"A top concern I hear from Ohioans across our state — second only to property taxes — is the accelerating pace of data center expansion," he said in a statement released by his campaign. "The data center industry has badly failed to earn the trust of millions of everyday Ohioans."

Among the complaints he said he has heard are rising electric bills, noise, pollution and "the absence of clearly defined economic benefits for Ohio families." Ramaswamy even called for data center companies to cover the power bills of people who live nearby.

This followed Ohio Democratic candidate for governor Amy Acton's plan for a "conditional moratorium" on data centers released last month along with a broadside that "Ohio cannot trust Vivek Ramaswamy to protect communities from his fellow big-tech billionaires."

toggle caption Thomas Simonetti/AFP via Getty Images

In Michigan's 7th Congressional District, Democrat William Lawrence didn't set out to campaign against data centers. But it quickly became a key plank in his platform because voters kept bringing it up to him.

Sponsor Message

"It wasn't something that I expected to be part of the campaign last August because data centers weren't on our radar," said Lawrence, who won in a primary against two more moderate Democrats. "But there have been four data centers proposed in the district since I declared my candidacy."

In Wisconsin, calling for a moratorium on data center construction has helped Francesca Hong build a broad coalition as she runs for the Democratic nomination for governor. She talks about data centers a lot and voters are noticing.

"It's time to press control+alt+delete to put a stop to this AI data center crisis, a full moratorium until we have the new regulations we need to protect our energy costs, our economy, our environment," Hong said in a video released by her campaign.

Voting ends Tuesday in Wisconsin and recent polls show Hong favored to win.

At a recent Hong campaign event, supporter Peggy McCrumb didn't hesitate when asked why she backs the candidate.

"I don't think anyone wants data centers, and she's the only one who stands up against it," McCrumb said. "So she's actually listening to what people want."

Hong is a democratic socialist. But this issue cuts through the usual partisan divides, says Amanda Litman, the founder of Run For Something, which works with Democrats running for state and local office.

She says these data centers are the most tangible, physical representation of the threat people perceive from AI, whether it's higher energy prices or making jobs obsolete.

"We're hearing it from urban, from rural, from suburban," Litman said of data center anxiety. "We're hearing it in red states, blue states, purple states. It's all kinds of communities, which I think is really speaking to how visceral people feel this is coming for them."

World.title: Senate votes to confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general
World.content:
Senate votes to confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general

toggle caption Eric Lee/Getty Images

The Senate voted to confirm Todd Blanche as U.S. attorney general, elevating the Justice Department's No. 2 leader and President Trump's former personal lawyer to head the entire 100,000-plus person department.

The Senate vote, early Saturday morning, was 50-49 in favor of Blanche. All Democrats, as well as Republican Sens. Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski, voted against him.

Blanche overcame a final speedbump on Friday after securing key support from Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana. With the absence of Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and Murkowski's opposition, Cassidy's vote was crucial in securing a glidepath for Blanche.

Cassidy, who lost his renomination bid to a Trump-backed challenger, acknowledged concerns over Blanche's judgment in exempting the president from IRS audits and said he was particularly troubled by the Department of Justice bringing suits against the president's perceived political enemies. But he said his decision to back Blanche was not a referendum on the president.

Sponsor Message

"Mr. Blanche is not perfect, and he will tell you this," Cassidy said on Friday. "But the choice is not between perfection and Mr. Blanche. It is between Mr. Blanche and another acting attorney general who may not run the department effectively under President Trump and who indeed may not be as good as Mr. Blanche."

Blanche's nomination cleared a series of other hurdles, including concerns from lawmakers of both parties about the department's controversial $1.8 billion Anti-Weaponization Fund. The fund, created as part of a settlement between Trump and the IRS over the president's leaked tax returns, was meant to compensate people who alleged the federal government had been weaponized against them.

Blanche first verbally promised that the anti-weaponization fund wasn't moving ahead after it faced legal challenges. But two Republican members of the Senate Judiciary Committee who are both also leaving Congress — John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — said they wanted written assurances the fund was dead, and held up the committee's vote on Blanche's nomination. Blanche provided that written statement on Aug. 2, saying the order establishing the Anti-Weaponization Fund "is rescinded and shall have no force or effect."

Cornyn praised Blanche's willingness to work with him and Tillis, and said the DOJ needs a permanent head; Blanche had been serving in an acting capacity after Trump pushed out Pam Bondi.

"President Trump needs someone in this role, as well with a strong legal mind, but who also is close enough to him to give him confidential legal advice to tell him hard truths," Cornyn said before the committee vote. "I would advise Mr. Blanche not to be afraid to capitalize on that earned trust when necessary for the good of the country."

Sponsor Message

In a second written statement on Aug. 2, the Justice Department clarified the scope of protections from a tax audit that were part of the same Trump-IRS settlement and shielded Trump, his family and his companies from any tax audits or enforcement for prior tax returns. That statement from the DOJ said those audit protections only apply retroactively, and are limited to Trump, two of his sons, and the Trump Organization — instead of including a potentially larger, more nebulous group of "affiliated individuals" and companies.

Legal experts and Democrats questioned whether such statements would stand up in court, as they have not been signed by all parties to the settlement, including Trump himself.

"These assurances are not worth the paper they're written on," Brandon DeBot, policy director at the Tax Law Center at NYU Law, told NPR's Ryan Lucas. "They don't pull back on the attempts to give the president and his affiliates unauthorized immunity from tax audits. And they don't do anything new to stop the president from trying to bring back the fund."

In fact, Trump earlier this week said the fund would have been "very fair" and could have given "some solace" to Trump supporters who were prosecuted for the Jan. 6, 2021, riot on the U.S. Capitol.

"I view that fund as a positive, and a lot of Republicans do too," the president told reporters.

Background as Trump's personal attorney

Justice Department veterans, legal experts, and some members of Congress have also criticized other facets of Blanche's leadership of the DOJ as well as his fitness to be attorney general.

"Todd Blanche claims he was Donald Trump's personal attorney but is continuing to act as if he's still Donald Trump's personal attorney," Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California, told NPR's Steve Inskeep. "The American people deserve better."

Trump hired Blanche as his personal attorney in 2023 to defend him from criminal charges over hush money payments, mishandling classified documents, and attempting to overturn the results of the 2020 election. After Trump returned to the White House last year, he nominated Blanche as deputy attorney general.

Sponsor Message

Under Blanche's tenure, the Justice Department pursued Trump's promised campaign of retribution against his perceived enemies. It charged former FBI Director James Comey with making threats against the president in a photo of seashells Comey posted online. It also charged the Southern Poverty Law Center over payments it made to confidential informants to infiltrate extremist groups.

The department has opened an investigation that centers around the lawsuits the writer E. Jean Carroll brought and won against Trump for sexual abuse and defamation.

And the Justice Department's track record in court has also challenged the presumption of regularity: courts' assumption that DOJ officials are acting properly and in good faith, and that they're making accurate factual representations in court.

Under this administration, federal judges have repeatedly expressed concerns about the Trump administration not complying with court orders or providing representations in court that aren't backed by the facts. And the department has also seen several high-profile cases unravel recently, including dropping vandalism charges against a former Olympic canoeist and others over the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

The Justice Department has defended its track record in court and accused judges of overstepping their authority.

Democrats and some Republicans, including Sen. Tillis, had also been vocal in criticizing Blanche's handling of the scandal around sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and demanding that Blanche meet with Epstein survivors. Blanche did so for the first time last month to assuage those concerns.

But survivors after the meeting urged the senators to block Blanche's nomination, with one, Annie Farmer, saying she "found him abrasive, condescending, and intentionally noncommittal to survivors," according to her July 16 statement.

With assistance from NPR's Ryan Lucas and Barbara Sprunt.

World.title: Entire community of Summerland, B.C., ordered to evacuate due to fast-moving wildfire
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The District of Summerland, B.C., declared a state of emergency on Saturday, stating the Bald Range wildfire poses a risk to life and safety. The entire municipality has been ordered to evacuate.

The entire District of Summerland, B.C., home to more than 12,000 people, has been ordered to evacuate as the nearby Bald Range wildfire spreads.

The wildfire has been declared "out of control" by authorities and covers 50 square kilometres, according to available estimates.

There are currently 104 active blazes in B.C. The cause of the Bald Range fire isn't yet known.

The entire District of Summerland has been ordered to evacuate as the Bald Range wildfire continues to grow.

The district declared a state of emergency on Saturday, stating the wildfire poses a risk to life and safety.

The fire started about 15 kilometres northwest of Summerland, which is on the southwest end of Okanagan Lake, around 250 kilometres east of Vancouver.

The Bald Range fire grew to 50 square kilometres in three hours after it was first detected at 5:30 p.m. PT on Friday, said Erick Thompson with the Regional District of Okanagan-Similkameen's emergency operations centre.

The Bald Range fire is expected to grow overnight, and Highway 97 may be closed, according to officials. (Jay Bertagnolli/CBC)

Evacuation orders have been issued by the Regional District of Central Okanagan, the Regional District of Okanagan-Similkameen and the District of Summerland.

Authorities expanded evacuation alerts in the Central Okanagan early Saturday morning.

In a video briefing, Thompson said the fire poses an immediate threat to those in the evacuation zone, which now encompasses all of Summerland.

He said at least 55 people have been rescued by air support.

The Bald Range wildfire near Summerland is seen on Friday. An offifical with the Regional District of Okanagan-Similkameen's emergency operations centre said it was one of the 'quickest-moving, fastest-growing' wildfires the area had seen. (Submitted by Gail Rella)

Thompson said the fire is showing aggressive Rank 5 behaviour, meaning that it has a fast-moving flame front with "long-range spotting" that can ignite new fires.

He added it was one of the "quickest-moving, fastest-growing" wildfires the area had seen.

B.C. Wildfire Service currently has the wildfire stage characterized as "out of control."

The regional district spokesperson said people should prepare for Highway 97 to be closed.

The B.C. Wildfire Service said that winds were carrying embers up to a kilometre ahead of the main body of the fire.

'Embers on the seats'

In an interview with CBC News, Ashley Jestin said her house burned in the fire. Her home was located at the corner of Fish Lake Road and Princeton Summerland Road.

She said when her husband came home from work at about 4:30 p.m., he saw flames and smoke on the hill by their home, and they began getting packed.

"By the time we got out, we had embers on the seats of our car," Jestin said.

Jestin said they had only minutes to leave before their home was surrounded by flames, and they left before she heard any evacuation alerts or orders had been issued.

The Bald Range wildfire is just one of 104 active blazes in the province. (Submitted by Gail Rella)

Taylor Colman, a fire information officer with the B.C. Wildfire Service, said the fire is spreading up slope, and its growth was accelerating on Friday evening.

"The conditions on site are extremely dry and the forest fuels are very receptive to ignition and there's wind coming out of the south and southwest — which is driving the fire to the north and northeast," said Colman.

The B.C. Wildfire Service has deployed air tankers, helicopters and ground personnel. Tactical evacuations were initiated as the fire moved toward structures, said Colman.

According to the 2021 census, Summerland's population is over 12,000.

B.C.'s Interior Health, the regional health authority, confirmed that it's monitoring the situation and working to relocate 48 residents from Summerland's long-term care facility, Dr. Andrew Pavillion. Efforts are underway to relocate another 190 residents from Summerland Seniors Village.

"This is an evolving situation, and we are working closely with municipalities, regional districts and the B.C. Wildfire Service to ensure precautions are underway to protect patients, clients and individuals in long-term care," Interior Health said in a statement.

The Bald Range wildfire is just one of 104 active blazes in the province, and officials say an investigation into its cause remains ongoing.

World.title: On America's northern border, the threats are not unidirectional
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Clad in a black bulletproof vest, a gun clasped to his hip, Tim Thayer gently pushes down the throttles of four 350-horsepower engines — and the 18,000-pound U.S. Customs and Border Protection boat jumps to life on the Detroit River.

Thayer is a marine interdiction agent, part of a team that patrols the waterways that make up the Canada-U.S. border in this part of the country.

He's assigned to the Detroit sector, an area that encompasses Michigan, Ohio, Indiana and Illinois. The border with Canada here is entirely water — all 1,388 kilometres of it — which poses a unique challenge.

A peculiar quirk in the geography of the two countries is that Windsor, Ont., lies south of Detroit, separated by the river and connected by two bridges and a tunnel, with some seven million people crossing back and forth here alone annually.

A U.S. Customs and Border Protection boat is shown navigating the Detroit River, near Windsor, Ont., on Aug. 4. (Willy Lowry/CBC)

On a warm Wednesday afternoon, Thayer scans south, looking toward the Windsor shoreline, his eyes searching for anything out of the ordinary.

"When we do our enforcement patrols out here on the Detroit River, what we're seeing is both people, narcotics and guns going back and forth between the U.S. and Canada," he said.

During the Prohibition era of the 1920s and '30s, the Windsor-Detroit corridor was the main route smugglers used to bring alcohol into the U.S. illegally from Canada.

While illegal activity on the Detroit River is perhaps not nearly as bustling today, the sheer number of recreational boaters who are frequently out presents a challenge for law enforcement.

WATCH | Trump's fentanyl claims aren't materializing at this Canada-U.S. crossing: Trump’s fentanyl claims aren’t materializing at this Canada-U.S. crossing | Duration 2:05 U.S. President Donald Trump declared a national emergency at both the northern and southern borders in 2025, citing the fentanyl crisis to justify tariffs levied against Canadian and Mexican imports. Ottawa, for its part, has committed roughly $1.3B in multi-year investments to beef up border security with the U.S. At the Detroit-Windsor border, the CBC’s Willy Lowry takes a look at how the U.S. handles things on their side of the fence.

"We saw how many boats today? And every boat could be a smuggler unless we stop every single boat," asked Kris Grogan, chief of external communications at CBP's air and marine operations.

"You have to use intelligence and partnerships to be able to secure this area up here."

Trump's claims aren't materializing

Just days into his second term in 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump accused Canada of failing to prevent drugs, especially fentanyl and human traffickers, from entering the U.S., using the flow of drugs as justification to declare a national emergency and slapping 25 per cent tariffs on an array of Canadian goods under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) of 1977.

In February of this year, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down those tariffs.

And while Trump has painted a picture of a porous and dangerous border, the reality is much more complicated.

In 2025, U.S. border officials in the Detroit sector seized more than 4,200 kilograms of illegal drugs, including nearly 15 kilograms of fentanyl, according to statistics provided by CBP. But the statistics don't reveal the direction the drugs were travelling.

"It's really not that big of a problem for inbound," said Lavarah Miller, a CBP watch commander on duty when CBC News toured a brand new American port of entry facility at the newly opened Gordie Howe International Bridge.

"A lot of the stuff that we actually get, we get a lot of it going out."

A view from the new American port of entry facility at the just-opened Gordie Howe International Bridge, which runs between Windsor, Ont., and Detroit. CBC News recently spent two days with U.S. Customs Border and Protection agents stationed in the region. (Willy Lowry/CBC)

And guns, too, are travelling north, recent statistics show.

In 2024, 87 per cent of the guns recovered in crimes in Ontario were traced back to the U.S, according to figures compiled by Ontario Provincial Police. In Toronto, police say 88 per cent of guns recovered were illegally smuggled into the country.

"Firearms, for sure. But also, the United States is the middle ground for drugs coming up into our country from Mexico and South America," said Kelly Sundberg, a professor of criminology at Mount Royal University in Calgary.

While the flow of drugs and weapons between the two countries is primarily northward, Sundberg said, Canada still poses a threat to the U.S. — just not the one Trump continues to accuse Canada of.

"There is virtually no fentanyl getting smuggled into the United States, especially when you compare it to what's coming in from Mexico," he said. "Nevertheless Canada does have some serious issues with staffing [at our border] — we don't have enough officers.

"The officers we do have need to be better educated, better trained, better selected, better equipped. There needs to be a significant investment in the human side of our border security."

A tale of 2 borders

Canada's fentanyl czar — a role created in the early days of the trade war to try and assuage Trump's concerns about the northern border — has also pushed back against suggestions that Canada poses a major drug-trafficking threat.

In an interview with CBC's The House in June, Kevin Brosseau pointed to new data from CBP that shows less than half a kilogram of fentanyl was seized at the Canada-U.S. border in May, compared to 358 kilograms at the Mexico-U.S. border.

The total amount of fentanyl seized by U.S. officials so far this year at the Canadian border is approximately three kilograms. At the Mexican border, it's approximately 3,221 kilograms.

Despite ongoing political tensions between Washington and Ottawa, the U.S. border agents who spoke with CBC News over our two-day tour insisted the working relationship with their Canadian counterparts has remained unchanged over the last 18 months.

"Locally, we still have great partnerships with those agencies right across the water," said Tim Balkus, the patrol agent in charge of the Detroit sector.

Meanwhile, Thayer nods his head as an RCMP boat flies past, the Gordie Howe bridge looming large in the distance — a symbol of both how strong and strained the bond between the two countries is today.

World.title: Canada, U.S. shadow Chinese research ships in the Arctic as concern grows over Snow Dragons' presence
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Both Canada and the U.S. have been quietly shadowing two Chinese icebreaking research ships in Arctic waters off Alaska over the last couple of weeks.

The Xue Long (Snow Dragon) and Xue Long (Snow Dragon) 2 sailed north through the U.S. exclusive economic zone in the Bering Sea in July, according to the U.S. Coast Guard.

The appearance of Chinese research ships every summer in the Arctic Ocean over the last few years has been a subject of growing concern among security and defence officials.

Data compiled by Steffan Watkins, an independent research consultant and ship tracker, shows a Royal Canadian Air Force CP-140 surveillance plane has been operating out of Alaska since early July.

The Department of National Defence confirmed Friday that the plane has been watching the activities of the two Chinese vessels in tandem with the Americans.

"The Canadian Joint Operations Command is actively monitoring maritime traffic in the Arctic, including the vessels Xue Long and Xue Long 2," defence spokesperson Cheryl Forrest said in a written statement.

"Both vessels are currently operating outside of Canada’s exclusive economic zone," Forrest added, referring to the area of ocean beyond territorial waters where the country has sovereign rights to resources and jurisdiction over activities like research and protection of the marine environment.

WATCH | From 2025: Canada monitors Chinese research vessel: Why is the Canadian military closely monitoring a Chinese research vessel? | Duration 3:48 The Canadian military and possibly the Coast Guard are closely monitoring a Chinese research vessel that has breached Arctic waters for the second year in a row. CBC's Murray Brewster says the Coast Guard was 'following a parallel course' of the vessel, despite denying any 'shadowing.'

Last year, the Canadian military began a focused effort to better monitor northern waters and co-ordinate with allies in the Pacific Ocean, including the Bering Sea off Alaska, under the banner of Operation Latitude.

The Royal Canadian Navy has committed the frigate HMCS Ottawa and the Arctic offshore ships HMCS Max Bernays and HMCS Robert Hampton Gray, in addition to the air force's surveillance aircraft.

The defence department says Canadian Special Operations Forces Command personnel and the icebreaker CCGS Des Groseilliers are also taking part.

Buoys can track submarine activity

When asked about the Chinese ships on Thursday, Defence Minister David McGuinty said the Canadian military actively monitors the country's waters.

China, which has declared itself a near-Arctic state, has repeatedly said the deployment of its icebreakers to the region is strictly for peaceful scientific research, environmental monitoring and global climate change studies.

Both research ships, however, have been known to deploy advanced sonar and telemetry buoys. Western defence officials say these devices not only track environmental changes and undersea topography, but are also useful in tracking submarine activity.

"Those research ships could do so many different things," said Richard Shimooka, a defence researcher at the Ottawa-based Macdonald-Laurier Institute.

There are no major international undersea fibre-optic cables in the Bering Sea region, but there is a regional subsea network vital to Alaska. Shimooka said he wonders how much time the Chinese are devoting to mapping that grid, in the same way the Russians are doing in the Baltic Sea and the North Atlantic.

People attend the launch ceremony of China's first domestically built polar icebreaker Xue Long 2 (Snow Dragon 2) at a shipyard in Shanghai on Sept. 10, 2018. (Reuters)

Canada, Shimooka said, is playing an increasingly important role in the western Pacific at a time when the U.S. Navy is occupied with the Iran war. But, he cautioned, given the age of the Canadian navy's frigates and coast guard ships, the country can't do much more than it's currently doing.

"I wouldn't say we're stressed, but it certainly is kind of reaching the limits that we can sustain comfortably given the age of the Halifax class," he said.

Described as the "backbone of the Royal Canadian Navy," the Halifax-class patrol frigates are now between 30 and 40 years old.

'Testing our capabilities to respond'

Members of the House of Commons defence committee travelled to the Arctic in mid- to late July and Conservative defence critic James Bezan left convinced that the region needs more surveillance.

"We know we've had to have more assets in the Arctic to ensure that we are monitoring the movements of the People's Republic of China as they continue to increase their interest in our Arctic," said Bezan, who noted that China has also been increasingly co-operating and co-ordinating its air activity in the Arctic with Russia.

"They are definitely challenging and testing our capabilities to respond to these incursions."

The federal government has begun investing heavily in the construction of new destroyers and begun the process of acquiring Arctic-capable submarines. It also plans to deploy an undersea network of sensors.

Bezan said time is of the essence because the country's sovereignty is at stake.

"Russia and China do not recognize our maritime claims" in the Far North, including the Northwest Passage, Bezan said.

"So, we need to be investing in the Arctic. When you look at the vast amounts of resources, a high percentage of energy resources that are locked in the Arctic, including in the Beaufort Sea, we have to do more to protect it and defend against these adversaries."

World.title: U.S. booze might end up back on Canadian shelves, but have we lost the taste for it?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Deb Anderson can't remember the last time she bought a product from the United States.

Like many Canadians, the 65 year old from Prospect, N.S., said she's been alarmed by U.S. President Donald Trump's repeated threats against Canada — and she's been boycotting American goods in protest.

So when she read on Friday that Canada was prepared to lift a ban on American alcohol sales as part of its trade negotiations with the Trump administration, Anderson says she felt disappointed.

"But just because it goes back on the shelves doesn't mean that sales are going to go back to where they were. The damage has been done," she told CBC in an interview.

Anderson says the "constant badgering and unfair negotiation practices" from the U.S. have "really give us a bad taste for all things American."

Anderson doesn't appear to be alone in her feelings: Sixty-nine per cent of Canadians said they weren't likely to buy American alcohol if it goes back on store shelves, according to a Nanos Research poll published last month.

Support for a continued boycott of U.S. alcohol was highest in British Columbia, where 80.9 per cent of respondents said they were unlikely or somewhat unlikely to buy U.S. booze again if it's made available.

That was followed by 74.7 per cent of people in Ontario and 73.9 per cent of Quebecers who said the same, the poll found.

WATCH | Are the booze bans an effective pressure tactic?: Is the U.S. booze ban working? | Duration 3:31 With most Canadian provinces vowing to keep U.S. alcohol off store shelves in response to President Donald Trump’s latest tariff threats, CBC’s Eli Glasner asks: are the booze bans an effective pressure tactic or merely political symbolism — and an inconvenience for consumers.

Steep decline in U.S. alcohol imports

Industry sources with knowledge of Canada-U.S. trade negotiations told CBC News that the Canadian government was prepared to lift bans on alcohol sales as it negotiates possible concessions in exchange for U.S. tariff relief.

Trump has threatened to impose 50 per cent tariffs on some Canadian goods on Aug. 19 if Canada fails to lift some retaliatory trade measures against the U.S., including the alcohol bans.

Those bans date back to early last year, when several provinces removed U.S. alcohol from the shelves at their respective liquor boards in response to Trump slapping a 25-per-cent tariff on Canadian goods.

Ivan Gedz, who owns the bar Union Local 613 in Ottawa, says his stockpile of American booze ran out two months after U.S. supplies were taken off the shelves at the Liquor Control Board of Ontario (LCBO) last year.

But Gedz says customers at the bar, which had previously offered a wide range of American spirits, didn't bat an eye at not having access to bourbon and other alcohol made south of the border.

Instead, the U.S. alcohol ban encouraged patrons to try booze they'd never had before.

"There's nothing I love more than giving someone an Indian whisky and they're like, 'India? I didn't even know India made whisky,' " Gedz told CBC News in an interview. "They're producing excellent stuff — it's just we don't get a ton of it."

A proposal to halt provincial bans on American booze was revealed Friday as negotiators race to reach a deal before new U.S. tariffs take effect on Aug. 19. However, a poll last month suggested 69 per cent of Canadians said they weren't likely to buy U.S. alcohol even if it returns to shelves. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

Changing tastes?

The need to seek out alternatives is something that was seen in other parts of Canada, too.

Quebec's liquor board, the Société des alcools du Québec (SAQ), said in its 2026 annual report that "fans of U.S. wines have turned to counterparts from other regions" amid the ban.

"Canadian wines, including Quebec wines, have gained popularity and now rank ahead of Australia's," the report said, adding that Austrian wines were also becoming more popular in "a sign that customers are curious and open to discovering new countries of origin."

Nicole Raufeisen is director of operations at Grape Witches, a bar and wine bottle shop in Toronto that continued to sell U.S. wines it already had stocked when the ban came into effect.

"We've slowly ticked away through those products. I think we're down to maybe just one or two different wines," she told CBC in an interview on Friday.

If the ban is lifted, Raufeisen says she expects customers will again reach for wines they enjoy from the U.S., such as fuller-bodied reds from California. "People will go back because those wines are good, that market share is well-trodden, so to speak, and the visibility there is high."

But she added that demand for American wines can also be attributed to trade barriers between provinces.

While nine provincial premiers announced last month that they would introduce direct-to-consumer alcohol sales between provinces, Raufeisen says restrictions on wholesale wine sales between provinces remain a major challenge.

"If there were no interprovincial barriers to the wholesale movement of wines, then it's possible that no one would miss any of the American wines," she said, noting that B.C. wines are comparable to those from California.

WATCH | Trump said Canada has 'nasty leadership': Canada has 'nasty leadership,' says Trump as he praises U.S. tariff policy | Duration 0:40 U.S. President Donald Trump, speaking from Las Vegas on Wednesday, praised his government's use of tariffs and once again mentioned Canada, saying, 'I love the people' but that the country has 'nasty leadership.'

Back in Ottawa, Gedz says Union Local 613 would probably bring U.S. booze back if the ban is lifted as part of a wider trade agreement between the two countries.

But he says he doesn't expect American alcohol to be as popular as it once was because many Canadians "have exposed themselves to products that they may not have tried" without the ban in place.

"I'm just hoping that those customers maintain their willingness for experimentation," Gedz said. "And you know what? If we stick it to the Americans for a little while longer, I'm cool with that."

World.title: The world wants more Canadian-made water bombers. Can Canada build them fast enough?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As France battled what President Emmanuel Macron called its worst wildfire crisis since the Second World War , his government faced swift criticism over whether it was prepared for the scale of the fires.

But another, less likely target soon came into view: Canada.

"We don't have enough Canadairs," said Didou Deyres, vice-president of the forest fire defence department in Le Porge, where 183 homes burned in late July after flames swept through the pine forests outside Bordeaux.

France has 12 of the distinctive yellow water bombers, but Deyres said only seven were flying at the height of the crisis.

Had more firefighting capacity been available sooner — "on the ground and in the air" — things may have been different, he said.

Asked whom he blamed, Deyres smiled: "Canada."

"We have to work together with Canada to modernize the planes."

Deyres's answer was tongue-in-cheek, but it points to a real pressure building across Europe: demand for Canadian-made water bombers is growing faster than De Havilland Canada can deliver them.

Drought and successive heat waves have fuelled destructive fires across Europe, putting greater pressure on governments to expand their aerial firefighting fleets.

Didiou Deyres, the vice-president of the forest fire defence department in Le Porge, France, says the country lacks firefighting resources. (Verity Stevenson/CBC)

European countries have ordered 22 new Canadair 515 aircraft from De Havilland Canada since 2022. But after production of the aircraft line was dormant for nearly a decade, the first newly built planes are not expected to begin reaching European customers until 2028. France is expected to wait until 2032 for the second half of its order of four, according to the company.

France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said in June that he hoped those deadlines would be "respected."

The hand-built planes are unmatched in the firefighting aircraft market and are built to last for decades. They are agile even at low speeds and scoop water directly from lakes and other suitable bodies of water before returning quickly to a fire.

The aircraft can scoop roughly 6,000 litres of water in about 12 seconds.

"They really are the backbone of most European firefighting operations," said Neil Sweeney, De Havilland Canada's vice-president of operations. "The last few weeks have reminded everybody just how important these aircraft are."

Neil Sweeney, vice-president of corporate affairs for Westerkirk Capital, the company which holds De Havilland Canada, poses for a picture as De Havilland produces the Canadair 515 water bomber to combat wildfires, in Calgary, Alta., in August 2025. (Ahmed Zakot/Reuters)

The Canadair line had been dormant since 2015, when its former manufacturer, Bombardier, stopped building the aircraft with no orders pending. By the time De Havilland launched the new Canadair 515 program in 2022, much of the supply chain had disappeared, forcing the company to re-establish sources for the roughly 50,000 parts needed to build each aircraft, a process that takes about 10 months, according to one expert.

"The supply chain disappeared," said McGill University aviation management expert John Gradek. Suppliers had moved on, tooling had been dismantled and thousands of specialized parts once made for the aircraft had to be sourced again.

France's existing fleet has also come under strain this season. Although Canadairs are designed to remain in service for decades, Gradek said France has been flying its aircraft almost continuously during peak fire season, increasing maintenance demands.

After scooping water from the Seine River while fighting a fire in the Fontainebleau forest near Paris, pilot Grégory Prats complained that France had spent 2 billion euros ($3.2 billion Cdn) cleaning the river in time for the 2024 Olympics but had not invested enough in its firefighting fleet.

The question now is whether De Havilland should expand production before more governments commit to buying aircraft.

Sweeney told CBC News that De Havilland would build another production plant if it could sell 50 planes to Canadian governments.

But Gradek argues the company is being too cautious.

"Risk averse — and that's the Canadian way, right?"

Canadair firefighting planes fly over Fontainebleau forest, which was affected by wildfires near Noisy-sur-École, outside Paris, during a heat wave in July. (Stephane Mahe/Reuters)

Rather than waiting for governments to place more orders, Gradek said De Havilland could do more to modernize and streamline production. He argues the company needs to invest in greater manufacturing capacity if it wants to maintain its commanding position in the market.

No 'handouts'

Gradek also questions why the company hasn't entered into a public-private partnership with the federal government.

"This is an aircraft that would basically be able to address an evolving national emergency. And if it's a national emergency, we need national support," he said.

De Havilland sees it differently.

Sweeney said the privately held company is "not looking for handouts and not looking for subsidies — just orders."

Building another production line would require hundreds of millions of dollars in investment, he said.

"It's not like an automobile. You don't really build them on spec," he said. He noted that the planes are customized for each country ordering them.

Still, Gradek worries De Havilland risks losing the commanding position Canada has built over decades by waiting for firm orders before expanding production.

"The world loves your airplanes," he said. But with wildfire seasons growing longer and governments scrambling to rebuild their fleets, he argues Canada cannot assume that dominance will last.

"You have to go out there and spend the money to build these plants and the orders will come."

Competition on the horizon

That pressure is already emerging. European aerospace companies and startups, such as Positive Aviation and Kepplair, are racing to develop competing firefighting aircraft. France has taken matters into its own hands as well, retrofitting an A400M military transport aircraft to be able to dump up to 20,000 litres of water or fire retardant.

None of the new entrants has the Canadair's decades-long operational record, and Sweeney said De Havilland is aware of the competition. But the efforts underscore what Gradek sees as a narrowing window for Canada's only producer of large, water-scooping aircraft.

"The world is not going to wait for Canada," Gradek said.

World.title: Feds should devise way to reflect on COVID-19 response, says Canada's chief science adviser
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's chief science adviser says the federal government should devise a way to reflect on its response to the COVID-19 pandemic to better prepare the country and Canadians for future public health challenges.

"I think we have to respect how people feel, and then we need to meet them and hear them and understand where things stand," Mona Nemer said in an interview with CBC's The House airing Saturday.

"People are angry for different reasons around the COVID measures. Some are angry because they lost their livelihood. Others are angry because they lost loved ones. Others are angry because their kids didn't go to school. I think we need to understand all of this."

Nemer, an independent adviser who does not make government policy, said Ottawa's reflection must be apolitical and cannot be open-ended. In her view, it must tackle specific questions so the process doesn't drag on and people forget.

"Just like now, when people reflect on and are angry about some of the vaccine discussions, people forget that so many folks were dying every day before we had vaccines and how much vaccines saved lives, actually," she said.

WATCH | World not ready for another pandemic, report warns: The world isn't ready for another pandemic, report warns | Duration 1:57 A new report by a World Health Organization-backed board warns the world isn't ready for the next pandemic. It urges health authorities to come together to track risk, share vaccines, tests and treatments, as well establish funding for prevention, preparedness and response.

"We just need to have the proper context for these kinds of discussions and reflections. And we need to have the proper mindset to do it in a constructive manner, to better prepare the country and the population for future health challenges."

Nemer's comments come as Conservative MP Dean Allison plans to hold his own inquiry in September on the pandemic — specifically "listening to the testimony of Canadians injured by a COVID-19 vaccine."

Last month, Allison said "every Canadian deserves to be treated with dignity, respect and compassion. When people come forward with their concerns about their health, our first response should never be dismissal. It should be listening."

According to the inquiry's website, it will be non-partisan. Plus, other MPs and senators from all parties are eligible to sit as panel members.

Conservative MP Dean Allison announces an inquiry into Canadian Covid-19 vaccine injured persons on June 4, 2026. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

When asked about the level of trust Canadians have in authorities when it comes to questions around infectious diseases, Nemer said general trust in government and science is decreasing — a worrisome development, the adviser noted, but not undeserved.

"Nothing was perfect [with COVID], but nothing was horribly badly done either," Nemer said. "I think people distrust when they don't understand, or they have their perspective and it hasn't been confronted or discussed against other things."

World falling behind on Ebola response

During her interview, Nemer also expressed concern about the global response to other infectious diseases, including Ebola.

The outbreak was declared on May 15 by the World Health Organization, and the number of infections has been steadily rising. According to data from the government of the Democratic Republican of Congo, the number of confirmed cases has risen above 4,000.

Ebola is not new, but Nemer said there were no diagnostics ready to detect the virus for several months, which likely worsened the containment of the current outbreak.

Nemer said that the global community still has not learned key lessons from COVID. For example, she highlighted that pandemic preparedness should not be viewed as a standalone concept, but instead should be integrated into routine health services.

Furthermore, Nemer said there was an urgent pace to dealing with the COVID-19 pandemic, but that urgency has since subsidied despite other diseases popping up that pose significant threats.

"Since COVID, we've had mpox, we've had Ebola, we've had hantavirus — the list is long. [Bird flu] is still a threat," Nemer said.

"So I don't think that we can declare victory and move on to other things."

WATCH | Canada approves trial for mRNA Ebola vaccine: Canada approves trial for mRNA Ebola vaccine | Duration 2:04 Health Canada has approved a Phase 1 clinical trial for Moderna's potential mRNA vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola. If found safe and effective, the vaccine would be used in future outbreaks of the virus.

Nemer also acknowledged the collective fatigue when it comes to dealing with new viruses in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, but pointed out there will always be a need to prepare for future outbreaks — and it's better done now than in a crisis.

"I think the pandemic has also taught us important lessons about public trust [and] about the need to develop this trust during peacetime, meaning between pandemics or prior to pandemics," Nemer said.

"Because it's not during crisis that we're going to start developing the trust that is absolutely critical."

World.title: Why is gaming giant Roblox losing tens of billions in market value?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Roblox isn’t getting the high financial scores that it used to — not even close.

The popular gaming platform has lost approximately $97.5 billion Cdn in market value over the last year, according to stock market data. The company says the decline is partly because of changes in the games its users play and growing pains as it attempts to attract older gamers — but experts say more could be at play.

"I think there's actually a lot of things going on," said Aaron Langille, co-ordinator of the game design and simulation program at Cambrian College in Sudbury, Ont.

"I think it's sort of a platform getting a little bit older, and maybe making some decisions that didn't work out."

Roblox Corporation’s stock price is down approximately 70 per cent compared to this time last year, dropping from $129.63 US ($180.67 Cdn) to $36.96 US ($51.51 Cdn). The stock fell sharply following an earnings call last week where executives reported revenue below company expectations.

If you don’t have iPad-armed kids in your life, Roblox is a gaming and creation platform where users can play games created by other users. Released in 2006, the platform has since grown to 151.5 million daily users and 3.5 million game developers, according to company data.

Roblox offers racing games, obstacle courses, first-person shooters, platformers, board games and more. The vast majority are multiplayer, where gamers play with or against other gamers.

Roblox gamers tend to be younger. The company, which rolled out identity and age verification for users earlier this year, said in February that of the daily active users who had completed verification, 35 per cent were younger than 13 and 38 per cent were aged 13 to 17, making more than half of all active players non-adults.

CEO David Baszucki and CFO Naveen Chopra told investors last week that Roblox has fallen short of its expectations this year when it comes to getting users to spend — particularly those under 13. They said the shortcoming was partly because of changes Roblox has made in the platform’s game recommendation algorithm, but also because games that are popular now aren’t moneymakers compared to last year’s hits.

“If you just look at the percentage of hours consumed on the platform last year, that was coming from these very large and high-monetizing viral hits — it was very concentrated,” Chopra said on the call.

“Those games did appeal, in particular, to younger users.”

Concerns raised over safety

Roblox, which includes text and voice communication between users, is looking to broaden its appeal to include older gamers. The effort comes as governments, watchdogs and experts have raised concerns about safety of young users on the platform.

The RCMP’s National Child Exploitation Crime Centre received more than 1,000 reports involving Roblox between 2024 and 2025, according to the Mounties.

In February 2025, 16-year-old Penelope Sokolowski of Vancouver took her own life after online messaging with a violent cult called 764, which encourages self-harm. She first met a member of 764 on Roblox.

Public Safety Canada listed 764 as a terrorist entity last December, saying “members routinely use various social media and gaming platforms, particularly those with young and marginalized user bases, to lure, groom and extort youth to commit violent and sexual acts, including self-harm.”

Roblox reached an agreement with the state of Nevada in June to implement more stringent online safety measures for young users and to put more than $10 million US towards education and safety efforts.

Yulia Nevskaya, an assistant professor of marketing at Queen’s University in Kingston, Ont,, said the platform’s complexity makes it difficult to pin down the cause of its financial downturn beyond the company’s explanations, but said safety concerns could be a factor.

“Roblox is facing a lot of scrutiny over safety, especially for children, and the company recently introduced new rules for age and account verification, which some users see as intrusive,” she said in an email.

“That could also be leading to some user base loss and affect some game developers' willingness to supply games. It’s very messy.”

Baszucki and Chopra also emphasized positives on the earnings call. They said changes to Roblox’s algorithm have boosted user retention.

They added that the company has seen growth in international markets like Japan and India, and that there’s increased diversity in what games users are playing — three years ago, its Top 10 games accounted for 30 per cent of all gaming hours compared to 20 per cent today.

Baszucki, Roblox’s Winnipeg-born co-founder, said improved gamer retention and growth, especially among older gamers, will eventually pay off, despite the disappointing revenue numbers.

“I’ve never been more excited about our mission, and more excited and confident in the road ahead.”

David Baszucki, co-founder and CEO of Roblox Corporation, attends the Allen and Company Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference in Sun Valley, Idaho, on July 8, 2025. Baszucki said on a recent earnings call that Roblox is making the right decisions for long-term growth, despite disappointing numbers for the company recently. (Brendan McDermid/Reuters)

Cristiano Politowski, an assistant professor of computer science at Ontario Tech University in Oshawa Ont., said Roblox is unique among gaming companies since it has full control of the platform its games appear on, and its ability to manage its platform suggests the changes that hurt its stock price in the short-term are part of a genuine long-term strategy.

“As the kids say nowadays, they are cooking something,” Politowski said.

“This is one step back to go two forward later.”

But, unlike its young userbase, Roblox could be starting to show its age.

“Twenty years is actually a really, really long time,” Langille said.

“I think what they’re seeing is that as their players they had along with them from the beginning are changing what they want to play, and what they think of as fun, they’re having a little bit of a harder time attracting new players.”

World.title: The air travel industry was on the brink of disaster, but travellers are still taking to the skies
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It seemed like airlines were on the brink of disaster heading into the peak summer travel season, with the Middle East war causing chaos and uncertainty, closing airspace in many areas and sending fuel prices soaring.

For weeks, headlines seemed to point toward a doomsday scenario. Fuel prices more than doubled in April. Europe was on track to run out of jet fuel by June, the International Energy Agency warned. Many airlines — including those in Canada — cut less profitable flights as a result. Florida-based Spirit Airlines fully shut down in May.

Despite all those headwinds, the industry — and passengers' desire to fly — appears to have rallied. Europe avoided its crisis by finding other sources of fuel , while passenger traffic has held steady, expected to increase by 2.1 per cent this year.

This summer even saw a new record: July 23 had the most global commercial flights ever tracked — a whopping 153,359, according to Flightradar24, a live flight tracker.

"What we're seeing is increased scheduled air traffic," said Ian Petchenik, Flightradar24's communications director. "It's really as simple as that."

Peak travel season

Total air passenger demand fell 1.7 per cent in June, according tothe International Air Transport Association (IATA). However, this was a smaller drop than the preceding months, and much of it was concentrated in the Middle East, which saw a 13.9 per cent fall year over year.

There isn't one single explanation for the July record, experts told CBC News. But it was likely fuelled by demand from the Northern Hemisphere, Newsweek reported , as airlines have been deploying maximum capacity for the season when travel typically peaks.

The last Thursday or Friday of July is usually the busiest, says Petchenik, as many see it as the peak of the summer season, just before school begins in August in much of the U.S.

For this summer in particular, he says, many of those flights were likely booked well in advance.

LISTEN | Canada's domestic tourism boom: The Current 18:53 Why Canadian tourism is booming At a time when the overall economy is sluggish, the Canadian tourism sector is bucking the trend and projected to grow by 6% in 2026. We hear from some innovative Canadian travel businesses that are cashing in and from tourism and hospitality professor Wayne Smith about what is driving the growth — and what it would take to build on it.

"A lot of people looking at the state of the world … before prices really spiked and saying, 'Maybe we should book now to get ahead of any incoming price increases.' "

Canadian commercial flights increased over the summer, as well, by Flightradar24's count, rising by 16 per cent between April 1 and July 23 to hit 5,558. Global commercial flights increased by 11 per cent that same time period.

But the number of flights alone doesn't always paint the full picture, said Amra Durakovic of Flight Centre Travel Group Canada. That's because our total annual commercial flight count remains 20 per cent below 2019, she said, citing data from analytics firm Cirium.

The global increase in flights is likely driven by large, emerging economies like China and India, which are increasing their flights as their markets grow.

However, countries with more established flight industries — like Canada — have instead increased the size of the average plane, while phasing out smaller ones. That means more people are served in the end.

Tourists take selfies with a reflection of the Eiffel Tower in the Champ-de-Mars garden in Paris on July 28. Canadians heading to Europe this summer have tended to book flights last minute, adopting what industry experts refer to as a wait-and-see approach. (Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty Images)

Where Canadians are going

On July 23, most Canadian travel was domestic, accounting for more than a third of all bookings, according to Flight Centre data.

Durakovic says her firm hasn't seen that happen since before the COVID-19 pandemic, and she notes it's likely that people are rerouting trips that originally would have been to the U.S.

Still, the U.S. was the second most popular destination that day, at 19 per cent, followed by European countries like the U.K., Italy and Spain, at 18 per cent combined.

Durakovic also noted an interesting trend among Canadians heading to Europe: They tended to book their flights last minute, as opposed to the typical approach of booking in advance.

"They've adopted what we refer to as a wait-and-see approach," said Durakovic, who attributed the trend to ongoing uncertainty around factors impacting the industry, like fuel costs and contract disputes.

Meanwhile, summer travel through Flight Centre Canada to Japan is up 37 per cent year over year — a significant sum considering the East Asian country is a long-haul flight away, at a time when cost remains a priority for many.

Notably, that demand is extending into the winter months, Durakovic says, as Canadians are finding it can be more affordable to ski in Japan, largely due to the weak yen.

"That's what is largely driving a lot of Canadians' travel decisions is where are they going to find the best value?"

Tourists ride on horses at the fifth station of Mount Fuji in Fujiyoshida, Yamanashi prefecture on July 23, 2026. Japan has become a popular tourist destination for travellers seeking good value for their money. (Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty Images)

What lies ahead

So far, the Middle East war hasn't seemed to significantly affect summer plans outside that region. But that may change the longer it goes on, alongside events like the recent WestJet strike , for example, which can erode confidence in travelling.

"I think that the more uncertainty there is and the higher prices rise … we will see a pullback in demand," said Petchenik of Flightradar24.

He says that could also trigger a shift to more local travel: "You know, 'I am buying a ticket, but … I'm flying somewhere where the prices are reasonable and I have certainty that my trip isn't going to be affected by world events outside of my control.' "

WATCH | How the war affected flight prices in March: How is war in the Middle East affecting flight prices for Canadians? | Duration 3:37 The costs of the war in the Middle East keep adding up as gas and diesel prices have risen sharply around the world; the cost of jet fuel has also increased. For people planning trips, it can be a scramble to find something less expensive. McKenzie McMillan from The Travel Group Ltd. explains how the war is affecting flights and by how much.

As for ticket prices, expect them to continue increasing, according to IATA. Airlines are still profitable, but their margins are under severe pressure due to fuel prices and with few ways remaining for them to cut costs.

Durakovic says she still expects demand to remain high in the near future.

"Look, it's a lot, but when we travel, we all love it, right?" she said, noting that people are generally willing to cut other costs to afford travel. "It says a lot about how important travelling is."

World.title: Colby Cosh: Supreme Court to decide which comes first — Crown oath or Sikh faith
World.content:
Article content

Most of the other provinces have abandoned the explicit oath of constitutional allegiance for lawyers, or made that oath optional, although that’s kind of a funny thing to do with an oath if you think about it. My six or seven readers who are fellow atheist-monarchists ought to recognize that the “Wirring Question” is a legitimately hairy one. The oath of Canadian citizenship, like the oath in the statute governing Alberta lawyers, still requires a declaration of “true allegiance” to the King of Canada. Whenever that oath has been challenged in court, so far, it has been upheld on the grounds that this statement — while seeming to demand obedience to a living, breathing human being — is really just a symbolic commitment to the Constitution. (A republican, I suppose, can take such an oath in good conscience because it is a pledge to the King and his “successors,” who might not be monarchs at all.)

World.title: Conrad Black: Iran stands no chance against Donald Trump
World.content:
Article content

Under no circumstance will Trump accept a defeat from Iran, and there are no possible circumstances that will impose a defeat upon him. The most likely outcome is that Trump will state that negotiations are useless because the United States would honour an agreement and Iran would not, so there is no point negotiating one. Instead, the United States will maintain an air-tight land, sea and air blockade on Iran and strangle it economically (while the People’s Republic of China scrambles to find a replacement source of oil). The U.S. will also guarantee passage of shipping through the strait and any Iranian attack on that traffic will be responded to at once with a high multiple of applied force, probably including the destruction of at least one power plant on each such infraction. The Americans will continue this blockade until Iran convincingly agrees that it will end all pursuit of a nuclear military program, including the removal of enriched uranium, and cease the promotion of terrorism, specifically including Israel’s neighbours, and will not claim any right to control the international waterway of the Strait of Hormuz. Until it accepts those conditions, it will be throttled economically and severely punished for transgressions. This would assure the victory of the United States. It would not necessarily remove the incumbent government of Iran. Trump has renounced any interest in who governs any foreign country as long as that country does not threaten the legitimate interests of the United States and of the civilized world. This would not be at all a difficult policy to sell to the country, and it does not necessarily involve any American casualties or a substantial expenditure of ordnance, and it would certainly eventually attain all of America’s objectives.

World.title: De la Espriella sworn in as Colombia’s new president
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in in Colombia’s third largest city, Cali, under extreme security precautions.

De la Espriella was sworn in by the president of Congress, Senator Honorio Henriquez of the far-right Democratic Center party in the theater of the private University of Santiago de Cali.

The first part of the ceremony was attended by the Spanish King Felipe VI, multiple heads of state from Latin America and more than 60 ambassadors.

After being sworn in, De la Espriella went to the nearby Pichincha Battalion to assume the supreme command of the armed forces and hold his first speech as president.

The president vowed the security forces that he would be “an essential part of the miracle country” and vowed that at the end of his four-year mandate “authority will be felt in every corner of the country.”

De la Espriella also promised that “nobody will be persecuted for his opinions” and warned members of the “regime” of former President Gustavo Petro he would cooperate with “other States,” suggesting they could be extradited.

Both ceremonies were boycotted by Petro’s leftist political party, the Historic Pact, which organized political rallies elsewhere in Cali, and in the cities of Bogota and Barranquilla.

In Barranquilla, Senator Ivan Cepeda stressed the left does not recognize the incoming government because of De la Espriella’s US citizenship and his alleged debts with the US Department of Justice.

“De la Espriella, who once acted as an intermediary for drug traffickers and paramilitaries—from whose ill-gotten gains he has profited—has now become a figure who will be pressured by the United States, by his own government, and by its federal agencies to allow all kinds of foreign intervention in Colombia,” said Cepeda.

The leftist senator lost the elections to De la Espriella with a razor-thin margin of less than one percent. His supporters continue to seek a court order to nullify the election.

World.title: Colombia investigating governors, mayors over $941M corruption racket
World.content:
Prosecutors arrested 13 suspects and asked Colombia’s Supreme Court to investigate seven (former) governors over their alleged involvement in the embezzlement of COP3 trillion ($941 million).

The arrests and the investigation requests are related to the public-private partnership Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund, which was created by Martin Zuleta (U Party) and his family when he was mayor of La Paz, Cesar, in early 2021.

While supposedly serving the interests of La Paz, the Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund allegedly used forged documents to illegally appropriate funds from the General Royalties System with the help of governors from at least five provinces.

“So far, we’ve tracked 3 trillion pesos, of which it has been established that some were misappropriated through irregular contracts,” anti-corruption prosecutor Madeleyne Perez said at a press conference.

Among those whose cases were forwarded to the Supreme Court were the governors of Magdalena, Vichada, Amazonas Guaviare an Vaupes.

Former Governors Rafael Martinez of Magdalena and Alvaro Leon of Vichada will also be investigated by the Supreme Court.

Among those who were arrested is the mayor of Maria la Baja, a contractor and multiple (former) directors of the mixed fund.

The non-profit has been investigated since 2024 when authorities found irregularities in the construction of a high school in the Huila province, funds for school transport in Casanare and funds meant for indigenous reserves in La Guajira.

A report by the now-defunct radio station W from that year showed that Sierra Nevada had been hired by authorities from throughout Colombia for a wide variety of projects, avoiding any open bidding procedure.

W found more than 100 contracts between mainly local and regional government authorities and the non-profit.

According to Caracol, Zuleta was taken to hospital after his home was raided by prosecution officials and would be available to cooperate with the prosecutors investigating his alleged involvement in corruption.

World.title: Colombia’s left presents evidence suggesting De la Espriella won through fraud
World.content:
Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro and data analysts presented evidence suggesting that President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella won the election through the mass manipulation of tally sheets.

During a two-hour presentation, Petro claimed that almost all tally sheets that had been shared with his political party, the Historic Pact “lacked the Hash security lock,” which is inserted into official PDF documents to guarantee they can’t be changed.

The absence of a hash file implies that the so-called E14 tally sheets may have been altered, which appears to have happened, according to data analysts who accompanied the president.

Legal expert William Villanueva said that original tally sheets were scanned and subsequently reprocessed, removing the metadata that would allow them to determine whether the E14’s were uploaded or introduced digitally.

“We found documents marked ‘confidential’… and others that said ‘not digitized’ on a blank page, which—and this is important—were later republished with different information,” said one of the computer scientists.
