The goal is to boost marine and nearshore coastal conservation efforts, support integrated coastal management actions and mitigate negative impacts on sectors such as fisheries, public health and tourism.

The announcement came during an Aug. 3 meeting between Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco and his Japanese counterpart, Toshimitsu Motegi, in which they agreed to establish a working group to advance new areas of collaboration to strengthen bilateral relations in the political, economic, scientific and technological spheres.

In a joint statement to the media, they announced the launch of a high-level economic dialogue to boost bilateral trade, which, from January to May this year, amounted to US $9.9 billion, a 4% increase compared to the same period last year.

A few days earlier, President Claudia Sheinbaum pledged 2 billion pesos in federal funds (US $115 million) to battle an influx of sargassum in the state of Quintana Roo.

These funds will be directed toward sargassum control efforts spanning roughly 30 miles of beachfront spanning resorts including Cancún, Playa del Carmen, Puerto Morelos, Tulum and Mahahual.

El secretario de Relaciones Exteriores, Roberto Velasco (@r_velascoa), recibió a su homólogo japonés, el ministro de Asuntos Exteriores de @MofaJapan_en, Motegi Toshimitsu (@moteging), quien realiza una visita de trabajo a nuestro país. En reunión bilateral, ambos titulares de… pic.twitter.com/iaZwAhBjjV — Relaciones Exteriores (@SRE_mx) August 3, 2026

In October, Cancún will host the international EU-Caribbean Global Gateway Conference on Sargassum, with the aim of articulating joint strategies for the containment and management of biomass and sargassum.

The conference is expected to focus on regional cooperation, circular economy solutions and sargassum-harvesting technology.

With reports from Excelsior and MVS Noticias

World.title: The Mexican peso hits its strongest level against the dollar in 6 months
World.content:
Mexico’s currency gained 0.12% vs the U.S. dollar in Thursday trading, extending its rally to 10 straight days after the central bank left interest rates unchanged at its Aug. 6 monetary policy meeting.

The peso closed Thursday at 17.21 to the US dollar and dipped below 17.14 in early trading on Friday, an additional 0.58% gain and its strongest level against the U.S. dollar since Feb. 23.

Forbes México attributed Friday’s early action to a negative U.S. jobs report and said the peso is on pace to appreciate by 1.3% by the end of the week.

Mexico’s currency was also boosted by the central bank’s unanimous decision on Thursday to hold its benchmark rate at 6.50% for a second consecutive meeting, while hinting that rates would remain at the current level for the foreseeable future.

In a statement, Banxico’s board of governors said “headline and core inflation are expected to decline throughout the forecast horizon, albeit more gradually than previously anticipated.”

Headline inflation slowed in July for a fourth consecutive month though the central bank does not expect it to converge to its 3% target until late next year.

In a social media post, Gabriela Siller, director of analysis at Grupo Financerio BASE, said the peso is also appreciating “due to the carry-trade,” a strategy whereby an investor borrows money in a currency with a low interest rate and invests those funds into higher-yielding assets or currencies.

Siller said large global investors are borrowing in the U.S. and Japan, then investing in Mexico, indicating that the peso continues to benefit from a wide interest rate differential (Mexico’s 6.50% policy rate compares favorably to the U.S. Federal Reserve’s 3.50%-3.75% target range).

The newspaper El Economista said the U.S. jobs report (which noted that U.S. nonfarm payrolls fell by 23,000 jobs last month, following a downwardly revised increase of 20,000 jobs the previous month) prompted the market to reduce bets that U.S. interest rates will rise.

Monex Grupo Financiero concurred, saying in a statement that the peso’s advance against the dollar is “driven by the weakness of the dollar and a readjustment of expectations on the direction of the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy” at its next meeting in September.

With reports from El Economista and Forbes México

World.title: After crushing Panama, Mexico’s Under-20 team looks to clinch Olympics berth
World.content:
Close on the heels of El Tri’s impressive World Cup performance, Mexico’s Under-20 men’s squad has qualified for next year’s U-20 World Cup and is on the verge of earning an invitation to the 2028 Olympics.

At the same time, El Tri’s U-23 team has reached the final of the Central America and Caribbean Games where it will face Venezuela on Friday evening in Santo Domingo, the capital of the Dominican Republic.

México vs Panamá | 2026 Concacaf Men's Under-20 Championship Quarterfinals

Watch this video on YouTube

Coach Alex Diego’s U-20 team faces Canada on Friday night in Puebla with a spot in the final on the line. The winner will face either Costa Rica or Team USA who play earlier Friday.

Team Mexico earned its berth in the semifinals by manhandling Panama 4-0 on Wednesday, its fourth straight shut-out in the tournament, which features 12 teams from the Concacaf region competing for four tickets to the World Cup.

All four semifinalists automatically secured invites to the U-20 World Cup, so now the battle is for the lone remaining Concacaf berth in the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.

As the host nation, the U.S. receives one of the two Olympics spots reserved for Concacaf teams.

That means if Team USA defeats Costa Rica and Mexico gets past Canada, El Mini Tri will have clinched a trip to the Olympics regardless of the outcome in Sunday’s final. However, if Costa Rica upsets the Stars-and-Stripes, then Mexico would have to win the final to earn a spot in the Olympics.

Of course, coach Diego’s goal is to hoist the trophy on home soil, but to do so, El Tri will have to overcome a pair of key injuries and the suspension of its first-choice goalie.

Attacking midfielder Santiago Sandoval required surgery after breaking a finger during the team’s 2-0 victory over Costa Rica in the team’s second group stage match, ending his participation in the tournament.

Of equal concern is the status of winger Hugo Camberos, a rising star who has attracted attention from English Premier League clubs.

Camberos has scored in each of Mexico’s matches thus far, but limped off the pitch late in Wednesday’s match and his availability for the semifinal is in question.

The situation in goal for Mexico is of lesser concern since back-up goalie Cristo Navarrete kept a clean sheet in both starts since first-choice keeper Juan Liceaga was shown a red card in El Tri’s second match.

With reports from ESPN, FIFA, N+ and Concacaf

World.title: Meet the woman bringing adobe back to a Maya village
World.content:
Recently, on a trip to Valladolid, I met a woman named Debi Morris, who is bringing adobe back to the Maya village of Ek’ Balam by building a community center out of the all-natural, sustainable material.

Morris fell in love with Ek’ Balam years ago after a taxi dropped her off in the middle of town rather than at the Ek’ Balam ruins. She was captivated by the warm, welcoming people, the laughing children and the surrounding smiles. So she decided to give back using adobe.

What is adobe?

Adobe is a highly durable, all-natural building material that, with proper maintenance and moisture protection, can last for centuries. The proof is still standing in Yotzil, a tiny village in Yucatán. Other historic structures, such as New Mexico’s Palace of the Governors, built in 1610, still stand strong, proving adobe’s longevity.

Made of locally sourced natural materials, adobe recipes vary slightly from place to place depending on the soil and sand. In Ek’ Balam, it is made of high-clay red dirt, sand, dried grass, agave fiber, water and horse manure. Dried beforehand, the manure carries no odor. Builders also added a layer of fermented cactus juice, called baba de nopal, to waterproof the exterior walls.

Adobe also offers high thermal mass, making it ideal for escaping the heat of a Yucatán summer. Because of this thermal efficiency, adobe is growing in popularity as people look for ways to adapt to rising temperatures and reduce air conditioning usage.

Key characteristics of adobe

Composition: Typically consists of blended clay, sand, silt, a fibrous binder (such as chopped straw or agave fibers) and water to bind the mixture and prevent cracking.

Thermal mass: Thick adobe walls absorb heat during the day and slowly release it at night, providing natural climate control in hot, arid environments.

Sustainability: Sourced directly from the earth, adobe is non-toxic, biodegradable and fully recyclable.

Durability: Traditional adobe lasts for centuries but remains susceptible to water erosion, and so requires regular maintenance.

Adapting adobe to local soil

“You’re going to need patience. This is trial and error. There is no specific formula,” an expert advised Morris when she began.

She learned through trial and error that everything depends on local materials. For example, a builder cannot use the same formula in Mérida, even though it is in the same state of Yucatán, because the soil composition differs. In Ek’ Balam, one plot may have red dirt, while a neighboring plot contains entirely different mineral compounds.

“That was an eye-opener,” Morris said.

Not all red dirt works; the clay content must be tested first. “Thank God ours did, so that was a big blessing,” she said. Each layer requires experimentation.

Building in Ek’ Balam

Construction begins with the frame: two layers of wood with a layer of rock in between. Once the frame is set, builders apply the first layer of adobe — a mixture of red dirt, water and dried zacate, a local grass found in surrounding fields. The mixture is combined using hands and feet.

Next comes the layering process: rock, adobe, rock, adobe. After drying for two days, the structure is ready for a second layer consisting of red dirt, sand, water and dried grass. For this layer, the grass is treated with borax to repel insects.

The third layer contains red dirt, fine double-sifted sand, sifted horse manure and agave fibers, which are also treated with borax and cut into 1- to 2-centimeter pieces.

Finally, builders add baba de nopal, or prickly pear cactus extract. The extract is made by removing spines from cactus paddles, chopping them and fermenting them in water for at least 24 hours before straining.

Once the third layer is completed, it is sprayed with water several times a day for five days to retain moisture. On the eighth day, smoothed cracks are treated with warmed cactus extract for waterproofing. Before hurricane season, a final layer of natural linseed oil is applied for additional weather protection without compromising thermal performance.

Reviving an ancient practice

In 2004, Ek’ Balam consisted primarily of traditional palapas. Today, concrete homes have become common, but they trap heat, leading residents to joke that they feel like pizza ovens. Adobe offers a solution rooted in local heritage.

Although adobe construction was an ancient Maya technique, the knowledge was lost generations ago. Morris visited several villages asking abuelitos (grandfathers) if they knew how to make adobe. The answer was almost always, “My grandfather did.” In one nearby village, centuries-old adobe walls are still standing, proving the material’s regional durability.

As a result, Ek’ Balam has welcomed the return of this traditional building method.

Mexico Correspondent for International Living, Bel is an experienced writer, author, photographer and videographer with 500+ articles published both in print and across digital platforms. Living in the Mexican Caribbean for over seven years now, she’s in love with Mexico and has no plans to go anywhere anytime soon.

It is the only fixture involving a big Rio club today, and it is the one the city will be watching. If you are not going to the ground, the sensible plan is a bar with sound rather than a screen in a corner. Boteco Belmonte at Rua Teixeira de Melo 53 in Ipanema shows every Brasileirão fixture and takes table bookings from lunchtime, which is worth doing for a derby. Before kick-off, spend the cooler end of the afternoon on a compact Centro museum loop. The Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil opens Wednesday to Monday, 9 am to 8 pm, with free admission. Three minutes away, the Paço Imperial at Praça XV de Novembro 48 opens Tuesday to Sunday, 12 pm to 6 pm, also free. Both sit on the Praça XV VLT stop and pair naturally.

OUTDOORS — EARLY, NOT MIDDAY Jardim Botânico and Parque Lage Before the Heat The Jardim Botânico opens Tuesday to Sunday from 8 am to 5 pm, with a late noon opening on Mondays. Entry is R$40 for people resident in Brazil (about US$7.90) and R$80 for foreign visitors (about US$15.75), with a R$20 half-price band (about US$3.95). On a 35°C day the avenue of imperial palms is a morning proposition, not an afternoon one. Adjacent Parque Lage opens at 8 am and is free; its green-area closing time changed recently, so check before planning a late afternoon there. Coffee in the courtyard of the mansion is the shadiest seat in the Zona Sul, and the short trail towards the base of Corcovado is manageable early. Leave it alone after about 11 am today.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — CENTRO A Realistic Word on Weekend Desks A caveat before you set out: several of Centro’s best-known independent cafés, Curto Café on Rua da Assembleia among them, publish weekday-only hours and their Saturday opening is inconsistent. Ring ahead rather than trusting a listing. Be realistic about weekend coworking in Rio. Most dedicated spaces in Flamengo, Botafogo and Centro are staffed Monday to Friday and sell weekend access to members only, so a drop-in desk on a Saturday afternoon is the exception rather than the rule. If you need to work today, a café or a hotel lobby is the dependable answer — and confirm by phone before you travel across town.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — PORT MUSEUMS Museu do Amanhã and MAR, Indoors and Air-Conditioned For a climate-controlled afternoon, the Museu do Amanhã on Praça Mauá opens Thursday to Tuesday, 10 am to 6 pm, with last entry at 5 pm and closed Wednesdays. Tickets are R$40 full and R$20 half, roughly US$7.90 and US$3.95. Its future-themed galleries hold a solo visitor easily and work well with children. The Museu de Arte do Rio next door keeps the same closed day but different hours: Thursday to Tuesday, 11 am to 6 pm, last entry 5 pm, R$20 full and R$10 half (about US$3.95 and US$1.95), free on Tuesdays. The rooftop terrace looks straight over the port and is a good late-afternoon seat once the sun is off it.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM The Derby First, Then Lapa Kick-off is 9 pm, so an early dinner and a late night is the shape of it. Lapa is the obvious base afterwards: the bars under the Arcos run well past midnight on a Saturday and the crowd is at its densest between 11 pm and 2 am. Carioca da Gema at Av. Mem de Sá 79 runs from 9 pm to 3 am on Saturdays with live samba de raiz — check the cover on the door, as it varies by act. For a quieter option, Bar do Gomez in Santa Teresa, properly the Armazém São Thiago at Rua Áurea 26, is open Monday to Saturday from noon to 1 am and remains the neighbourhood’s beer-and-cachaça institution. Late hunger is handled at Casa Momus, Rua do Lavradio 11, open Thursday to Saturday from 11:30 am to 2 am. One practical note: the Santa Teresa tram runs in daylight only — the Dois Irmãos line operates 9 am to 5 pm at weekends from Estação Carioca — so plan a ride-hail for the hill after dark.

ALSO ON TODAY Centro Cultural dos Correios — “Roberto Burle Marx pelos amigos” — Centro — Tuesday to Saturday, 12 pm to 7 pm, free; the show runs until 22 August. Museu de Arte do Rio — rooftop and port galleries — Praça Mauá — 11 am to 6 pm, R$20 full and R$10 half (about US$3.95 and US$1.95); last entry 5 pm. Bonde de Santa Teresa — from Estação Carioca — the Dois Irmãos line runs 9 am to 5 pm at weekends; the Paula Mattos line runs daily 8 am to 6 pm.

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

Metrô lines 1, 2 and 4 run a Saturday schedule from 5 am to midnight, and 7 am to 11 pm on Sundays and holidays. The single-journey fare is R$7.90, about US$1.55 — the regulator approved a rise to R$8.20 in April, but a state decree has held the fare where it is. A contactless card or a Giro pass saves you the machine queue at the busy interchanges.

The VLT light rail runs roughly 6 am to midnight every day, with longer gaps between trains at weekends. For the derby, Engenho de Dentro is on the SuperVia line rather than the Metrô, and ride-hail surge around the ground is steep in the half-hour after the final whistle — walking ten minutes away from the stadium before you book is the cheap trick.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: Cais do Oriente at Rua Visconde de Itaboraí 8 in Centro serves a Saturday feijoada in a restored 19th-century warehouse a few minutes from Praça XV, which puts you within walking distance of both museums above. It is a sit-down lunch rather than a quick one, so allow a couple of hours.

Dinner: Bar do David in Chapéu Mangueira, above Leme, is the award-winning boteco worth the trip — note it is in Leme, not Santa Teresa, as some listings claim. In Lapa, the Rua do Lavradio strip stays open past midnight; Casa Momus at number 11 runs to 2 am on a Saturday. Most places take cards, but keep R$100, about US$20, in small notes for the street bars.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Today is a heat day, not a jacket day. The minimum is 17°C overnight but the maximum is 35°C, and the north-westerly makes the Centro streets feel closer than the number suggests. Drink more water than you think you need, and treat 11 am to 3 pm as indoor time.

Book the Jardim Botânico online through the official site to skip the Saturday-morning queue. Museu do Amanhã and MAR both stop admitting at 5 pm, so a 4:30 pm arrival is cutting it fine.

For the derby, leave the passport in the safe and carry a photo of it, take only one card, and agree a meeting point with anyone you are going with before you get to the ground. Rival colours are not a good idea at either end.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

If you are new and looking for people, apply one filter to anything you are sent: a real event has a date, a named venue and a booking link. A great many “weekly meetups” recycled through WhatsApp groups have none of the three, and several point at venues that closed months ago.

A word of caution on listings. Several nomad guides still point to Selina’s Lapa and Copacabana properties for rooftop mixers. Selina wound up its Brazilian operation in early 2025 and those two buildings now trade under different owners and different names, so check the venue exists before you cross town for an event.

08

Game Day

THE WEEKEND ROUND

Round 22 of the Campeonato Brasileiro runs across Saturday and Sunday. Tonight in Rio: Botafogo v Fluminense at the Nilton Santos, 9 pm BRT. Elsewhere today, Grêmio host São Paulo at 4 pm, Remo play Atlético-MG at 6:30 pm and Coritiba meet Chapecoense at 8:30 pm.

Sunday brings the rest, and two of them matter in Rio: Bahia v Vasco at 4 pm and Flamengo v Vitória at the Maracanã at 7:30 pm. The other Sunday fixtures are Cruzeiro v Mirassol at 11 am, Palmeiras v Internacional at 4 pm, and Bragantino v Corinthians and Santos v Athletico-PR, both at 6:30 pm.

Coverage is split between Premiere, SporTV, Globo, Record and Prime Video depending on the match, so check which one carries your fixture before you settle into a bar. There are no round-22 matches on Monday.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

Friday’s close split cleanly between New York and São Paulo. US July payrolls came in at minus 23,000 against a consensus near plus 80,000, which markets read as the end of the case for another rate rise: the Nasdaq Composite rose about 1.3% to 26,690.62 and the S&P 500 closed at a record 7,757.64, with the Dow up 0.28%.

Brazil did not join in. The Ibovespa fell 1.73% to 172,513, dragged by Petrobras, and closed the week down 3.08% — its worst week since May. The one part of the global move that did reach Brazil was the currency: the real firmed about 0.46% on the day to R$5.08 as the dollar softened. If you read elsewhere that a weak US jobs report lifted Brazilian assets, that is true of the real and not of the stock market.

The week ahead is an inflation week. Brazil’s IPCA for July lands on Tuesday 11 August, IBGE’s services-sector survey follows on Wednesday 12 August, and US July CPI is published the same Wednesday at 8:30 am in New York, which is 9:30 am in Rio. Anyone paid in dollars and spending in reais should watch the second of those rather than the first.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

THE DAYS AHEAD SAT 8 — 17–35°C, isolated showers — Centro museums by day, Botafogo v Fluminense at 9 pm. SUN 9 — 17–33°C, isolated rain — Bahia v Vasco at 4 pm; Flamengo v Vitória at the Maracanã at 7:30 pm. MON 10 — 16–27°C, cloudy — the cool change arrives; Pedra do Sal roda de samba from 7 pm, free. TUE 11 — 17–26°C, showers — IPCA for July in the morning; MAR free-entry day. WED 12 — cloudy — US July CPI at 9:30 am Rio time; IBGE services data; Museu do Amanhã and MAR both closed.

Background: Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight — August 7, 2026.

Background: Rio de Janeiro Daily Brief — Friday, August 7, 2026.

11

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

What is on in Rio de Janeiro today, Saturday 8 August?

The Rio derby. Botafogo host Fluminense at the Estádio Nilton Santos in Engenho de Dentro at 9 pm BRT, the headline fixture of round 22 of the Campeonato Brasileiro. It is the only big-club match in the city this weekend day, and bars across the Zona Sul will have it on with sound. Note that the Pedra do Sal roda de samba, which many listings still attach to any night of the week, runs on Mondays, from 7 pm to midnight and free, at Largo João da Baiana in Saúde. There is no Saturday roda there.

Which Rio museums are actually open today?

Open on a Saturday: CCBB (free, 9 am to 8 pm, closed Tuesdays), Paço Imperial (free, 12 pm to 6 pm), Museu do Amanhã (R$40 full, R$20 half — about US$7.90 and US$3.95 — 10 am to 6 pm, closed Wednesdays), MAR (R$20 full, R$10 half, 11 am to 6 pm, closed Wednesdays) and the Centro Cultural dos Correios (free, 12 pm to 7 pm), which is showing “Roberto Burle Marx pelos amigos” until 22 August. Closed today: the Real Gabinete Português de Leitura, which opens Monday to Friday, and the Museu Nacional de Belas Artes, whose single reopened space, the Galeria de Moldagens II, is open weekdays from 1 pm to 5 pm only.

How hot is it going to get, and what should I carry?

Alerta Rio has the city between 17°C and 35°C today, cloudy to partly cloudy, with isolated light to moderate showers and a moderate to strong wind from the north-west. That is the hot end of a Rio winter, not the crisp end, so carry water, sunscreen and a hat rather than a jacket. The change arrives Monday, when a southerly drops the maximum to 27°C under cloud, with Tuesday at 26°C. If you have an outdoor plan that needs sun, do it this weekend. Sunset today is at 5:34 pm.

Sources: Alerta Rio — extended forecast, CCBB Rio — visiting hours, Museu do Amanhã — hours and tickets, Museu de Arte do Rio — hours and tickets, Jardim Botânico do Rio — tickets, MetrôRio — fares, Riotur — Roda de Samba da Pedra do Sal, Exame — Brasileirão round 22 fixtures

World.title: São Paulo Daily Brief — Saturday, August 8, 2026
World.content:
São Paulo today starts wet and blustery: showers overnight and into the morning, easing through the afternoon, with gusts of up to 70 km/h.

Culture carries the day. The Pinacoteca is free across all three buildings, and Japan House on Avenida Paulista is free until 7 pm.

Wall Street rallied on a weak US jobs report and gold hit a seven-week high, but the Ibovespa fell anyway; the board carries the settled figures.

The day for an indoor morning near Luz, a long lunch, and Ibirapuera once the rain lifts.

Ibirapuera is the afternoon option once Saturday morning’s showers clear. Photo: The Rio Times archive.

Weather & What to Wear

THE WEEKEND

SAT 8 16–27°C morning showers, gusts to 70 km/h SUN 9 16–27°C cloudy MON 10 – TUE 11 — beyond the city forecast window

The city’s emergency-management centre has showers overnight and through Saturday morning, easing from the afternoon, with the temperature between 16°C and 27°C and humidity high all day. Gusts of up to 70 km/h are forecast through today, part of the windstorm alert that covers eleven states including São Paulo.

So: waterproof layer in the morning, and do not bother with an umbrella you mind losing — the wind will take it. Sunday stays cloudy at much the same temperatures. The city’s own forecast does not extend reliably past Sunday, so we are not printing Monday and Tuesday numbers we cannot stand behind.

Sunset today: 5:48 pm.

02

Day at a Glance

SNAPSHOT

— Weather: Morning showers easing, 16–27°C, gusts to 70 km/h. — Today’s pick: Free Saturday at the Pinacoteca, all three buildings. — Also free: Japan House on Paulista until 7 pm; MAC USP in Ibirapuera until 6 pm. — Markets: Wall Street rallied and gold hit a seven-week high; the Ibovespa fell 1.73%. — Football: São Paulo away to Grêmio at 4 pm; nothing at home today. — The day for: An indoor morning at Luz, then Ibirapuera when the rain lifts. A grey, gusty Saturday that pushes you indoors for the good half of the day — which in São Paulo is no hardship at all.

03

What to See & Do

SATURDAY IN SÃO PAULO

TODAY’S PICK — ART & THE CITY A Free Saturday Across the Pinacoteca, Then the Mercadão The Pinacoteca de São Paulo in Luz is free for everyone on Saturdays, across Pina Luz, Pina Estação and Pina Contemporânea. It opens 10 am to 6 pm with last entry at 5 pm, and closes on Tuesdays. No proof of anything is needed for the free rate, but the museum recommends booking a timed slot online, and before 11 am is the quiet window. Take the Metrô to Luz on Linha 1-Azul or Linha 4-Amarela and walk three minutes. On a wet morning this is the right first move of the day: three buildings, all indoors, all within a few minutes of each other. Afterwards, walk twelve minutes to the Mercado Municipal for a mortadella sandwich under the stained glass. The Mercadão is open 6 am to 6 pm on Saturdays. Bar do Mané has been making the sandwich since 1933 and now charges from about R$43, roughly US$8.50, for the 350g version; Hocca Bar next door does the pastel de bacalhau.

THE VIEW — IF THE CLOUD LIFTS Farol Santander, 26 Floors Above Anhangabaú Farol Santander at Rua João Brícola 24 opens Tuesday to Sunday, 9 am to 8 pm, with the last ticket sold at 7 pm. The observation deck and café sit on the 26th floor and the ticket is R$45, or R$22.50 concession — about US$8.85 and US$4.45. This is the one item on today’s list that depends on the weather. Check the cloud before you buy: on a grey afternoon the view is a wall of white, and there is no refund for that. If it stays overcast, swap it for the Museu do Ipiranga, open 10 am to 5 pm with last entry at 4 pm, R$30 full and R$15 half, about US$5.90 and US$2.95.

OUTDOORS — LATE AFTERNOON Ibirapuera and Beco do Batman, Once the Rain Eases Ibirapuera Park is open daily from 5 am to midnight, and the forecast has the showers easing from the afternoon, so this is a late-in-the-day plan rather than a morning one. MAC USP, in the Pavilhão Ciccillo Matarazzo inside the park, is free and open Tuesday to Sunday from 10 am to 6 pm, with an eighth-floor terrace that looks back over the marquise. The nearest station is AACD–Servidor on Linha 5-Lilás, about fifteen minutes on foot to Portão 5. Prêt no MAM, the café at the Museu de Arte Moderna inside the park, is the reliable coffee stop — note the name, since several guides list it as “Prêt no Parque”, which does not exist. Beco do Batman in Vila Madalena is free, open-air and best in the last hour of daylight. It is also the wettest-looking option on a day like today, so keep it flexible.

THE QUIET ALTERNATIVE Museu da Língua Portuguesa, Inside Estação da Luz The Museu da Língua Portuguesa sits inside the Estação da Luz, a two-minute walk from the Pinacoteca, and opens Tuesday to Sunday from 9 am to 4:30 pm, with visitors free to stay until 6 pm. Tickets are booked through Sympla. One correction worth making, because it circulates widely: the museum’s free days are Tuesdays and Sundays, not Saturdays. Today it costs R$25, or R$12.50 concession — roughly US$4.90 and US$2.45. It is still the best value on this list for a rainy hour, and the permanent gallery on the rhythm of Portuguese rewards slow attention.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Centro First, Vila Madalena After Bar Brahma at Avenida São João 677, on the corner of Ipiranga, is the classic Centro stop and a two-block walk from Farol Santander. It has been there since 1948 and the terrace runs all evening. Live music is usual on a Saturday, but the line-up is set week by week, so check the board at the door rather than trusting a listing. In Vila Madalena, Posto 6 at Rua Aspicuelta 644, on the corner of Mourato Coelho, has been running since 2002 and fills from about 8 pm on a Saturday. The Aspicuelta–Fidalga–Mourato Coelho triangle is the densest few blocks of bars in the city and works without a plan. A word on listings: several nomad guides still send people to a Selina rooftop in Vila Madalena. Selina’s Brazilian operation collapsed and that property is listed as closed for the whole of 2026, so it is not an option tonight.

ALSO ON TODAY Free Saturday at the Pinacoteca — Luz — 10 am to 6 pm, last entry 5 pm, free across all three buildings. Japan House São Paulo — Avenida Paulista 52 — 10 am to 7 pm at weekends, free entry. MAC USP — Pavilhão Ciccillo Matarazzo, Ibirapuera — 10 am to 6 pm, free, eighth-floor terrace. Museu do Ipiranga — Parque da Independência — 10 am to 5 pm, last entry 4 pm, R$30 full and R$15 half (about US$5.90 and US$2.95). Farol Santander — Rua João Brícola 24, Centro — 9 am to 8 pm, last ticket 7 pm, R$45 (about US$8.85).

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

Today is Saturday, so the municipal rodízio does not apply — it runs Monday to Friday only, in the 7 to 10 am and 5 to 8 pm windows. Every plate can circulate freely until Monday morning.

The single-journey Metrô, CPTM and ViaMobilidade fare is R$5.40, about US$1.05, up from R$5.20 at the start of January; the integrated bus-and-rail fare is R$9.38, about US$1.85. Lines 1-Azul, 2-Verde, 3-Vermelha, 4-Amarela and 5-Lilás all run a Saturday timetable. We have not found any planned engineering notice for this weekend, but a negative is hard to prove, so check the operator’s status page before a long journey.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: The Mercado Municipal is the obvious call on a wet Saturday and it is indoors: the mortadella sandwich at Bar do Mané from about R$43, roughly US$8.50, or the pastel de bacalhau at Hocca Bar. It closes at 6 pm, so this is lunch, not dinner. If you are on Paulista instead, the basement food court at Shopping Cidade São Paulo, at Avenida Paulista 1230, is the cheap and dependable option.

Dinner: Posto 6 in Vila Madalena for a long, loud Saturday evening, or Aizomê at Japan House if you want the opposite — note that Aizomê is a proper Japanese restaurant with prices to match, not a canteen. Reservations are rarely essential in Vila Madalena, but a message an hour ahead saves you a pavement table in the rain.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry a waterproof layer rather than an umbrella, given the gusts, and a fully charged phone for Pix. Contactless cards work at every venue on this list; a R$50 note, about US$10, is still useful at the smaller Mercadão stalls.

Book the free Pinacoteca slot and the Museu do Ipiranga ticket online in advance — the Ipiranga free Wednesdays also require a booking, which catches people out. Both museums stop admitting an hour before they close.

After dark, stick to the well-lit stretch between Bar Brahma and Farol Santander in Centro rather than the quieter side of Praça da República. In Vila Madalena the crowd itself is the safety, so stay on the busy blocks.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

São Paulo has a large and genuinely active expat and nomad scene, but it is worth applying one filter to anything you read: a real event has a date, a named venue and a booking link. A great many listings recycled across WhatsApp groups have none of the three, and several point at venues that have since closed.

The clearest current example is Selina. The chain wound up its Brazilian operation and the Vila Madalena property is listed as closed for all of 2026, yet its rooftop still appears in nomad guides as a weekly fixture. If you are new here, check the venue is open before you cross the city for a meetup.

08

Game Day

THE WEEKEND ROUND

Round 22 of the Campeonato Brasileiro is split across Saturday and Sunday, and the São Paulo clubs are mostly out of town or playing tomorrow. Today: Grêmio v São Paulo at 4 pm BRT at the Arena do Grêmio in Porto Alegre. Also today, Remo v Atlético-MG at 6:30 pm, Coritiba v Chapecoense at 8:30 pm, and the Rio derby, Botafogo v Fluminense, at 9 pm.

Sunday is the big local day. Palmeiras v Internacional kicks off at 4 pm at Palmeiras’ ground in Água Branca, Bragantino v Corinthians at 6:30 pm in Bragança Paulista, and Santos v Athletico-PR at 6:30 pm at Vila Belmiro. Cruzeiro v Mirassol opens the day at 11 am, Bahia v Vasco is at 4 pm and Flamengo v Vitória closes it at 7:30 pm.

Coverage is split between Premiere, SporTV, Globo, Record and Prime Video depending on the fixture, so confirm which one has your match before you commit to a bar. Vila Madalena screens most of them with sound.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

Friday’s close was good almost everywhere except São Paulo. US July payrolls fell by 23,000 against a consensus near plus 80,000, and markets took it as the end of the argument for another rate rise: the Nasdaq Composite rose about 1.3% to 26,690.62, the S&P 500 closed at a record 7,757.64 and the Dow added 0.28%. Gold jumped 2.1% on Friday to about US$4,348 an ounce, a seven-week high, and finished the week up roughly 7.5%.

Brazil went the other way. The Ibovespa fell 1.73% to 172,513, weighed down by Petrobras, and ended the week 3.08% lower — its worst week since May. The currency did follow the global move: the real firmed about 0.46% on the day to R$5.08 as the dollar softened. If you see it written that the weak US jobs report lifted Brazilian assets, that holds for the real and not for the stock market.

The week ahead is about inflation. Brazil’s IPCA for July is published on Tuesday 11 August, IBGE’s services survey follows on Wednesday 12 August, and US July CPI lands the same Wednesday at 8:30 am in New York, which is 9:30 am here. For anyone earning in dollars and spending in reais, the second number is the one that shows up in your budget.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

THE DAYS AHEAD SAT 8 — Showers easing, 16–27°C — free Saturday at the Pinacoteca; Grêmio v São Paulo at 4 pm. SUN 9 — Cloudy, 16–27°C — Palmeiras v Internacional at 4 pm; Museu da Língua Portuguesa free. MON 10 — Pinacoteca open, MASP and most museums closed; a good admin day. TUE 11 — MASP free until 8 pm and Museu da Língua Portuguesa free; IPCA for July in the morning; Pinacoteca closed. WED 12 — Museu do Ipiranga free with advance booking; US July CPI at 9:30 am São Paulo time; IBGE services data.

Is the Pinacoteca really free today, and do I need to book?

Yes. Admission to the Pinacoteca de São Paulo is free for everyone on Saturdays, across all three buildings — Pina Luz, Pina Estação and Pina Contemporânea. The museum opens 10 am to 6 pm, with last entry at 5 pm, and closes on Tuesdays. You do not need to prove anything to get the free rate, but the museum recommends booking a timed ticket online, and arriving before 11 am avoids the worst of the queue. Take the Metrô to Luz on Linha 1-Azul or Linha 4-Amarela and walk three minutes.

What is free today and what is not?

Free today: the Pinacoteca, Japan House on Avenida Paulista (10 am to 7 pm at weekends) and MAC USP inside Ibirapuera (Tuesday to Sunday, 10 am to 6 pm). World.title: Colombia’s New President Says the Wealth Tax Will Go — What That Means if You Live There
World.content:
Colombia · Taxes

Key Facts The pledge. President Abelardo De La Espriella said in his inaugural address on 7 August that the wealth tax will be abolished: “we must stop punishing those who invest and generate wealth.”

President Abelardo De La Espriella said in his inaugural address on 7 August that the wealth tax will be abolished: “we must stop punishing those who invest and generate wealth.” Not law. It is an announcement. Abolition requires a structural tax reform passed by Congress, and no bill has been filed.

It is an announcement. Abolition requires a structural tax reform passed by Congress, and no bill has been filed. Also announced. A decree freezing public spending, the recovery of Ecopetrol as a priority, and the re-authorisation of fracking.

A decree freezing public spending, the recovery of Ecopetrol as a priority, and the re-authorisation of fracking. Why it matters to you. The impuesto al patrimonio is the levy that reaches foreign tax residents in Colombia on their worldwide assets above the threshold.

The impuesto al patrimonio is the levy that reaches foreign tax residents in Colombia on their worldwide assets above the threshold. The setting. He gave the address from the Cantón Militar Pichincha, a military garrison, rather than from Bogotá.

Colombia’s new president says the wealth tax will go. It is the levy that reaches foreign residents’ worldwide assets — and it is an announcement, not a law.

The Colombia wealth tax is the first thing the new government named. In his inaugural address on Friday, Abelardo De La Espriella said the impuesto al patrimonio would be abolished as the centrepiece of a structural tax reform, because the country “must stop punishing those who invest and generate wealth”. For foreigners weighing Colombian tax residency, no other line in that speech matters as much — and none is further from being law.

Colombia’s New President Says the Wealth Tax Will Go — What That Means if You Live There. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the Colombia wealth tax pledge actually is

De La Espriella took the oath at 3 p.m. on Friday at the Universidad Santiago de Cali, then delivered his first address from a military garrison. The economic content was the part that matters to anyone with assets in Colombia. He named a structural tax reform, and named its headline measure: the wealth tax goes.

Alongside it he said he would sign a decree freezing public spending “in the coming hours”, called the recovery of Ecopetrol an absolute priority, and confirmed that Colombia will re-authorise fracking under what he called responsible and sustainable technical standards.

Be clear about what this is. Abolishing the impuesto al patrimonio is not something a president can decree. It requires a tax reform bill through both chambers of Congress, and the previous government’s own tax reform died there in July. No bill has been filed. What exists today is a stated intention from a president on his first day.

Why the wealth tax matters to foreign residents specifically

Colombia taxes its tax residents on worldwide income and worldwide assets. You become a tax resident by spending more than 183 days in the country across any rolling 365-day period, and the clock does not reset at the calendar year.

For most foreigners the income side is manageable, because Colombia gives credit for tax paid abroad. The asset side is the one that catches people out. The wealth tax applies to net worth above the threshold, wherever in the world that wealth sits — a house in Europe, a pension pot, a brokerage account. For a retiree or a remote worker with accumulated savings, it can turn a comfortable cost-of-living arbitrage into an expensive one.

That is why this announcement is worth more attention than a typical tax headline. It is not a rate tweak. It is the specific provision that most often decides whether someone lets the 183-day clock run out or leaves before it does.

Colombians have already had one scare on this. In December the outgoing government used emergency powers to cut the entry threshold from 72,000 UVT to 40,000 UVT, a change that would have brought the total number of people liable to around 105,000, including plenty of foreign residents who had never expected to file. The Constitutional Court suspended the decree in January and struck it down in April, and the threshold reverted. That episode is worth remembering for two reasons: the wealth tax is the lever Colombian governments reach for first, and the court is the backstop that decides how far they get.

What to do about it, which is mostly nothing

Do not restructure anything on the strength of an inaugural speech. Between an announcement and a promulgated law sit a filed bill, two chambers, committee stages and, in Colombia, a reasonable chance of a Constitutional Court challenge. The previous administration’s reform cleared none of that.

What is worth doing now is knowing your own position. Count your days honestly across the rolling year, not the calendar year. Know whether your net worth would sit above or below the current threshold. For 2026 that line is 72,000 UVT, and with the UVT fixed at COP 52,374 for the year it works out to about COP 3.77 billion, or roughly US$1.19 million at Friday’s rate. Above it the rate starts at 0.5 percent and rises in bands. The threshold is written in UVT rather than pesos precisely so that it moves with inflation every January, which means a portfolio that sits comfortably below the line one year can cross it the next without you doing anything at all. If you are close to either line, that is a conversation with a Colombian accountant, not a decision to take from a news story.

The other thing worth watching is the offset. A government that removes a tax and freezes spending in the same week has to find the money somewhere, and the same speech promised mega-prisons and a harder security posture, neither of which is cheap. What replaces the wealth tax in the reform bill will tell you more than its removal does.

The wider signal

Read this alongside what the outgoing government did in its final fortnight. On 4 August the environment ministry signed a resolution closing 42 percent of the country to new mining and oil contracts. On 20 July it filed a bill to ban fracking outright. Within three weeks Colombia has produced both of those and a new president promising the opposite on both counts.

For anyone modelling Colombian exposure, the lesson is not which side wins. It is that Colombian tax and resource policy now changes with the political cycle rather than through settled law, and that instruments made by decree or resolution can be unmade the same way. Price the volatility, not the position. This is general information, not tax or legal advice.

World.content:
Argentina · Markets

Key Facts The number. Argentina’s country risk closed at 451 basis points on Friday, up 3 percent on the day and the highest since June.

Argentina’s country risk closed at 451 basis points on Friday, up 3 percent on the day and the highest since June. The streak. The Merval fell for a sixth straight session and is down roughly 5 percent so far in August. New York-listed Argentine shares lost as much as 5.6 percent.

The Merval fell for a sixth straight session and is down roughly 5 percent so far in August. New York-listed Argentine shares lost as much as 5.6 percent. The oddity. All of it happened while Wall Street rallied and the dollar weakened after a soft US jobs report — the rest of Latin America went up.

All of it happened while Wall Street rallied and the dollar weakened after a soft US jobs report — the rest of Latin America went up. The tell. The blue-dollar gap has collapsed to about 0.3 percent, but the CCL gap has widened to about 5.4 percent.

The blue-dollar gap has collapsed to about 0.3 percent, but the CCL gap has widened to about 5.4 percent. The line. The wholesale dollar again failed to break 1,500 pesos, closing at 1,498.50 with the central bank a net buyer of dollars.

The wholesale dollar again failed to break 1,500 pesos, closing at 1,498.50 with the central bank a net buyer of dollars. The date. INDEC publishes July inflation on Thursday 13 August at 4 p.m., with consensus near 2.0 percent.

Argentina country risk hit 451 basis points on a day the rest of Latin America rallied. The gap between the blue dollar and the CCL says who is doing the selling.

Argentina country risk closed at 451 basis points on Friday, its highest since June, on a day when a weak US jobs report lifted almost every other asset in Latin America. The Merval fell for a sixth straight session. When a market drops on a good global day, the reason is at home — and the clearest signal is hiding in the exchange rates.

Argentine shares fell for a sixth session while the rest of the region rallied on the US jobs report. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What Argentina country risk did while everyone else rallied

Friday should have been a good day for Argentine assets. US payrolls came in far below expectations, the dollar sagged, and money moved into emerging markets. Brazilian, Mexican, Chilean and Peruvian assets all firmed.

Argentina went the other way. Country risk — the spread investors demand to hold Argentine sovereign debt over US Treasuries — rose 3 percent to 451 basis points, its highest since June. The Merval closed lower for a sixth consecutive session, taking its August decline to close to 6 percent in pesos, and Argentine ADRs in New York fell by as much as 5.6 percent.

A market that falls on a good global day is telling you something local. This is not the dollar, the Fed or commodity prices. It is Argentina.

The two gaps, and why the difference matters

The most useful number here is not the headline spread. It is the divergence between Argentina’s parallel exchange rates.

The blue dollar — the street rate, the one tourists and small savers use — closed at 1,525, five pesos lower on the day and its weakest since 16 July, against a retail official near 1,520. That is a gap of roughly 0.3 percent. By Argentine standards it is nothing. For most of the past decade that gap has been measured in tens of percent.

The contado con liquidación, the rate at which institutions move money out of the country legally by buying securities locally and selling them abroad, closed near 1,579. That is a gap of about 5.4 percent against the wholesale rate, and it is widening.

Read together, those two numbers say the retail panic is gone and the institutional exit is not. Households are not queuing for dollars. Funds are trimming Argentine paper and taking the money out. That is a slower, quieter kind of pressure than a currency run, and it is harder for a government to talk down.

The 1,500 line

The wholesale dollar ended a four-session rise and again failed to break 1,500 pesos, closing at 1,498.50, a peso lower on the day. The central bank was a net buyer of about US$16 million in that session, roughly 4 percent of the dollars on offer, so this was not a defence funded by selling reserves. The retail rate remains well below the band ceiling of 1,852.73 pesos, which is the level at which the central bank would be obliged to step in.

Holding a line is cheaper than restoring one, but it is not free, and every day spent defending a round number is a day of reserves not spent on something else. The question for the next fortnight is whether 1,500 is a level the authorities have chosen or a level the market has yet to test properly.

What it means if you live in or earn in Argentina

If you are paid in dollars, the practical picture has not changed much this week: the blue and the official are effectively the same rate, so the old arithmetic of changing money on the street no longer buys you anything meaningful. Use whichever channel is convenient and legal for you.

If you are paid in pesos, the date to put in your diary is Thursday 13 August. INDEC publishes July inflation at 4 p.m., and consensus sits near 2.0 percent on the month. That figure feeds directly into rent indexation, pension adjustments and UVA loan balances, so it lands on your actual budget rather than on a screen.

If you hold Argentine assets, the honest read is that the market decoupled from the region this week for domestic reasons, and the CCL gap suggests the money leaving is not retail. Neither of those resolves before the inflation print. This is general information, not investment advice.

If you are moving money in or out, the spread that matters now is the CCL, not the blue. A wedge of about 5 percent between the wholesale rate and the rate at which securities move dollars offshore is the real price of getting capital out of the country, and it has been widening rather than narrowing all week. That is a cost worth checking before you time a transfer, and it is the number to watch if you are weighing whether to bring savings into Argentina at all.

World.content:
The Short Version In short: Your LatAm expat and nomad daily guide for Saturday, August 8. Colombia’s new president used his first hours to promise the abolition of the wealth tax and to re-authorise fracking, and a weak US jobs report pushed the Mexican peso to a five-month high and the Peruvian sol to a four-month high. 01 Colombia’s opening move. All of it is announced, none of it is law. 02 The dollar slipped. US payrolls fell 23,000 in July against a consensus of about +80,000, and September rate-hike odds dropped from roughly 57 to 44 percent. 03 This weekend. Medellín’s Desfile de Silleteros closes the Feria on Sunday afternoon, and Cali opens the 30th Petronio Álvarez the same day. What changed since yesterdayColombia moved from ceremony to policy: the new government named the wealth tax as its first target and confirmed fracking will return. The US jobs report came in far weaker than expected, lifting the peso and the sol. Argentina went the other way, with country risk climbing to 451 while the rest of the region rallied.

Good morning. Your LatAm expat nomad daily guide opens on what Colombia’s new government said it will do to taxes, a soft US jobs number that moved every currency in the region, and a weekend of parades.

01 Visas & Residency

Where What changed What it means for you Colombia The new government says it will abolish the wealth tax as the centrepiece of a structural tax reform, and announced a decree freezing public spending. Nothing has passed Congress. The wealth tax is the levy that catches foreign tax residents on worldwide assets above the threshold, so this is the single biggest change to the calculus of becoming a Colombian tax resident in years — if it survives Congress. Do not restructure anything on an announcement. Colombia Fracking will be re-authorised under what the president called responsible and sustainable technical standards. Nothing for your visa. It matters for energy costs and for anyone with upstream exposure, and it will draw an immediate court challenge. Region-wide No visa or residency rule changed anywhere in the region on Friday or overnight. The rules that bind you today are the ones that bound you last week — Argentina’s border insurance check, Brazil and Panama’s insurance conditions on visas, and the tighter tourist-stay enforcement across the region.

02 Cost of Living & Money

Markets are closed for the weekend, so the rates below are Friday’s close — except the Colombian peso, where the official rate is set daily and carries through today. The direction of travel came from Washington: US payrolls fell 23,000 in July against a consensus of about 80,000 gains, with May and June revised down by a combined 103,000 and participation at a five-year low of 61.4 percent. The dollar sagged and every currency in the region firmed.

Currency Per US$ Read Brazilian real 5.09 firmer on the US data Mexican peso 17.14 five-month high for the peso; intraday 17.09 Colombian peso 3,157 official rate in force today Chilean peso 915 barely moved Peruvian sol 3.38 four-month low for the dollar Argentine peso 1,520 retail; blue near 1,525, CCL near 1,579 Uruguayan peso 40.25 stable

If you earn in dollars and spend in pesos or soles, this is the worst level since March in Mexico and since April in Peru. If you have a local obligation you were planning to fund, the arithmetic just got worse. The Fed is on hold at 3.50 to 3.75 percent, and the market cut the odds of a September hike from about 57 percent to about 44 after the jobs print — an unusual direction for this region to be reading. Mexico’s Banxico held at 6.50 percent on Thursday, its second hold in a row.

Argentina is the exception and it is worth watching. Country risk closed at 451 basis points, up 3 percent on the day and the highest since June, with the Merval down for a sixth straight session while Wall Street rallied. The blue-dollar gap has collapsed to under half a percent, but the CCL gap has widened to about 5.6 percent — the tell that the pressure is on institutional money leaving rather than retail.

03 What’s On

Sunday is the big day. Medellín’s Feria de las Flores closes with the Desfile de Silleteros, 2 p.m. to 7 p.m., in its 69th edition, with around 700 silleteros carrying flower arrangements that can weigh over 100 kilos along a 2.4-kilometre route. Get there early and check the route on the day — local outlets are giving different versions of it.

Cali opens the 30th Festival Petronio Álvarez the same day with the commemorative parade “Bundeando pa’ la Casa Grande”, with more than 1,600 participants from 23 Pacific-coast colonias. The main programme — the music competition, the traditional-expressions showcase and the Caserío Pacífico — runs 12 to 17 August at the Unidad Deportiva Alberto Galindo.

In Brazil, Sunday is Dia dos Pais. Restaurants in Rio and São Paulo will be full and reservations scarce, so book today if you have not. São Paulo also has the Heritage Festival and the Festa de Nossa Senhora Achiropita, the Italian street festival in Bixiga. In Mexico City, the Festival de Culturas Indígenas, Pueblos y Barrios Originarios is running free in the Zócalo until 23 August, with a large food pavilion.

04 Art & Culture

The Petronio is the cultural event of the Colombian year for anyone interested in Afro-Pacific music, and the 30th edition adds a Global Afro-Diasporic Summit and an anniversary exhibition. If you are in Cali this week, the free programming around the Unidad Deportiva is the part most visitors miss.

Medellín’s silleteros are the older tradition — campesino flower growers from Santa Elena who once carried their stock into the city on their backs, now carrying arrangements as artworks. It is the one day of the year the city genuinely stops.

05 Food & Coffee

Two practical notes. In São Paulo and Rio, Father’s Day Sunday is the single busiest restaurant day of the Brazilian winter — if you want a table anywhere good, today is the last realistic moment to book. And in Cali, the Caserío Pacífico at the Petronio is the best week of the year to eat Pacific-coast food outside the coast itself, from encocados to viche.

06 Community & Safety

Brazil. The cyclone has moved out to sea, but INMET’s windstorm alert runs through today across eleven states including Rio, São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Espírito Santo, with gusts of up to 100 km/h possible on the Rio and São Paulo coasts. The Port of Santos channel was shut for about 90 minutes on Friday and ferry services were halted. Expect residual delays at Santos Dumont and Congonhas and rough seas. The serious damage was in Rio Grande do Sul on Thursday: one person killed, five injured, 118 municipalities reporting damage, more than 1,800 people out of their homes and around 229,000 properties still without power on Friday afternoon.

Cali. The drone ban over Cali and neighbouring municipalities runs until 11:59 p.m. tonight, enforced with anti-drone systems, and downtown road closures hold through today. If you are heading to Sunday’s Petronio parade, expect closures to be lifting only through Sunday morning. Our guide to the Cali restrictions has the detail.

07 What to Watch — August 8–17

Sat Aug 8 Drone ban over Cali and neighbours ends at 11:59 p.m.; INMET wind alert across eleven Brazilian states.

Sun Aug 9 Medellín’s Desfile de Silleteros, 2 p.m.; Cali opens the 30th Petronio Álvarez; Dia dos Pais in Brazil.

Tue Aug 11 Brazil’s IPCA inflation for July, from IBGE at noon. Inflation is running 3.36 percent year to date against 4.26 percent for all of 2025.

Wed Aug 12 Brazil retail trade survey; the Petronio main programme opens at the Unidad Deportiva Alberto Galindo in Cali.

Thu Aug 13 Argentina’s INDEC inflation for July, 4 p.m. Consensus is around 2.0 percent on the month. This one feeds straight into rent indexation, pensions and UVA loan balances. Colombia’s cabinet meets in La Guajira.

Mon Aug 17 Festival Petronio Álvarez closes in Cali.

01 America loses jobs, and Wall Street cheers

The most important number of the month landed with a jolt. The United States economy actually shed 23,000 jobs in July, a stark miss against forecasts of an 80,000 gain and the first monthly decline in years. Wages cooled too, rising just 3.2% over the year, below expectations.

Ordinarily a shrinking jobs market would frighten investors. Instead, stocks rallied to fresh records — the S&P 500 closed at an all-time high, the Nasdaq jumped 1.3%, and even smaller companies advanced. The logic was simple: a weak labour market takes the pressure off the Federal Reserve, and investors quickly concluded that a rate rise, feared only weeks ago, is now firmly off the table.

Bond yields and the dollar fell as traders repriced the outlook for cheaper money, while gold jumped 2.11% and the market’s fear gauge sank to unusually calm levels. It was a near-perfect mirror image of early June, when a blockbuster jobs report sent shares tumbling on fears of higher rates. The same machinery, running in reverse, this time delivered a celebration.

02 A weaker dollar hands Brazil an opening

For Brazil, few developments are as welcome as a Federal Reserve expected to hold or lower rates. When American rates look set to fall, the dollar softens and higher-yielding markets like Brazil become more attractive — and the market’s response on Friday, with the dollar and US yields sliding, pointed exactly that way.

The domestic backdrop is strengthening the case. Brazilian wholesale prices fell again in July, a monthly drop of 0.86% that deepened an existing deflation, while car production rebounded. Across the region the story rhymed: Mexican core inflation slipped below 4% for the first time in months. With inflation fading at home and the external threat from US rates easing, Brazil’s central bank has room to keep lowering the Selic rate from its current 14.00%.

Investors are already positioning for it. Foreign bets on the real climbing in value jumped sharply last week, reaching their highest in months — a clear signal that global money expects the currency to strengthen as the interest-rate gap with the United States narrows in Brazil’s favour. After a year in which the hawkish Fed was the chief obstacle, a cooling US jobs market may prove the moment the balance tips toward Brazil.

03 The paradox — unemployment fell because workers vanished

Buried in the jobs report was a genuine riddle. Even as the economy lost jobs, the unemployment rate did not rise — it fell, to 4.1%. On its face that looks like good news layered on bad, but the explanation is far less comforting.

The rate fell because people stopped looking for work altogether, and those no longer searching are not counted as unemployed. The share of Americans in the workforce slipped to 61.4%, and nearly 1.4 million people have left the labour force this year alone. A jobless rate that improves because the workforce is shrinking is a statistical mirage, not a sign of health. It also hands the Federal Reserve a genuine dilemma: the falling unemployment rate hints at a stable jobs market, while the outright loss of jobs points to a weakening one. Which signal the central bank chooses to believe will shape its next move — and the market has already placed its bet on the gloomier reading.

04 What to watch today and this week

Next week: US consumer price figures, the next major test of whether inflation is cool enough to let the Federal Reserve ease.

US consumer price figures, the next major test of whether inflation is cool enough to let the Federal Reserve ease. This week: Comments from Fed officials, for signs of how seriously they take the surprise drop in employment.

Comments from Fed officials, for signs of how seriously they take the surprise drop in employment. This week: The path of the dollar and US bond yields, the clearest gauges of shifting rate expectations and the main channel to Brazil.

The path of the dollar and US bond yields, the clearest gauges of shifting rate expectations and the main channel to Brazil. Ahead: Whether foreign inflows into Brazil and other emerging markets accelerate as bets on US rate cuts grow.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did stocks rise when the jobs report was so weak?

Because a weak labour market makes the Federal Reserve less likely to raise interest rates, and possibly more likely to cut them. Lower rates reduce borrowing costs and make shares more attractive, especially fast-growing technology companies. Investors judged that the loss of 23,000 jobs all but removes the threat of a rate rise that had worried markets, so they bought shares — sending the S&P 500 to a record. It is a case of apparently bad economic news being treated as good news for markets.

How can unemployment fall while the economy loses jobs?

The two figures come from different surveys and measure different things. The unemployment rate only counts people who are actively looking for work. In July, the rate fell to 4.1% not because more people found jobs, but because many stopped searching and left the workforce entirely — the participation rate dropped to 61.4%. People who are not looking are not counted as unemployed, so the rate can fall even as the number of jobs declines. It is a sign of a discouraged workforce, not a strong one.

What does a softer US jobs market mean for Brazil?

It is broadly positive. When the US economy weakens and the Federal Reserve is expected to lower rates, the dollar tends to soften and investors look for higher returns in emerging markets like Brazil. This supports the real and can attract foreign capital. Combined with falling inflation at home — Brazilian wholesale prices dropped again in July — it gives Brazil’s central bank more room to keep cutting its own interest rate, while a narrower rate gap with the US still leaves Brazil offering attractive returns.

Why are foreign bets on the real rising?

Investors use certain financial contracts to bet on whether a currency will strengthen or weaken. Last week those positions shifted sharply toward the real strengthening, reaching their highest in months. The reasoning is that as the US Federal Reserve moves toward cutting rates while Brazil’s inflation falls under control, the gap between the two countries’ rates works in Brazil’s favour, making the real more appealing. Rising bets of this kind often precede, and can help drive, actual gains in the currency.

Does this weak report guarantee a US rate cut?

Not necessarily. While markets have taken a near-term rate rise off the table, the picture is mixed. The economy lost jobs, which argues for easier policy, but the unemployment rate fell, which some Fed officials may read as a sign the labour market is still stable. The central bank will weigh both signals along with upcoming inflation data before deciding. So while the report makes a rate rise far less likely, it does not by itself lock in a cut — the coming weeks of data will be decisive.

Key Facts Chile’s S&P IPSA slipped 0.17% on Friday, a pause after Thursday’s close at the highest level since April

a pause after Thursday’s close at the highest level since April The week still finished 2.18% higher, making Chile the region’s strongest performer over the five sessions

making Chile the region’s strongest performer over the five sessions July inflation slowed sharply, with consumer prices up just 0.1% in the month and the annual rate falling from 4.3% to 3.5%

with consumer prices up just 0.1% in the month and the annual rate falling from 4.3% to 3.5% Two big earnings misses capped the session, as Cencosud dropped 0.49% after posting a quarterly loss and CMPC saw profits fall 89% from a year earlier

as Cencosud dropped 0.49% after posting a quarterly loss and CMPC saw profits fall 89% from a year earlier The dollar sank at the open, losing close to 10 pesos — though it closed down just 3.81, at 912.03 — after the United States reported a contraction of 23,000 jobs in July

Today’s Focus Chile spent the week doing everything right and then stopped to catch its breath. Inflation came in lower, the government’s reconstruction package passed, and the IPSA closed Thursday at its highest since April. Friday brought a marginal fall of 0.17%. The reason was partly caution ahead of the weekend and partly two large companies reporting figures the market did not like. None of that spoiled the week. The index still finished 2.18% higher, the best showing in Latin America over the five sessions. What matters today. Chile is the one market in the region whose gains this week came from its own economy rather than from an American data release.

01 The session in one read

The IPSA eased 0.17% on Friday, a marginal decline that followed a week of solid gains. Over the five sessions the index rose 2.18%, and it came into Friday having closed at its best level since April.

The morning suggested otherwise. The index opened 0.5% higher at 11,327.42 points, led by Santander at 2.1%, Bci at 1.5% and the lithium producer SQM-B at 1.5%, all heavyweight names.

It gave that back through the day. Diario Financiero described a market waiting for weekend news on the Middle East, while volatility widened in the United States after the July employment figures.

Two company reports did the rest. Cencosud fell 0.49% after a quarterly loss, and CMPC finished flat after profits collapsed, which took the shine off an otherwise constructive week.

Assessment — A pause, not a turn MEDIUM The distinction that matters is where Chile’s week came from. Mexico rose on an American data release and Brazil fell on the same one, but Chile advanced on domestic news: inflation falling from 4.3% to 3.5%, an earnings season delivering operational surprises, and a reconstruction package with tax reductions that the market read favourably. A 0.17% decline on the final day, driven by two identifiable company results and by caution before a weekend of geopolitical headlines, does not undo that. The variable to watch is copper, which eased on Friday and remains the single largest external influence on Chilean assets.

02 The week’s numbers

Measure Level Change Read S&P IPSA, Friday — −0.17% Marginal fall after Thursday’s April high S&P IPSA, week — +2.18% Best performer in Latin America Thursday’s close 11,275.15 +1.05% Highest level since April USD/CLP 912.03 −0.42% Fell close to 10 pesos at the open, pared to 3.8 by the close Annual inflation, July 3.5% from 4.3% Monthly rise of 0.1%, below the 0.2% expected Copper — −2.1% Eased on Friday; Chile’s largest export

The inflation figure is the number of the week. A fall from 4.3% to 3.5% in a single month is a large move, and by The Rio Times’ calculation it takes the annual rate 0.8 percentage points closer to the central bank’s 3% target.

The equity move should be read alongside it. An index that gains 2.18% in a week when inflation drops and a stimulus package passes is behaving rationally rather than speculatively.

03 Why it moved — good domestic news, then a pause for the weekend

The week’s foundation was laid at home. July consumer prices rose 0.1% from June, below the 0.2% expected, and the twelve-month inflation rate slowed from 4.3% to 3.5%.

Politics helped rather than hindered, which is not always the case. Parliament approved the government’s National Reconstruction Project, whose tax reductions and other stimulus measures were generally well received by market participants.

Earnings season added a third leg. Diario Financiero noted that results had brought positive operational surprises, and that combination carried the index to its best close since April on Thursday.

Friday interrupted the sequence for two reasons. The first was external: traders were waiting to see what emerged from the Middle East over the weekend, with the Strait of Hormuz still the dominant geopolitical question.

The second was corporate. Cencosud reported a loss of 36,500 million pesos for the second quarter when the market had on average expected a profit of 67,200 million, and the shares fell 0.49%.

CMPC gave a variation on the same theme. It sold more than expected in the quarter to June, but earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of nearly US$270 million came in below consensus and profits fell 89% from a year earlier to US$8.7 million.

04 The day’s movers

Driver Level / Move Change Note Santander Chile (BSANTANDER) — −1.11% Led at the open, then gave it all back Bci (BCI) — +1.5% Second bank among the early leaders SQM-B (SQM-B) — −0.77% Lithium producer; opened higher, closed lower CMPC (CMPC) — 0.0% Profits down 89% to US$8.7m; sales beat Cencosud (CENCOSUD) — −0.49% Quarterly loss of CLP 36,500m against expected profit

The opening leaderboard and the closing one told different stories. Santander, Bci and SQM-B all rose more than 1.5% in early trading, and between them they carry enough weight to lift the whole index.

The retail side pulled the other way. Cencosud’s loss was the session’s clearest negative, and its chief executive warned of aggressive competition in the Chilean market, which matters more for the sector’s outlook than the single quarter does.

CMPC is the more interesting case. The forestry group beat on revenue but missed on operating profit, and the 89% fall in net earnings shows how much pressure pulp and paper prices have put on margins.

05 The peso and the copper link

The dollar fell sharply at the open, losing close to 10 pesos after the United States reported that employers had cut 23,000 jobs in July against expectations of an 80,000 gain. The dollar pared most of that, settling at 912.03 pesos, a fall of 3.81 pesos or 0.42% on the day.

The mechanism runs through two channels at once. A weaker dollar lifts most emerging currencies, and lower American rate expectations reduce the pull of dollar assets.

For Chile there is a third channel that matters more than either. Copper is the country’s largest export, and the metal’s price sets the terms for export earnings, mining profits and, ultimately, the currency.

That link cut against the peso on Friday. Copper eased about 2.1% on Friday, having been higher earlier in the week, which takes some of the support away.

The inflation data works in the currency’s favour on a longer view. With the annual rate down to 3.5%, the pressure on the central bank has eased considerably from where it stood at the start of the year.

06 The regional scoreboard

Index Country Change IPC Mexico +0.82% IPSA Chile −0.17% Merval Argentina −0.45% Ibovespa Brazil −1.73% COLCAP Colombia closed

Friday was a day of small moves everywhere except Brazil. Mexico rose 0.82% because its market reads American data as its own, while the Ibovespa fell 1.73% as investors moved money out of emerging markets and into American technology shares.

Chile’s 0.17% decline sits closer to Argentina’s 0.45% fall than to either extreme, but the weekly picture is what separates them. Chile gained 2.18% over the five sessions while Argentina fell for a sixth consecutive day, and Colombia did not trade at all on Friday because of the Battle of Boyacá holiday.

07 The technical picture

The index has spent the week reclaiming ground it lost earlier in the summer, and Thursday’s close was the highest since April. That makes the April peak the reference point that now matters rather than any nearby round number.

Friday’s decline was too small to signal anything on its own. A single 0.17% move after a 2.18% week is noise, and the pattern only becomes meaningful if the pause extends into the coming sessions without a clear external trigger.

The genuine risk sits outside the chart. Copper eased on Friday and the Middle East remains unresolved, so the index enters next week with its domestic story intact and its external one open.

08 What to watch

Copper: The metal eased on Friday and remains the single biggest external influence on Chilean shares and the peso.

The metal eased on Friday and remains the single biggest external influence on Chilean shares and the peso. The Strait of Hormuz: Traders paused before the weekend specifically to see what emerged; any resolution moves oil and with it the whole region.

Traders paused before the weekend specifically to see what emerged; any resolution moves oil and with it the whole region. The rest of earnings season: Cencosud and CMPC both disappointed on Friday, and the results still to come will show whether that is a pattern.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the S&P IPSA?

It is Chile’s main stock index, tracking the most heavily traded shares on the Santiago Exchange, including SQM, the big banks and the retail groups.

Why did the index pause after such a strong week?

Investors were waiting for news out of the Middle East over the weekend, and two large companies reported disappointing quarterly figures on the day. The week as a whole still finished 2.18% higher.

What happened to Chilean inflation?

Consumer prices rose 0.1% in July, below the 0.2% the market expected, and the annual rate slowed from 4.3% to 3.5%. That is a substantial improvement and it supported both shares and the peso.

Why is copper so important to the Chilean market?

Chile is the world’s largest copper producer, so the metal’s price shapes export earnings, the peso and the profits of the mining companies in the index. Copper eased about 2.1% on Friday.

What was the Reconstruction bill that lifted the market?

It is the government’s National Reconstruction Project, approved this week, which combines tax reductions with other stimulus measures. Investors welcomed it, and it was one reason the index reached its highest level since April on Thursday.

World.title: Mexican Stocks Jump as Weak US Jobs Data Lifts Miners and Peso
World.content:
Key Facts Mexico’s S&P/BMV IPC rose 0.82% to 66,938.64 points, a gain of 542.49 points that ended a run of four losses in five sessions

a gain of 542.49 points that ended a run of four losses in five sessions The peso closed at about 17.12 per dollar, its strongest level since 18 February, after a weak United States jobs report knocked the dollar lower

its strongest level since 18 February, after a weak United States jobs report knocked the dollar lower Mining names led the advance, with Peñoles and Grupo México riding a precious-metals rally that took gold 2.11% higher

with Peñoles and Grupo México riding a precious-metals rally that took gold 2.11% higher Mexico’s central bank held its rate at 6.50% on Thursday, a unanimous second consecutive pause, and pushed its inflation target date out to late 2027

a unanimous second consecutive pause, and pushed its inflation target date out to late 2027 The single session wiped out August’s losses, leaving the index roughly flat for the month after being down 0.81% a day earlier

Today’s Focus Mexican shares had their best day in weeks on Friday, and the reason came from Washington. American employers shed jobs in July instead of adding them, and a market that trades in step with the United States took that as good news.

The S&P/BMV IPC climbed 0.82% to 66,938.64 points, adding 542.49 points and breaking a run of four falls in five sessions. The peso went with it, reaching its strongest level since February.

The gains were concentrated where the dollar’s weakness bites hardest. Precious metals rallied, and Mexico’s big miners carried the index.

What matters today. The same American jobs number that pushed money out of Brazil pushed it into Mexico, which is the clearest illustration this year of how differently the region’s two largest markets are wired.

01 The session in one read

The IPC finished Friday at 66,938.64 points, up 542.49 or 0.82%, on volume of 113,357,974. It was the index’s first convincing session in a week that had otherwise been a slow drift lower.

The shape of the day was one-directional. The index opened at 66,394.89, which was also its low, ran to 67,185.88 at the top and gave back only part of that into the close.

The turn was imported. United States employers cut 23,000 jobs in July against forecasts of an 80,000 gain, and June was revised down to just 20,000, which pushed expectations of a Federal Reserve rate rise from September into October.

Wall Street rose on that reading and Mexico followed, with the Dow up 0.28%, the S&P 500 up 0.62% and the Nasdaq up 1.30%. Brazil, wired differently, fell 1.73% on the same news.

Assessment — The right side of a weak American number MEDIUM Mexico benefits twice from a soft United States labour report: the dollar falls, which lifts the peso and the metals its miners dig, and the rate outlook softens, which lifts everything else. That is why Friday’s gain was led by Peñoles and Grupo México rather than by anything domestic. The caution is that none of this originated in Mexico, so the durability of the move depends on American data rather than on the local economy, and the index is still 0.8% below where it sat in late July.
