World.title: Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed against Japan
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed against Japan Jonathan Drennan August 8, 2026 — 11:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Aidan Ross 5.5 The Wallabies are still struggling to provide a regular tag-team partner for Angus Bell, and the search continues. Ross was busy in defence with 11 tackles, but was barely used in open play, making just four metres with the ball. Josh Nasser 6 Nasser was strong from the set piece and provided a solid lineout with his throwing. Didn’t let anyone down, especially after the recent impressive form of Brandon Paenga Amosa. Harry Wilson leads his team around the field. Getty Images



Allan Alaalatoa 5.5 It was brutal conditions for any front rower in Osaka, and, like Ross, was busy in defence as the Wallabies struggled to deal with early Japanese onslaughts. Made nine tackles and had little chance to do much else. Josh Canham 8 Canham just keeps getting better and better as a Test second-rower. Athletic, great hands and even put in a clearing kick from the Wallabies line. Won five lineouts, including a crucial steal off Japan ball. Canham is beginning his Test career but already is looking like he has been a Wallaby for years.



Miles Amatosero 3 Amatosero was given a big opportunity with his first Test start and was red-carded for a high shot on Japan captain Warner Dearns. Amatosero could argue that Dearns’ body height changed dramatically, but it was still careless and could have proven far more costly to the Wallabies. Rob Valetini 6 A quieter outing for Valetini, who struggled in brutal conditions. Made 14 tackles but only made 12 metres, far below what the breakaway would normally make in a Test.



Fraser McReight 6.5 Wasn’t able to dominate at the breakdown, but did lead his team with 21 tackles and scored a try in a tireless performance. McReight put in a tireless performance. Getty Images Harry Wilson 5.5 Had 10 carries but only made 8 metres, in simple maths, averaging 0.8 metres per carry. Also seemed to get on the wrong side of Irish referee Eoghan Cross and conceded two penalties. The captain’s effort can never be faulted, but it wasn’t an easy night.



Ryan Lonergan 6 Lonergan has had an outstanding season so far for the Wallabies, but it was a very tough night with a slippery ball for a halfback. Provides the Wallabies with an accurate goal kicker, which proved crucial in the end. Missed four tackles. Declan Meredith 4 The playmaker struggled badly with his kicking on exits, getting low metres and leaving the Wallabies under pressure. Showed his inexperience when taking a quick tap and completely mis-kicking it to himself, when the Wallabies were putting Japan under huge pressure in the scrum near their try line, and a yellow card was possible. Harry Potter 8.5



The Wallabies’ best on the night. Potter struggled with the Waratahs this season, but was the pick of the Wallabies backline. Scored a try and looked dangerous with the ball, beating four defenders with three line breaks. Difficult to drop now. Harry Potter makes a break for the Wallabies Getty Images Hunter Paisami 7 Some huge defensive hits from Paisami, even if he does sometimes shoot out of the line too quickly. Also made a brilliant pass for Tom Wright’s try and was dangerous with the ball in his hands. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii 5



Just could not get himself into the game, making a poor pass early, which Harry Potter did well to scoop off the ground and still score a try. Made a ruck turnover and didn’t stop trying, but did look vulnerable against quick Japanese attack in defence. Surely it is time to give him a go on the wing to utilise his strengths aerially and in attack. A huge talent that needs another chance to show it somewhere else on the field. Max Jorgensen 6 Scored a try and was solid when he attacked. Also made a ruck turnover. Tom Wright 7



Made a huge play, putting his body on the line to win a ruck turnover on 38 minutes with Japan certain to score. Scored a try, although also guilty of some handling errors on a humid night. Tom Wright scored a try, but was also guilty of some handling errors. Getty Images REPLACEMENTS Billy Pollard 5.5 Made a mess of a set play with a pass with the Wallabies pressuring the Japanese defence, but played a role in a strong bomb squad scrum that caused havoc for Japan.



Angus Bell 7 Gave away two penalties, but also made a crucial turnover on the ruck and played his part in a strong scrum. Carried the ball for 22 metres and was exactly what was needed to take the game to Japan late. Taniela Tupou 7 Made a huge hit at the end of the game to knock the ball out of Japanese hands and win the game; also ended up scoring the decisive try. Tupou was having a field day in the scrum and would have loved an opportunity to do more of them. Provided the perfect ballast off the bench. Isaac Henry, Tate McDermott, Hunter Paisami, Taniela Tupou and Angus Bell await the national anthem. Getty Images



Jeremy Williams 6.5 Brought a desperately needed calmness to the Wallabies and the Force second rower is clinical in his work; it was his clean-out that paved the way for the Tupou try. Charlie Cale 6 Finally given a chance to wear the Wallabies jersey and was busy, topping the Wallabies carries per minute with 0.22. Tate McDermott 6



Had looked rusty in his previous Tests, but was back with his sniping best against Japan. Busy and helped fight the Japanese speed with his own blistering tempo. Ben Donaldson 6 Came on at fullback, but would have liked to have been given more time to impress at five-eighth after Meredith’s wobbles. Isaac Henry N/A Wallaby 999 was desperate to make an impression, but only had eight minutes to do it. Will have lots more opportunities in Test rugby. World.title: Mistakes abound, but Wallabies’ win provides plenty of satisfaction
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Opinion Mistakes abound, but Wallabies’ win provides plenty of satisfaction Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author August 8, 2026 — 11:00pm

August 8, 2026 — 11:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Get that up yer, Eddie. The Wallaby win over Japan in Osaka was satisfying on a dozen levels at once. Most importantly, of course, is the fact that it was indeed a WIN, a victory if not a triumph, but that rarest of breed in recent times, a (W) next to the Wallaby name on the scoring ledger as the final whistle blew. And it was terrific that it came in the first match of new Wallaby coach Les Kiss’s tenure. The Wallabies’ lineouts were excellent, and Josh Canham turned in a near Man of the Match performance. Getty Images But right up there in terms of satisfaction was that it was against a side coached by Eddie Jones, who in fact was negotiating to take that very position while having carriage of the Australian team in the 2023 World Cup. The result was that our side was a complete shambles, and he left behind the smoking ruins of what might have been.



But here, three years later, our blokes registered a small payback against a Japanese side good enough to have easily defeated Italy and even threatened Ireland in recent times. The win to the Goodies, came despite several things not going the Wallabies’ way. The first thing was playing in such heat and humidity; it was clear from the first that in terms of sheer energy expended, not to mention hugely skilful play, the habituated locals were always going to be a handful. We were also a man down for twenty minutes – following lock Miles Amatosero being dispatched for high contact - which exhausted the surviving fourteen further. Ryan Lonergan kicks the ball. Getty Images And finally, we had an error rate that would kill a brown dog. Balls were kicked out on the full, knocked on and dropped behind with alarming regularity, even while the Japanese kicks were twice allowed to bounce and we kept making mistakes just when the try-line beckoned. Against that?



Related Article Wallabies ‘We found a way’: Wallabies defy heat, red card to get home over Eddie’s Japan Well, against that both our scrum and lineouts were excellent, and the surviving lock, Josh Canham – sort of rhymes with CANNON - turned in a near Man of the Match performance, stealing balls in the lineout, winning his own, ripping the balls off them in the maul, and constantly penetrating their line with death-or-glory charges. In the back row, Fraser McReight had his usual strong game while, off the bench, Taniela Tupou scored a great try which – if I were him – I’d describe as “a 50-metre carry, sidestepping my way through,” but was closer to a five-centimetre carry, followed by falling over the line with the ball in hand. The point was, after marvellous lead-up work by the entire team, it was Tupou who was there at the death to finish the job against a valiant Cherry Blossoms team that simply refused to quit. It was also Tupou who pulled off a massive tackle in the final seconds, making his opponent spill the ball, which finally put the game to rest. Angus Bell also had a great game off the bench, as did Jeremy Williams, and in some ways Kiss’s bench might have been stronger than the starting side they replaced, which saw the Wallabies finish strongly and not fade badly, which they have also been wont to do in recent times. In our back-line we saw the virtues of new coach Les Kiss’s stated desire to have less structured play, to have his charges work less with zones and channels and more with – stop me if this is too complex – running to where the bloody gaps are! Related Article Wallabies Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed against Japan



Time and again they did that, led by Max Jorgensen, and the results were there for all to see. The diminutive winger – and Tom Wright at fullback – were standouts for us, while the other winger Harry Potter had another strong game, as did Ryan Lonergan at halfback. When Tate McDermott came on to replace him at half in the final twenty minutes, he did what he does best, launching a series of darting runs from the base of the scrums, rucks and mauls and always laying the ball back. At fly-half, Declan Meredith struggled, and it was frankly a surprise that he played the full eighty minutes, as hard as he did try. (Carter Gordon, who was a revelation against Ireland last month, before injuring himself, will likely be back next week, in the return bout against Japan in Townsville.) Joseph Suaalii also struggled at times to hold on to the ball, though as captain Harry Wilson noted at game’s end, in those conditions the ball was like soap. Whatever. It was a WIN, did I mention? And not only that, the Wallabies second in succession! Get that up yer, Eddie. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Rabbitohs deny Eels greatest comeback in NRL history
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Rabbitohs deny Eels greatest comeback in NRL history Jasper Bruce and Justin Chadwick Updated August 8, 2026 — 10:12pm ,first published 5:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Parramatta have come within a sliver of the greatest comeback in NRL history, but have gone down 28-24 to South Sydney, who moved one step closer to a top-eight finish. But the manic victory looks to have come at a cost as young Souths halfback Ashton Ward injured his hamstring attempting a sideline conversion in Saturday’s first half. Loading Alex Johnston crossed for three tries as Souths took an imperious 28-0 halftime lead in the veteran winger’s first game at Allianz Stadium since breaking the NRL’s tryscoring record. The Eels lost Brian Kelly to the sin bin for a professional foul after just 92 seconds and conceded three tries without him, then watched as gun fullback Isaiah Iongi went down with a knee injury just before the break.



But against all odds, and with no realistic finals hopes to play for, Parramatta were hoisted back into the contest by off-contract journeyman Ronald Volkman. Ronald Volkman celebrates a try. Getty Images With Josh Addo-Carr deputising at fullback and hooker Ryley Smith in the centres, five-eighth Volkman’s attacking nous threatened to help the Eels pass the standing record for biggest NRL comeback (26 points). After Tallyn Da Silva crossed for the Eels’ first try, Volkman kicked through for Smith to nab their second before spinning past Matt Dufty for a four-pointer of his own. When Jordan Samrani soared over makeshift winger Jye Gray and slammed Volkman’s kick down, Parramatta were within four points.



After forcing a dropout in the final minutes, the Eels looked set to go for the killer blow, but the returning Tallis Duncan regathered the Rabbitohs’ short restart. In the same set, veteran Cody Walker kicked a 40/20 to put Souths out of trouble and on the attack for the final exchanges of a calamitous game. Brandon Smith celebrates a Rabbitohs try. Getty Images In Indigenous Round, Walker had been integral to the Rabbitohs’ early lead, most memorably slamming a kick into the goalposts that Tevita Tatola regathered for a fantastic try. The win lifts Souths back into seventh place to finish a weekend during which top-eight rivals Manly and Canterbury suffered potentially costly defeats.



They will likely make finals if they win two of their remaining four games, but have tough matches against Canterbury, the Warriors and Sydney Roosters on the run home. Earlier, Manly endured a dark day in Perth, conceding a whopping 42 consecutive points as their finals hopes took an almighty hit in a 42-20 loss to Melbourne. The Storm were horrible early on Saturday, with their completion rate sitting at just five of 12 as the Sea Eagles scored the opening two tries of the match to race out to a 14-0 lead. Loading But it was all one way traffic from that point on, with Melbourne piling on six unanswered tries either side of half-time to turn the contest on its head.



Manly’s fifth loss on the trot leaves their finals hopes on life support. Kieran Foran’s men now nurse a 9-11 record, meaning they will have to win their last four games to have a legitimate chance of making finals. In a further blow for the Sea Eagles, prop Taniela Paseka limped off in the first half after suffering a suspected MCL injury. Sualauvi Fa’alogo celebrates a try for Melbourne. Getty Images The Storm snapped a three-game losing streak, but at 9-12 they need to win their remaining three games and rely on other results to go their way in order to sneak into the post-season.



Fittingly, Melbourne’s Nick Meaney was a perfect nine-of-nine with the boot in a place he will soon call home. Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 NRL gives Perth Bears cap concessions to boost marquee pitch as inaugural jersey revealed The centre will join Perth next season and there were plenty of Bears fans in attendance to watch their future star. Perth coach Mal Meninga led around 1000 supporters on a pre-match ‘Bear Walk’ in the rain to HBF Park to signify the venue will soon become a ‘Bear Pit’. The NRL’s newest franchise launched their home jersey on Friday, with the red-and-black hooped strip paying tribute to the first-ever North Sydney Bears side of 1908, when the club was a foundation member of the NSW Rugby Football League. World.title: Won’t back down: Petty’s last laugh at Voss in Dees’ statement win; Bailey Smith shrugs off scandal in Cats’ win
World.content:
Loading

Melbourne backed born-again forward Harrison Petty for his gleeful take-down of former tormentor Patrick Voss on an afternoon that the Demons announced themselves as a serious premiership threat. Petty was a crucial key forward in the finals-like MCG clash, kicking three goals to help Melbourne down top-of-the-table Fremantle by four points – 17.11 (113) to 17.7 (109). Harrison Petty kicks three goals against Fremantle. Getty Images But it was after his first goal that he made his statement, rubbing his freshly shaved head in delight – an obvious broadside at Voss for his antagonistic treatment of Petty earlier this year. Following that round-two match at Optus Stadium, Voss was charged with misconduct and fined $1500 for mocking Petty by rubbing the then defender’s hair and simulating a crying action.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘It’s not 1980 – the coach doesn’t run everything these days’: Scott speaks on concussion scandal It prompted the AFL to instruct umpires to start paying free kicks against players who rubbed the head of an opponent. But there was no taunting Petty on Saturday. He was crucial in the Demons’ fighting win – they trailed by three points a half-time, eight points at three-quarter-time and fell 15 points in arrears during a tense final term. Teammate Bailey Laurie, who kicked three valuable goals of his own, called Petty’s actions “awesome”. “Last time, I think he got his head rubbed, so I mean, he’s probably got the laugh today. So I’m sure he’ll be pretty happy with that one,” Laurie told The Age.



Coach Steven King was also full of praise for Petty. “I think it’s just him embracing who he is, being authentic. He’s on the big stage, you know,” King said. “[There’s] nothing wrong with shaving your head. I think it looks great. It wasn’t something I was aware that was going to happen. But I think that just shows where Petts is at. “He’s enjoying his footy. He’s proud of who he is, who he plays for, and yeah, it’s a good sign for him that he’s engaged in the game, and it means something to him.”



While Voss was at the opposite end of the ground to Petty, he was making a statement of a different kind. The damaging Dockers forward kicked four straight goals for the match. His teammate Jye Amiss also booted five without registering a behind. View post on X Their accuracy was unnerving for the Demons in an opening half that both sides piled on 21 goals between them in a mouth-watering shootout. At the long break, the Dockers led 11.2 to the Demons’ 10.5. “I think Kingy said we were plus-20 something in contest, and there were periods of the game we played really well, but we knew they were kicking all these goals that were pretty good. Like, tip your hat to them,” Laurie said.



“But all the stats were saying that if we kept doing what we were doing, we’d be right there at the end, which we were.” It was a game of fluctuating fortunes. Fremantle kicked four of the first five goals, Melbourne answered with the next four, the Dockers hit back with three in succession, and then Melbourne clawed their way back with four in a row. All this before half-time. Max Gawn has a fierce battle against Fremantle’s Luke Jackson at the MCG. Getty Images Then the midfields took turns in sharing dominance.



For most of the afternoon it was hard to split All-Australian ruck contenders and 2021 premiership teammates Max Gawn (16 disposals and 33 hitouts) as he did battle with Luke Jackson (17 disposals and 26 hitouts). “They’re both unique,” King said. “You could call both of them ‘unicorns’, I guess. Max has done things we haven’t seen. I think ‘Jacko’ now, the way he plays and follows up, he’s like an extra midfielder for them. Bailey Laurie celebrates the Demons’ win with coach Steven King. AFL Photos “I just think they’re both unbelievable footballers, and what a privilege it was to come here today to watch them both compete against each other.” The indefatigable Gawn played out the final term without a break as he willed his team over the line – they did not hit the front until the 21-minute mark of the final term on the back of a Bayley Fritsch snap.



But the Dockers had their chances. Jordan Clark and Matthew Johnson spilled marks in the last minute, while the enigmatic Fritsch was paid a mark right on the boundary line in the dying seconds that could easily have been ruled out-on-the full, allowing the Dockers one last roll of the dice. But none of that mattered to the Melbourne-dominated crowd of 40,938 who erupted in full voice as the final siren sounded. View post on X As they belted out the theme song, Fritsch kicked a behind, bumping the final margin to four points and bringing his total for the game to 2.5. Outside of Pickett, there were crucial bit-part players everywhere for the Demons who not only landed their biggest scalp of the season and improved their MCG record this year to 10-1, but have given themselves a chance at a top-four finish.



Tom Sparrow racked up 24 disposals and two goals, Koltyn Tholstrup blanketed the dangerous Murphy Reid, Harvey Langford took a mark-of-the-year contender, while hard-running wingman Harry Sharp managed three of his own, including a 60-metre bomb on the run from the boundary and a brilliant soccer goal in the pulsating final term. “I was saying to some of the boys throughout the game, as a spectator, that would have been unbelievable game to watch,” Laurie said. “To play my part in that was nice. It was very satisfying. We’re a special group, and anything’s possible.” King agreed, beaming with pride after winning a game at the MCG with a finals-like intensity against a team they rated as “the best team in it”. “I think for us it was a scalp we needed to take,” he said. “We needed to signify to the opposition that we’re here. We’re not just shooting to play a final. We want to make it count.“

- Danny Russell



Ollie Dempsey was again in standout form for the Cats. AFL Photos Young gun pushes his All-Australian claims Jon Pierik Star Geelong wingman Ollie Dempsey has put forward another case why he should be an All-Australian after helping the Cats to a 67-point win over Essendon at GMHBA Stadium on Saturday. Wearing his typical headband around his long blond locks, and dashing around in two different-coloured boots, Dempsey had 19 disposals and four goals, including a sharp snap in the second term after pouncing on a loose ball.



The win, including the percentage boost, ensures the Cats remain in the hunt for a top-four finish. They have North Melbourne and Richmond over the final two rounds. After a week of turbulence at the Cats given the Jake Kolodjashnij concussion scandal, superstar onballer Bailey Smith relished the chance to talk about anything but – heaping praise on Dempsey. “[He’s] All-Aus, surely. Just don’t take my wing spot. You can have the bench – just kidding,” Smith told Kayo Sports after the game. Dempsey said dismissed talk of an All-Australian nod but thanked those lobbying for him. “I’m not really thinking about it, it’s nice hearing all those things in public, but I’m just worried about getting the next two wins,” Dempsey told Kayo.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘It’s not 1980 – the coach doesn’t run everything these days’: Scott speaks on concussion scandal The Cats quickly got to business against an opponent which initially was overwhelmed, but continued to fight, and reinforced that eventually there may be light at the end of the tunnel when a new coach is installed. The Bombers pressured as best they could, and had numbers around the ball. But they were goalless until just under two minutes remaining in the first half. They rallied in the third term, but the Cats cruised to their 10th-straight win over the red and black. Dempsey has the most goals of any wingman this season, his ability to slip forward causing rivals nightmares. He said he had not given any thought to earning a maiden green blazer. View post on X



“It’s always great fun playing at home,” Dempsey told Kayo Sports. Cats premiership great Tom Hawkins said Dempsey was a multi-faceted player. “He still gets back and defends, he is not just an attacking wingman. He supports the defence as well,” Hawkins said in commentary. Dempsey’s fellow forward Ollie Henry also booted four goals in a fine tandem act. Geelong pair Sam De Koning and Mark Blicavs shared the ruck duties, the former pushing forward when possible, but counterpart Vigo Visentini had a bagful of hitouts and was particularly impressive after half-time. He worked hard at stoppages and around the ground before leaving the field late after a heavy hit from behind. He, surely, will be a piece the new coach wants to harness.



Editor's pick Opinion

AFL 2026 The Cats are not the cultural beacon they once claimed to be Caroline Wilson Football columnist for The Age Veteran Cat Tom Stewart began in the middle at the opening throw-up, but spent most of the evening in his customary role of patrolling half-back. Smith’s excellent form continued. He was a metres-gained monster with 38 disposals, providing drive when the rain fell, while James Worpel and Tom Atkins provided grunt in close. Worpel could yet be under pressure should Max Holmes return from injury. The battle between impressive youngsters Nate Caddy and Connor O’Sullivan was one to watch, and something the football world will enjoy over the next decade. Caddy is a fighter and still wants the ball delivered to him no matter the strife his time is in. O’Sullivan had his moments in defence, this clash an even one. The Bombers have redeployed Zach Merrett back into his customary role in the midfield over the past month, and he was typically busy. In what could be his final weeks at the club, the former skipper had 29 disposals and 401 metres gained.



Sam Durham was quiet, but rookies Dyson Sharp, who found plenty of the ball, and Jacob Farrow, with two goals, continued their development. The Bombers host the Swans next Sunday, and could yet pinch one more victory, at home against Port Adelaide, to close what has been a largely dismal campaign. World.title: Mistake to omit creative arts technologies from new school subjects, drama teachers say
World.content:
The drama teachers' association says the government has made a mistake by omitting technologies that support the creative arts from its list of new industry-led school subjects.

The nine subjects would be developed by industry skills boards to provide clear pathways to further training and jobs for secondary school students in Years 12-13.

Whakaari Aotearoa Drama New Zealand said it should have included a subject that covered areas like lighting, sound, staging, costume, and set design.

The organisation's president Annette Thomson said failing to do so would sever students' pathway into industries such as film and television that had critical skill shortages.

Whakaari Aotearoa Drama president Annette Thomson. Supplied / Whakaari Aotearoa Drama NZ

She said currently teens could earn credits toward an NCEA qualification while they participated in backstage roles like lighting or sound for school productions, but that would not be possible under the new qualification being introduced in 2029 because students would have to study entire subjects and there was no subject that covered those skills.

Thomson said the decision endangered the government's plan to grow the creative sector's economic contribution to $22 billion a year by 2030.

"We feel like they're not really thinking about some of these things that are actually important. They do actively contribute to GDP and to our students," she said.

"All we're seeing is a cutting, a reducing, a narrowing of subjects in the arts."

World.title: What's gone wrong for Milford's Active Growth Fund?
World.content:
Milford's Active Growth Fund has long been one of the success stories of KiwiSaver, reliably at the top of performance tables in its category and delivering strong returns year after year.

But in recent times, it's started to slip - and quickly.

While it's still the best performing growth fund over 10 years, with a return of 10.2 percent a year, it was the worst performer over the most recent three months according to research firm Morningstar, returning 5 percent compared to 12.5 percent for the best performer.

It was 28th over one year, with a return of 7.8 percent, compared to 21.5 percent for the top fund.

Steven Le, associate director at Morningstar, said Milford had taken a deliberate step back to a "somewhat defensive" position relative to other fund managers in terms of its allocation to technology and the US, both of which have been strong performers recently.

But he said Milford was still a strong manager. "They do a lot of good things, robust research, they cover a lot of ground. They have boots on the ground in several regions including Australia and the research they conduct is quite comprehensive. We think they're doing good things and we have a positive view of them as a business as well as a positive view of the strategy."

Do I have to buy that extended warranty? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

There have been concerns that the fund has become too big. Le said those were legitimate because as funds grew larger investment managers were forced to extend their reach.

Since 2020, New Zealand equities exposure in the fund had more than halved. He said that trend was likely to continue as Milford tried to manage capacity in smaller local markets.

"Milford is undoubtedly a major player in the New Zealand market. The scale and growth of the business have enabled ongoing investment in its research and investment capabilities over time, which are key contributors to our positive view of the business and a number of its strategies.

"That said, the considerable growth of the business and several of its strategies does come with associated risks. In particular, the firm has expanded into new segments, such as global equities, and when a fund manager broadens its capabilities beyond its traditional areas of expertise, it is something we pay close attention to. To date, we have not identified any issues that we think would materially impact investors, but it's an area we are actively monitoring."

He noted that Milford's wide-ranging mandate for the fund allowed it to change its split between growth and income assets with discretion.

The allocation to equities fell as low as 60 percent in December 2022, while it sat at 76.3 percent as of November 2025. Le said although reduced US equities exposure could dent returns, as in recent times, it was beneficial during the April period last year when the fund returned 0.1 percent when the category index fell 1.6 percent.

Milford head of KiwiSaver Murray Harris. Supplied / Milford

Milford recently held a webinar for financial advisers about the fund, at which they were told that Milford intended to stick with its strategy, which aimed to deliver 10 percent annual returns over a seven-year period.

Milford head of KiwiSaver Murray Harris said the session was an opportunity for advisers to hear directly from and ask questions of the investment team about recent performance, portfolio positioning, the market environment and the outlook for the strategy. "Advisers place significant trust in us when recommending our funds to clients, and it is important that we are open, accessible and transparent about performance, investment decisions and portfolio positioning."

Milford said it had seen some movement of investment funds into higher-risk categories, such as people moving from growth to aggressive, and balanced to growth.

World.title: Charities raise money for Kaimanawa muster, save horses from culling
World.content:
Kaimanawa wild horse charities have raised enough money for a fourth muster of the year, and found enough homes for a small group of animals living in an ecologically sensitive area of the North Island's central plateau.

The fourth muster was required because a group of about 15 horses is living away from the main herd, on Defence Force land near Waiouru.

Three musters have taken place earlier this year to help limit herd numbers, which current sit at about 500.

The Kaimanawa Wild Horse Advisory Group - including the Department of Conservation and the charities, Kaimanawa Heritage Horses and the Kaimanawa Legacy Foundation - recently decided that a muster of those horses could take place if the charities raised the money for it.

If they didn't it was possible aerial culling would have been used.

Legacy Foundation founder Kelly Wilson said the charities had raised about $60,000, which was enough, although the cost for the latest muster had since increased by about $19,000.

The charities would have to cover that cost.

Legacy Foundation founder Kelly Wilson. Nick Monro

Eighteen homes had agreed to take wild horses if needed. Wilson said no one knew the exact number that would be taken from the site, so it was good to have flexibility.

"It's a huge relief," Wilson said.

"Our fundraising to do the muster would be pointless if we didn't have homes for them to go to."

She said it would be interesting to see how easily the horses could be trained as, unlike horses from the main herd, they'd had little contact with people.

Trainer Morgan Chandler-Bruce would work with six or seven of the horses at Wilson's sanctuary, near Taupō.

Wilson said a week before applications for horses had closed, the charities had only received one for the five stallions likely to be mustered, and they were short of homes for mature mares.

However, private sponsors put up the money for eight horses, to cover most of the costs of training them. Applications then followed.

"We are hugely appreciate of the public for the donations received to enable the muster to go ahead, as well as the homes that have stepped forward to offer these special Kaimanawa horses homes," she said.

DOC project lead Sarah Tunnicliffe. Dan Jones

DOC project lead Sarah Tunnicliffe said the department was finalising logistics of the muster and setting up temporary yards for it.

World.title: Whanganui opts out of Head Start pathway ahead of deadline
World.content:
Whanganui District Council has voted not to submit a proposal on local government reform ahead of the Head Start deadline on Sunday.

It has instead signed a regional Memorandum of Understanding with its neighbours - Rangitīkei and Ruapehu - committing to working proactively towards locally-led reform.

Mayor Andrew Tripe said Whanganui needed more time to consider its options.

"We need robust modelling to help us understand the implications, opportunities and long-term outcomes. That work, alongside continued conversations with our communities and partners, will help shape the next phase of this process," he said.

"For our council, the priority is making sure decisions deliver the best outcomes for Whanganui and the region and we'll continue working constructively with our regional partners while keeping the community involved as the picture becomes clearer."

The government would decide next month which Head Start proposals should move on to a detailed design phase, before final decisions were made in 2027.

Whanganui, meanwhile, would now fall into the group of Back Stop councils for whom reform would begin after the 2028 elections.

Tripe said continuing to work with interested councils didn't predetermine any outcome or limit councils from exploring alternatives.

"What it does do is give us a structured way to continue to work together, build a stronger evidence base and consider different options before any decisions are made."

Tripe said over the past three months, mayors and council chief executives in the region and nearby had met regularly to discuss opportunities and challenges presented by the government's Simplifying Local Government reforms.

The council had also commissioned and considered data and technical analysis, engaged with iwi and hapū partners, and asked the community for its initial thoughts.

"We've had many productive discussions and begun to build up an information base," he said.

"That work has strengthened our understanding of the issues and, in particular, the opportunities. It's shown there's more work to do before any structural changes can be properly considered. In addition, it gives us the opportunity to think bigger than the Head Start pathway to reimagine local government in and for the future."

Tripe said for some councils change was more straightforward because amalgamation discussions were well advanced and Head Start was primarily for those councils.

"But for most, it makes sense to take the time to build a robust evidence base and work carefully through it so we can make the best decision for our communities now and in years to come."

World.title: Privacy experts warn of gaps in NZ law, as camera glasses hit Kmart shelves
World.content:
Privacy experts are warning that wearable camera technology, dubbed by some as "pervert glasses", expose significant gaps in New Zealand's laws.

University of Canterbury professor Annette Mills said the devices, which were often marketed as smart glasses, were "essentially a computer on your face", combining cameras, microphones, speakers and AI-powered functions in everyday wearable technology.

The Anko Camera Glasses. Supplied / Kmart

Her warning comes as Kmart begins selling its Anko Camera Glasses for just $99, a price point expected to make the technology far more accessible than premium smart glasses such as Meta's Ray-Ban range.

She said that while the glasses offered some benefits, especially as assistive technology for people with disabilities, the technology's growing popularity raised serious privacy concerns.

"We expect to be recorded in some places, such as by CCTV cameras in supermarkets," Mills said.

"But we certainly don't expect to have that everywhere we go."

Mills said that unlike smartphones, which required users to visibly raise a device before taking a photo or recording video, smart glasses could capture footage far more discreetly, making it difficult for bystanders to know whether they were being filmed.

She said overseas cases had already shown how wearable cameras could be misused, including secret recordings in bathrooms and people approaching women in public before uploading the footage to social media without their consent.

Mills said future developments, including facial recognition technology, could make the privacy implications even more significant.

"You could literally look at someone and say, 'Tell me everything there is about this person'. That can make someone feel very vulnerable."

Laws designed for organisations, not individuals

Mills believed New Zealand's privacy framework had a fundamental weakness when it came to wearable technology.

"Our privacy regulations are primarily aimed at protecting individuals, but they are targeted at organisations and what organisations do," she said.

"They are not set up to deal with personal information collected by individuals."

While existing laws could apply to intimate recordings, harmful digital communications and some forms of stalking, Mills said many everyday uses of camera glasses may fall outside current legal protections.

Her concern extended beyond what people record.

Once footage was uploaded to cloud services, it could be processed, analysed and potentially shared in ways many users - and the people they record may not fully understand.

"I think we need to come up with not just regulations that deal with the use, but also controls that deal with the deployment of these devices," she said.

University of Canterbury professor Annette Mills. Supplied / University of Canterbury

Minister of Justice Paul Goldsmith said the government may consider "taking advice on the matter" in the next parliamentary term.

'Serious privacy harms'

The Office of the Privacy Commissioner said the Privacy Act was largely focused on regulating the actions of businesses and organisations, not individuals and it applied regardless of what technology was used.

"Tools like CCTV, drones, and smart glasses make it easier for individuals to record each other. If individuals do not use them in a responsible manner, that can lead to serious privacy harms," a spokesperson said.

It said that individuals using glasses to film covertly should be aware that their actions might breach the Privacy Act if the collection, use or disclosure of the personal information was highly offensive to a reasonable person.

"Other laws are also likely to be relevant, such as the Harmful Digital Communications Act, stalking offences or other crimes under the Crimes Act."

Surveillance concerns extend beyond the wearer

Meanwhile, University of Auckland commercial law professor Gehan Gunasekara raised questions about the companies behind the devices.

University of Auckland commercial law professor Gehan Gunasekara. RNZ / Phil Pennington

His concern was not simply that individuals may misuse camera glasses, but that platforms operating the technology could collect vast amounts of information about where people went, what they looked at and how communities behaved.

"The platform also knows all of that information," he said.

"They can map trends, see where people travel and the kinds of stores they shop at."

Even where companies anonymised data before using it to improve artificial intelligence systems, Gunasekara said the aggregated information remained commercially valuable and raised broader questions about privacy and data sovereignty.

A 'game-changing' technology for blind New Zealanders

However, not everyone saw the technology as a threat.

Blind Low Vision New Zealand chief executive Andrea Midgen described AI-enabled smart glasses as the most significant technological advancement her community had seen.

Blind Low Vision chief executive Andrea Midgen. Supplied / Blind Low Vision NZ

The glasses could read street signs, restaurant menus and other visual information aloud while allowing users to keep both hands free for a white cane or guide dog.

"This is the most exciting game changer thing that we've had in technology for our community ever," Midgen said.

She acknowledged privacy concerns but said they stemmed from how people chose to use technology, rather than the technology itself.

"This is just a different form of what already happens with smartphones," she said.

'Use responsibly' - Kmart

A Kmart Group spokesperson confirmed that its Anko Camera Glasses were available to buy in New Zealand.

"The Anko Camera Glasses are part of an established and increasingly mainstream category of wearable technology, with similar products available globally from major technology and eyewear brands. Like other products in this category, they allow users to capture photos and video while also providing audio and connectivity features," the spokesperson said.

"As with any device capable of recording images, we expect customers to use the product responsibly, respectfully and in accordance with applicable laws and community expectations around privacy."

World.title: Brian Tamaki says police have revoked his firearms licence
World.content:
Destiny Church leader Brian Tamaki says police have revoked his firearms licence.

On Saturday, the church leader announced on social media that police had decided he was no longer a "fit and proper person".

He said police issued a notice revoking his firearms licence on Friday.

"I am now prohibited not only from possessing my own firearms, but from possessing or using a firearm even under the supervision of a licensed firearms holder."

Acting Executive Director of Firearms Safety Authority Bruce Bird said police were unable to comment on an individual case or licensing decisions.

"However, speaking generally, decisions about suspending or revoking a firearms licence are based on a legal standard of whether a person is 'fit and proper' to possess a firearm."

Bird said fit and proper decisions were guided by circumstances outlined in section 24A of the Arms Act.

Tamaki said he would be seeking a review of the decision.

"I now have 28 days to apply for a review ... you can be certain that I will," he wrote on social media.

Tamaki's comments about India

On Saturday, Tamaki claimed his licence had been revoked in response to statements he had made concerning Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

"I was speaking passionately. I was protesting. I was challenging what I believed needed to be challenged," he said.

"This follows the temporary suspension issued to me on 30 June and the subsequent submissions made by my lawyer opposing that suspension."

In June, police confirmed they had served a temporary firearms licence suspension notice at an Auckland property. Authorities declined to comment on the specifics.

At the time of the suspension, Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour said he was sure the police had acted within the law.

"I got zero time for Brian Tamaki," he said. "If he's got any complaints, he should take them through the proper legal channels and possibly stop being a dickhead."

Earlier that month, Tamaki accused Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi of purging Christians in the South Asian nation.

"He [Modi] is currently purging India of all Christians and burning church buildings down," Tamaki had said in a video posted on social media.

"I think we should reciprocate in kind. Let's purge New Zealand of Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims. And, while we're at it, if they're burning churches down, why don't we burn mosques and their temples down? Tit for tat."

Ethnic Communities Minister Mark Mitchell then labelled the comments as the "actions of a scared bully" and said police would assess the remarks.

World.title: Councils across country meet to finalise amalgamation proposals ahead of deadline
World.content:
Councils face deadline to propose amalgation agreements Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Councils across the country have been meeting to finalise their amalgamation proposals or face the process being dictated to them by central government.

Sunday marks the deadline for district councils to submit their proposals to amalgamate with at least one other nearby authority.

On announcing the three-month Head Start process in May, Local Government Minister, Simon Watts and Resource Management Act Reform Minister, Chris Bishop had a stark message for councils.

"Today we are giving council's a clear choice. Lead your own reform or we will do it for you," Bishop said.

This week, Hamilton District Council voted 12 to three to not participate - meaning the district would end up in a backstop process controlled by central government to ensure reforms still went ahead.

Councillor Andrew Bydder told Morning Report council didn't want to put forward a proposal and have the government think they were happy with it.

"Getting into the tent might leave us stuck in the tent which is not desirable when the tent is a brothel with a minister who wants to pimp us out," Bydder said.

Earlier in the month, Hamilton mayor Tim Macindoe told RNZ he was reluctant to cede control of the process but could not support rushing into an arrangement which did not suit his city.

Tim Macindoe. RNZ / Richard Tindiller

However this week he told councillors he received a phone call from Watts which ruled out his council's involvement in back stop decisions if they did not take the first step of submitting a proposal ahead of the deadline.

"He was also quite clear during our discussion that back-stop councils will not be at the table for that process," Macindoe said.

Down south, Christchurch City Council unanimously agreed to submit on the Head Start process.

They chose to retain the city's current city boundaries while taking on Canterbury Regional Council's functions.

But earlier in the week, councillor Melanie Coker warned the changes could cost millions to implement.

"Functions between councils that join will need to reviewed, combined, resized and this doesn't come for free. Any savings may be decades away and are not guaranteed," Coker said.

But in a Wellington City Council meeting yesterday, mayor Andrew Little said council reform was a necessary step to help address existing problems with long term infrastructure plans, economic growth and the region's ability to cope with the challenges of climate change.

Andrew Little. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"Put aside Head Start. Put aside the dodgy process. can we still address those challenges under the status quo? My view is not," Little said.

On Friday. a statement on behalf of the Wellington and Wairarapa Mayoral Forum outlined how the region could approach the merger.

Two proposals would come from councils of the region. One a region-wide proposal (supported by Wellington City Council, Hutt City Council, Porirua City Council and South Wairarapa District Council) and another proposal for Wairarapa (supported by Carterton District Council and Masterton District Council).

The statement said the proposals would convey the positions of individual councils and the forum was requesting the "door remains open" for alternative arrangements for Kapiti Coast District Council and Upper Hutt District Council.

Late last month, Taupo mayor John Funnell described a proposed Western Waikato Unitary Authority as a "hostile takeover" which would leverage his district's financial strength while ballooning ratepayer debt to nearly ten times current levels.

He said his council had decided not to engage in the Head Start process.

Funnell said he understood concerns that stepping away from the Head Start process could see a merger dictated by central government but said councils who wished to merge with Taupo should come through the front door.

"We're three months out from an election - I would say to Minister Watts 'be careful'.

"I've seen the communications from our residents of the district here and there's a fair bit at stake for everyone here.

"I think the residents are quite clear they want to have their concerns taken in consideration and they want to make sure that the investments that this council has made over many years can put them in a good position as protected - and there's many ways of doing that - but it needs time."

Watts said the government had been clear from the outset that this was a "voluntary process", giving councils the chance to put forward locally led proposals.

"Many councils and mayors have embraced that opportunity, working constructively across their regions to consider how local government can be better organised to deliver stronger services, lower costs and better value for ratepayers.

"We're undertaking the most significant reform of local government in a generation because the current system has become increasingly complex, costly and fragmented, and too often isn't delivering the outcomes that ratepayers expect."

He said no final decisions have been made regarding any backstop as any design would be informed by "the lessons from the voluntary Head Start process."

"I will have more to say once submissions have been received and we have had the opportunity to carefully consider the proposals put forward."

World.title: Souths hang on to deny Eels remarkable comeback
World.content:
South Sydney concedes 24 unanswered second-half points but manage to hold on for a 28-24 victory, which consolidates the Rabbitohs' place in the league's top eight.

On a day of incredible NRL fightbacks, the Eels almost delivered the biggest of all time after trailing 28-0 at the break.

Earlier the Dolphins came from 24-0 down to beat the Broncos 40-32 in a remarkable Battle of Brisbane, while the Melbourne Storm came back from 14-0 down to hammer Manly Warringah 42-20 in Perth.

In Sydney though, the Eels looked as far from mounting a fight back as any team could be after a dire first half.

Alex Johnston's hat-trick, coupled with tries to Tevita Tatola, Brandon Smith and Jye Gray had Souths well on top at the Sydney Football Stadium.

Souths lost halfback Ashton Ward to a hamstring injury just before the break, while the Eels had Isaiah Iongi carried off with a knee injury in a brutal match played at an incredible pace.

But after the break, the Eels turned their form around dramatically, Tallyn Da Silva, Ryley Smith and Ronald Volkman scoring three tries in the space of six minutes to open the second stanza.

Jordan Samrani scored too, setting up a remarkable finale.

However, a magical 40:20 from Cody Walker with just over a minute on the clock secured the victory for Souths.

"It's just one of those ones that came off," Walker told Fox Sports after the match.

"I'm just happy with the two points, we needed that.

"We had players playing everywhere, we lost our halfback in the first half so we just had to win that and we did it.

"I'm pretty proud of the boys' effort."

Sea Eagles 'not good enough'

Sualauvi Fa'alogo helped ignite the Storm after they trailed 14-0 in the first half in Perth. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Earlier, the Sea Eagles lamented a horror performance that all but eliminated them from finals contention, needing to win their last four games to have a legitimate chance of making the top eight.

Manly coach Kieran Foran questioned his team's hardness and apologised to the club's fans after shipping 42-straight points in East Perth.

The Storm were horrible early in Saturday's match, with their completion rate sitting at just five of 12 as the Sea Eagles scored the opening two tries to race out to a 14-0 lead.

But it was all one way traffic from that point on, with Melbourne piling on six unanswered tries either side of half-time to turn the contest on its head.

"We can't explain it. I just don't feel that there's a real hard edge about our approach to our footy at the moment," Foran said.

"You know, 14-0 up, you should be in control of that game of footy. You should be able to put the foot on the throat and maintain a level of control.

"I feel very, very sorry to our fans.

"We had a lot to play for today. There was a lot on the line.

"There was good reason to turn up and put in a really good performance. And after about the half an hour mark, that just wasn't good enough.

"I had a bit to say [to the players] just before, but I'll keep most of it in house."

The Storm snapped a three-game losing streak, but at 9-12 they need to win their remaining three games and rely on other results to go their way in order to sneak into the post-season.

Dolphins bite back to beat Broncos

BRISBANE, AUSTRALIA - AUGUST 08: Connelly Lemuelu of the Dolphins is congratulated by team mates after scoring a try during the round 23 NRL match between Dolphins and Brisbane Broncos at Suncorp Stadium, on August 08, 2026, in Brisbane, Australia. (Photo by Bradley Kanaris/Getty Images) (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

The Dolphins produced arguably an even greater fight back in front of over 50m,000 supporters at Lang Park.

The Broncos tore out of the blocks in the derby, racing into a 24-0 lead early on, only to see the Dolphins flip the script with a remarkable second half display.

Tabuai-Fidow won the Battle Medal as man of the match, scored his second try in the 68th minute with stunning leap above Reece Walsh from a Katoa bomb to give the Dolphins a 36-32 lead, the first time they had hit the front.

"It's obviously a special round for myself, being a proud Torres Strait Islander," he said.

"So to get the win in this [Indigenous] round and especially against the Broncos, it's something special."

The Broncos, already out of finals contention, lamented the familiar defensive errors that have cost them the chance to defend their premiership crown this season.

"We just need to be better around our defence," coach Michael Maguire said.

"We all need to take ownership. Are we capable of being better than where we are? I believe so, definitely."

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

World.title: Why broadcasting row has Tour de France Femmes fans 'pissed off'
World.content:
The catchcry of the Tour de France Femmes by its lead sponsor, Zwift, is pretty simple: Watch the Femmes.

By and large, the viewership data shows that people are doing exactly that.

And why wouldn't they?

After a riveting seven days of racing so far, capped by Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney's masterful ascent of the legendary Mont Ventoux, the top three riders in this year's race are separated by just 39 seconds.

Six different riders have claimed stage victories so far, with the overall race lead changing hands three times since the opening stage.

The 2024 champion, Niewiadoma-Phinney, holds a 15-second advantage over Demi Vollering, the woman she beat two years ago by a measly four seconds.

This is a race that has had it all.

The three-way battle between Demi Vollering, Marlen Reusser and Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney has captivated fans this year. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

But fans, as yet, cannot watch the race in its entirety, with just three of the nine stages of this year's race televised from start to finish.

The lack of comprehensive live coverage is a growing pain that the women's edition of the Tour de France is hoping to overcome as the fifth edition of its most recent iteration comes to a close in Nice this weekend.

It is something that women's riders' union, The Cyclists' Alliance (TCA) — whose president is Australian former world and Olympic champion Grace Brown — has criticised throughout the race.

"For the biggest race in women's cycling, partial coverage is no longer enough," TCA wrote in a social media post.

The 'accursed' mountain that stands apart this Tour de France The ascent to hell on the punishing slopes of Mont Ventoux is one of the Tour de France's most formidable and iconic theatres.

"Fans will still miss the attacks, the tactics, and the moments that could define the race."

Broadcaster Orla Chennaoui, who hosts the coverage for TNT Sports in the UK, was less diplomatic.

"I'm getting really annoyed now. I'm getting really, really pissed off," she said on an Instagram reel that she titled: Women's sport done a disservice Editions #4957.

"What the heck? There is so much excitement and interest in the Tour de France Femmes.

"The riders, the race have proven over and over again how dynamic and dramatic this sport is.

"I have never seen my [social media] algorithm so flooded with excitement, with joy, with celebration for this race.

Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney won her first Tour de France Femmes stage on the slopes of Mont Ventoux. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

"It's everywhere, on Instagram, podcasts popping up all over the place, YouTube videos, more written articles that I would ever have imagined when I started covering women's cycling 10 years ago.

"And we still, despite this, despite how proven the interest is, we cannot get live TV coverage.

"ASO [Amaury Sport Organisation], what are you doing? Why can we not get to watch all stages live?"

The astonishing story behind the women's Tour The Tour de France Femmes produced one of the closest finishes in cycling stage race history last year. But when the women's Tour was first revived, it was called "ugly".

Chennaoui said there was a "huge will" from broadcasters to show the race in its entirety every day in that post, which she acknowledged she may get in trouble for and be asked to delete.

All 21 stages of the men's Tour de France were broadcast live in their entirety.

On the same day that the third stage of the women's Tour de France Femme was half-shown, stage one of the men's Tour de Pologne World Tour race was shown in full, all five hours, four minutes and 11 seconds of what was a flat, 234.2-kilometre race.

The duration of the Tour de France Femmes broadcast has increased to 27 hours and 40 minutes for this year's race, up five hours and 20 minutes from what was shown live in 2024.

However, TCA noted that France Télévisions data showed a 40 per cent increase in viewership from 18.3 million in 2024 to 25.7 million in 2025.

"The demand is undeniable," TCA said.

"We are asking for the coverage to catch up."

One of the pre-race favourites, Demi Vollering crashed early in the stage. (Getty Images: Alex Broadway)

That post was put up in the hours before stage three took place, a stage won by Norway's Sigrid Haugset with an 88km breakaway attack.

However, the move that saw the Norwegian break away from the peloton was completely missed, as the TV cameras had not started rolling.

Additionally, one of the pre-race favourites, Vollering crashed early in the stage, an incident that was, again, missed by the cameras, and could have huge repercussions for the rest of the race.

"That was disappointing," former world champion on the track and the road Lizzie Deignan told the For The Love Of Cycling podcast.

"There's no substitute for footage. You can't get a feel of the race, of the tension, of the atmosphere."

According to organisers, this year's Tour de France Femmes is being broadcast in 190 countries, including by SBS in Australia.

France Télévisions keeps the supporters of women's cycling in the shade with their coverage. (Getty Images: NurPhoto/Romain Doucelin)

However, SBS and the Tour's other broadcast partners around the world can only show the footage they are provided with.

France Télévisions handles production and distribution of the broadcast on behalf of the Amaury Sport Organisation [ASO].

The ASO is also responsible for the men's Tour de France, as well as other major cycling events, including two of cycling's monument one day races, Liège-Bastogne-Liège and Paris-Roubaix.

The organisation was heavily criticised for its coverage of the women's edition of Paris-Roubaix earlier this year, with less than 90 minutes of the three-and-a-half hour race shown.

"Paris-Roubaix this year, regardless of what they are going to say about TV numbers, was a step backwards," Chennaoui said in her Instagram reel.

"They're still doing a disservice to women's racing."

Tour de France Femmes race director Marion Rousse says things are moving in the right direction. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

As for the Tour de France Femmes, Deignan, who won the 2020 edition of La Course by Le Tour de France, a one-day precursor to the current women's multi-stage Tour, said the lack of coverage was a return to the "old days" of following professional cycling.

"It was very hard to follow from home," Deignan said of stage three of this year's Tour.

"It was like being back in the old days, refreshing news feeds, trying to figure out what's going on."

Cycling Weekly spoke to race director Marion Rousse about the criticism, and she said the race was moving towards full broadcast coverage.

"We're giving serious consideration to broadcasting all the stages in full in the future because the women deserve it," Rousse told Cycling Weekly.

"It works well in terms of audience figures.

"We're currently giving it real consideration, which is a step forward. Things are moving in the right direction."

World.title: Crows get home after almighty Tigers scare in the wet
World.content:
Izak Rankine stars as Adelaide manages to get the job done against Richmond in torrential rain at Adelaide Oval.

The Crows struggled for most of the night against Richmond, but Rankine's 37-disposal, 19-contested possession, 12-clearance game, capped with a huge goal from beyond 50, dragged the home side over the line as Adelaide won by nine points, 9.9 (63) to 7.12 (54).

Jason Horne-Francis hobbled off the field in Port's 97-point loss to Sydney, as Geelong made light work of Essendon, triumphing by 67 points at Kardinia Park.

Port Adelaide star Jason Horne-Francis gave his team a big injury scare when he limped off in the final quarter against Sydney. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Jason McCawley)

Earlier on Saturday, a huge final quarter from Harry Petty helped Melbourne claim a four-point win over the AFL's ladder-leaders Fremantle.

Petty kicked 3.2 for the afternoon, including two in the final quarter as Melbourne emerged 17.11 (113) to 17.7 (109) winners in one of the games of the season at the MCG.

Prior to the action on Saturday, AFL boss Andrew Dillon addressed Geelong's concussion saga, ending a couple of days of silence from the league.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: AFL chair apologises for his part in Cats concussion contract saga
World.content:
AFL Commission chairman Craig Drummond has apologised for his part in Geelong's controversial concussion contract with defender Jake Kolodjashnij.

Drummond was Geelong president two years ago when premiership defender Kolodjashnij signed a contract in which he took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from court action down the line.

It is understood Kolodjashnij's agent was not aware of the contract, and neither the AFL Players Association (AFLPA) or AFL were informed at the time.

It is also understood that while Kolodjashnij passed an independent medical test, he was still considered at risk of future complications from head injuries.

Jake's twin brother, Kade, was forced to retire from the game in 2020 due to ongoing concussion problems.

"I was president of the Geelong Football Club in 2024," Drummond said.

"This was an extremely complex and sensitive matter, and obligations to both the player and the club were very carefully considered by the Geelong board.

"Jake's welfare was central to all discussions, and I have been thinking of him particularly over the past few days.

Cats face 'please explain' Geelong is finally issued a 'please explain' over its controversial concussion contract with premiership defender Jake Kolodjashnij.

"While the player was medically cleared to play, the club engaged in lengthy discussions including with him, his family, doctors and insurers about his future and the potential risks of returning to play.

"Regardless of the player's agreement, the club went too far in adding a waiver into an informed consent document and it will be removed."

Drummond said it was an error to keep the process quiet, and clarified that he would not be involved in AFL discussions about the matter.

"As the club has also acknowledged, there was also a process failure in relation to lodgement of the agreement with the AFL and the AFLPA," Drummond said.

"I have not and will not be involved in any deliberation in relation to this matter and its assessment under the AFL rules and regulations.

"I apologise for the mistakes made in this very complex situation."

Speaking to ABC Sport ahead of the Saturday games, AFL boss Andrew Dillon reiterated that it was a complex situation.

"This is an issue that is really complex and in this one in particular it's complex and unique," Dillon said.

"But concussion and the effects that has on players or participants in contact sports ... is an issue that's confronting contact sports worldwide.

"What we have here is a player that has suffered multiple concussions, went before an AFL concussion panel, ultimately over a period of months was cleared as fit to play.

"Through that period, over a number of months, Jake's worked with the club doctors, independent medical experts, the club, and the club board and management to make sure that he understood their were risks to continue playing, not withstanding that you've been cleared medically fit to play.

"That was the intent behind what was going on."

Dillon said the please explain was around why the concussion agreement sat alongside his playing contract.

"We've gone to Geelong under the rules and asked them why it wasn't lodged with us," Dillon said.

"So we're waiting to hear back from Geelong on that."

The Cats are expected to be fined over the contract saga after initially being cleared of wrongdoing.

World.title: Surprise parents' visit inspires new leader in Tour de France Femmes
World.content:
Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney launched a decisive attack up Mont Ventoux to win the seventh stage of the Tour de France Femmes and take the overall lead from Marlen Reusser.

The 2024 champion was in tears as she put on the yellow jersey and now leads 2023 champion Demi Vollering by 15 seconds and Reusser by 39 with two stages left.

"I'm just so tired and so blown away with what just happened," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"When I started climbing I looked to the right and I saw my parents standing on the roadside. They came today by surprise. I saw my father yelling for me and I thought I had to make him proud."

Reusser and Vollering could not follow Niewiadoma-Phinney when she broke away about 9km from the top of Ventoux, one of the most iconic climbs in cycling with its barren, lunar aspect.

It was a first Tour stage win for Niewiadoma-Phinney, who won the 2024 edition without claiming a stage. Gritting her teeth in the final few hundred metres, the Polish rider dug deep and with the sun gleaming behind her, raised her arms after crossing the line.

She then almost lost balance through fatigue and had to be helped off her bike. Moments later, she was all smiles as she sat on the road and poured cooling water over her head.

"I never chase victories for the sake of winning, I target them because I like this beautiful feeling I have right now," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"I came here (before) to Mont Ventoux with my friends and my husband, and we rode up the climb three times.

"The feeling of reaching the top of this mountain was amazing. From that moment, I just wanted to experience that feeling again. The pure joy of riding, as if I was a kid."

Vollering dropped Reusser in the closing stages of the 15.7km ascent of Ventoux, which has featured several time on the men's Tour. In one of the darkest days in Tour history, British rider Tom Simpson died after collapsing during a tortuous ascent in 1967.

World time trial champion Reusser battled gamely but lost valuable time in the title fight. The Swiss rider finished the stage fourth as Vollering and two-time Giro d'Italia winner Elisa Longo Borghini of Italy both placed ahead of her.

There were three smaller climbs heading to Ventoux, which was ranked as a Hors Catégorie ascent — the hardest category — and had a gradient of nearly 9 per cent.

Vollering moved ahead first, and Reusser and Niewiadoma-Phinney joined her as others lagged behind. Niewiadoma-Phinney then attacked and, although Vollering stood up in her saddle to chase her the new race leader was riding a brilliant tempo and proved too strong.

"My idea was that I had to make it to Chalet Reynard on my own," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"Because from then on the headwind would be quite strong and the chasers would try to stay on each other's wheel for as long as possible."

The eighth stage is a flat 172km route for sprinters finishing in Nice, where the race ends after another mountain stage on Sunday night.

Stage nine features four sharp climbs of Col d'Èze, nestled in the hills overlooking the Principality of Monaco.

Two years ago, Niewiadoma-Phinney beat Vollering on the final stage to win the race by just four seconds.

World.title: AFL issues Cats a 'please explain' over defender's concussion contract
World.content:
Geelong has been handed a belated 'please explain' notice from the AFL after initially avoiding sanction over its controversial secret deal with defender Jake Kolodjashnij, a player with a history of concussions.

In 2024, Geelong struck a secret agreement with Kolodjashnij, who on Friday evening identified himself as the player in question, whereby he took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from court action down the line.

The bombshell concussion case emerged on Thursday and pressure mounted on the league and Geelong after the AFL didn't hand down any punishment that night.

On Friday afternoon, Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking said he had signed off on the deal and confirmed the 'please explain' notice.

Geelong's Steve Hocking said the club would provide information to the AFL about Kolodjashnij's contract. (AAP Image: Erik Anderson)

"I take responsibility for the fact that we didn't lodge it with the AFL and the (AFL)PA," Hocking told reporters in Geelong.

"… I have received a letter of 'please explain' from the AFL in relation to this matter, so we'll deal with that over the coming days."

Hocking said not registering the deal was a "misstep" and was uncertain what consequences Geelong would face.

"We've got a 'please explain' letter, and at the appropriate time we'll work through that with the AFL," he said.

"We'll have to respond to that, and then it'll be up to the AFL, and whatever that is, we'll accept."

Later on Friday, Kolodjashnij issued a statement through Geelong, confirming he was the previously unnamed player.

"While I appreciate the efforts made not to identify me, the speculation has left me feeling I needed to address this personally," Kolodjashnij said.

"I participated fully in the AFL's independent concussion panel process, respected its independence, and was comfortable with the outcome. I have continued playing AFL football since.

"What disappoints me most is that my private medical information has been made public. Everyone deserves the right to keep their confidential medical information private.

"… I am healthy, feeling good, and focused on playing my role for the team for the remainder of the season."

The 2022 premiership defender, 30, has played 209 games.

Kolodjashnij's twin brother Kade, who played for Gold Coast and Melbourne, retired prematurely in 2020 due to concussion.

On Thursday night, calling it a "complex and unique case", the AFL had insisted it was "satisfied that the letter was not used by Geelong to allow a medically unfit player to return to play".

Geelong also issued a statement, saying they would remove the waiver from the contract.

"The club was not attempting to vary the terms of the AFL standard playing contract, or attempting to avoid its responsibilities under health and safety laws," the Geelong statement read.

Grief-stricken mother of star footballer reveals AFL executive phone call West Coast Eagles star Adam Hunter's mother Joanne Brown says AFL executive Laura Kane reached out to her, but the grieving mother says the phone call was "too little, too late".

New AFL Commission chair Craig Drummond was the president of the Geelong board when the deal was struck.

Drummond was not mentioned in the AFL statement.

Drummond did not front the media and issued a three-line statement on Thursday night calling concussion a "challenging medical and legal issue for all contact sports globally".

Many AFL players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern and former number one draft pick Paddy McCartin, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

Several deceased players, including Danny Frawley, Shane Tuck and Graham 'Polly' Farmer, were posthumously diagnosed with degenerative brain disease Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE).

There is also a multimillion-dollar concussion class action against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.
